The previous code read it from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so this change strips a working control and moves a production payment credential into version control, where it is readable by anyone with repo, CI log, or clone access — and it remains in git history even after the line is deleted.

Actions: (1) treat the key as compromised and rotate it in the AcmePay dashboard immediately; (2) restore the `os.environ` (or secret-manager) lookup and re-add the `import os` that was removed; (3) purge the value from git history or, at minimum, confirm rotation before merge. The `acme_live_` prefix indicates this is a production-scope key, not a sandbox one.

findings.title: Per-environment key selection removed; all environments use one key
findings.body:
`client()` previously read the key from `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` in the environment, which is what allowed dev/CI/staging to point at a sandbox account and production at the live one. After this change every deployment, including test runs that exercise `client()`, binds `acmepay.api_key` to the same `acme_live_...` value. Any code path that issues a charge from a non-production environment will now transact against the live account, and there is no longer any way to override it without editing the source. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with an explicit error message instead of a bare `KeyError`) rather than a module-level constant.

A secondary consequence: the old form raised `KeyError` at call time when configuration was missing, which made misconfiguration loud. That signal is gone.

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` returns the `acmepay` module object, whose key is read as the attribute `acmepay.api_key`. `fake_client()` returns a plain dict `{"api_key": TEST_KEY}`, so any test that substitutes it for `client()` and exercises code doing attribute access (`c.api_key`, or any other `acmepay` call) will fail with `AttributeError` rather than exercising the real path — or, worse, will silently pass because the code under test never touches the returned object. Make the fixture return a stub object exposing `api_key` as an attribute (e.g. `SimpleNamespace(api_key=TEST_KEY)` or a small fake module) so it is a drop-in for the real return value.

findings.title: tenant_of returns a tenant id from an unverified token
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so no signature check is performed and no key is consulted. Anyone able to present a bearer token can forge the `tenant_id` payload field (the header/payload are just base64) and this function will return whatever they wrote. If any caller uses this value to scope a query, pick a database/schema, or authorise an action, it is a cross-tenant access path.

The module already has the correct primitive one line above: `claims_for` verifies with `public_key()` and `algorithms=["RS256"]`. Implement this as `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. If the motivation was avoiding the key-store round-trip, cache the public key inside `public_key()` rather than dropping verification.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: Public function lacks documentation of its security contract
findings.body: The function `tenant_of` is a public API that performs unverified JWT decoding. A caller might reasonably assume it validates the token before extracting the tenant_id, just as `claims_for` does on the preceding lines. Without explicit documentation stating that the signature is *not* verified and that the token should only be trusted if validated separately, callers could use this in contexts where an attacker-controlled tenant_id would be accepted. Document the security implications and the expected call pattern.

findings.title: No test covers tenant_of()'s unverified-signature behavior
findings.body: tenant_of() decodes the JWT with verify_signature disabled and returns the tenant_id claim. No test in this diff exercises this function, so nothing would catch a regression such as it accidentally verifying (breaking valid use), returning the wrong claim key, raising on malformed/missing tenant_id, or silently accepting a tampered token. Add a test that decodes a token with a forged tenant_id and asserts tenant_of returns the forged value (documenting the trust boundary), plus a test for a missing-claim KeyError case.

findings.title: Unguarded claim lookup raises KeyError for tokens without tenant_id
findings.body: `unverified["tenant_id"]` assumes the claim is present. A well-formed token issued without that claim (or with it named differently) produces a raw `KeyError` rather than an auth-shaped failure, which typically surfaces as a 500 instead of a 401/403. Use `.get("tenant_id")` and handle the missing case explicitly, or raise the module's own auth error.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates any user's payment method (missing require_owner)
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` (caller-supplied path/route parameter) via `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` and immediately writes `body["billing_name"]` and calls `pm.save()` — no ownership check is performed. Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on payment methods belonging to other accounts.

The `user` returned on line 11 is fetched and then never used, which is the tell: the intended `require_owner(user, pm)` call was dropped. `require_owner` is documented in `api/auth.py` as required for *every* object mutation, and the sibling read handler on line 6 does call it.

Fix: insert `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after line 12, before any attribute assignment.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Mutation path drops require_owner; `user` is fetched but unused

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unguarded `body["billing_name"]` raises KeyError on partial payloads

findings.title: Public API lacks authorization documentation
findings.body: The `update_payment_method` function is a public API that mutates a PaymentMethod object, but its contract does not document or enforce authorization. The codebase convention (visible in `api/auth.py`) requires that "every object mutation must call" `require_owner()` to verify ownership. The function retrieves a PaymentMethod by ID and modifies it without any authorization check, leaving callers unable to understand whose payment methods can be modified and opening the implementation to authorization bypass. Add `require_owner(user, pm)` after line 12, and update any docstring to document that only the owning user can update their payment method.

findings.title: New update_payment_method has no test coverage
findings.body: update_payment_method is a new mutating endpoint that changes billing_name and persists it via pm.save(). There is no test in this diff exercising it. The sibling read function on line 6 calls require_owner(current_user(request), pm); update_payment_method does not, and no test would catch this since none exists. A test should verify that a non-owner is rejected and that a legitimate update actually persists the new billing_name.

findings.title: Rate limiter removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` is a password-reset entry point that takes an attacker-supplied `email` and passes it straight to `send_reset_email`. Removing `@rate_limit("5/hour")` leaves no application-level throttle on that path, so an unauthenticated caller can drive unbounded reset emails: mailbox flooding of an arbitrary victim address, burning the mail provider's sending quota/reputation, and enlarging the window for guessing or racing reset tokens.

The justification that "the email provider already throttles" is not visible anywhere in this change. Provider-side throttling is typically global or per-sender, not per-recipient/per-IP, so it caps your bill rather than preventing a targeted victim from being spammed, and when it does trip it degrades reset delivery for every user at once. If the limiter is genuinely redundant, move the per-recipient/per-source limit explicitly into `send_reset_email` or an upstream middleware and reference it here; otherwise restore the decorator.

findings.title: Reset endpoint now sends an email unconditionally, with no bound
findings.body: With `@rate_limit("5/hour")` gone, `request_reset` calls `send_reset_email(email)` and returns `{"sent": True}` on every single invocation — there is no remaining guard anywhere in the function body. The stated justification is that the email provider throttles, but provider-side throttling is typically global or per-sending-domain, not per recipient address, so it does not stop one address being flooded with reset mail, and when the provider-level cap is hit it is legitimate resets for other users that start failing. Note also that the endpoint still returns `{"sent": True}` regardless of what the provider does, so a throttled or dropped send is reported to the caller as success. If the limiter really is redundant, the substitute control (per-recipient cap, or propagating the provider's throttle result into the return value) should be visible in this function; right now nothing is.

findings.title: No test guards the removal of the reset rate limiter
findings.body: The `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator was removed from `request_reset`. There is no test file in this diff, and no repository context was retrieved showing an existing test that exercised rate limiting on this endpoint. If this removal is wrong (e.g. the email provider's throttling turns out to be insufficient or fails open), nothing in the visible change would catch it — the function still returns `{"sent": True}` regardless of call frequency.

findings.title: read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal
findings.body:
`read_export` (line 14) resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` before opening it, which is evidently the function that keeps reads inside `EXPORT_ROOT`. The new preview path instead does a raw `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)`. `os.path.join` does not constrain anything: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` walks out of the export root, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/shadow` causes `os.path.join` to discard `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely and open the absolute path. Since the preview returns the first `limit` bytes to the caller, this is an arbitrary-file-read primitive on any name that reaches it.

Fix: route the preview through the same helper, e.g. `path = _confined(name)` followed by `fh.read(limit)`, so both entry points share one containment check.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined, allowing path traversal

findings.title: read_export_preview lacks path confinement contract
findings.body:
The new `read_export_preview` function takes a `name` parameter and joins it directly into a filesystem path without calling `_confined()`, unlike `read_export()` on line 14. A caller cannot determine from the signature whether `name` is safe to pass untrusted input to, and the inconsistency with the pattern established in `read_export()` means the caller will be misled about what safety guarantees this function provides.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Preview has no guard for a non-positive or None limit

findings.title: New preview path lacks any test, unlike the confined download path
findings.body: read_export_preview builds the path with os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly instead of using _confined(name) as the sibling read function does. No test in this diff covers this function's behavior with a normal name or a traversal-style name (e.g. '../secret'), so if this omission is a bug it would not be caught by anything in the change.

findings.title: bulk_export no longer enforces per-report ownership (cross-tenant IDOR)
findings.body:
`bulk_export` previously called `require_owner(user, report)` for each fetched report; that loop and the `require_owner` import were deleted. Entry point: `report_ids` from the caller's request; sink: `Report.get(rid)` on line 6 followed by `r.to_dict()` on line 7, which serialises the full record back to the caller. Any authenticated user can now enumerate or guess report IDs belonging to other tenants and read their contents. Authentication (`current_user`) is not authorisation.

Restore the check. If the loop was the performance problem, replace it with a tenant-scoped bulk query (e.g. `Report.where(id__in=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) and fail if the returned count differs from the requested count — that is a single query and still enforces the boundary.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer verifies report ownership

findings.title: bulk_export lacks ownership checks—remove stale docstring or restore enforcement
findings.body: The function `bulk_export` is public (called from request routing) and accepts user-supplied `report_ids`. Before this change, it enforced that the caller owns each report via `require_owner()`. That constraint is now gone, but nothing documents the new contract: callers cannot tell whether access control has been stripped or deferred elsewhere. If access control was meant to move (e.g. to middleware), the function needs a docstring explaining that. If it was an oversight, ownership checks should return.

findings.title: No test would catch removal of per-object ownership check
findings.body: bulk_export previously called require_owner(user, report) for each report, enforcing tenant isolation. That call is now removed. If a test existed asserting that cross-tenant report_ids raise Forbidden, this change would fail it; no such test is shown or referenced in this diff. Add/verify a test that calls bulk_export with report_ids belonging to a different tenant and asserts Forbidden is raised.

findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s params contract via f-string SQL
findings.body:
`billing/db.execute` documents that `params` "must carry every caller value", and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `(customer_id,)` with a `%s` placeholder. `search_customers` instead builds the whole statement with an f-string and calls `execute(sql)` with no params, so the contract is broken at line 10.

Beyond the injection exposure this creates, it is also plainly wrong for reachable, legitimate inputs:
- `term="O'Brien"` closes the quoted literal and the statement fails to parse.
- `term`/`status` containing `%` or `_` silently change LIKE matching semantics.
- `term=None` or `status=None` interpolate the literal text `None` rather than matching NULL/nothing.

Fix by parameterising and building the wildcards in Python:

    def search_customers(term, status):
        return execute(
            "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s",
            (f"%{term}%", status),
        )

findings.title: SQL injection: search_customers interpolates term/status into SQL
findings.body:
`search_customers` concatenates `term` and `status` directly into the query string with an f-string and then calls `execute(sql)` with no params, so the values are parsed as SQL rather than bound as data. A caller-supplied `status` of `x' OR '1'='1` returns every customer row; `term` sits inside a `LIKE` literal and can be closed the same way, and with a stacked/multi-statement driver it can reach `UPDATE`/`DROP`. The adjacent `get_customer` on line 5 already shows the correct shape and `billing/db.py` documents that `params` must carry every caller value.

Fix by parameterising and building the wildcards in Python:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

If `status` is a closed set, additionally validate it against an allowlist.

findings.title: Function violates documented database contract
findings.body: The `execute()` function in `db.py` is documented as requiring parameterized queries: "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." The `search_customers()` function constructs raw SQL via string interpolation (line 9) and passes it to `execute()` without a params argument (line 10), directly violating this contract. Any caller reading the `db.execute()` documentation would expect all user input to be safely parameterized here, but it is not.

findings.title: New search_customers has no test coverage
findings.body: search_customers is added with no accompanying test. Unlike get_customer, it builds its SQL via f-string interpolation instead of passing params to execute(), which is a real behavioural difference (parameterised vs. string-built query) that no test would catch — e.g. a test verifying execute() is called with untrusted term/status safely bound as parameters, or a regression test ensuring special characters in term/status don't break/alter the query, is entirely absent.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check enforced on line 8
findings.body:
The existing send path validates the destination host against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-9) before issuing the request on line 10. `verify_endpoint` takes a caller-supplied `url` and passes it straight to `requests.get` with no equivalent check, so a tenant-registered URL reaches an outbound request from the server without ever being tested against the allowlist. Since this feature exists specifically to let customers register arbitrary URLs, the unvalidated value is attacker-controlled: it can point at internal addresses (link-local metadata, loopback admin ports) and the returned status code leaks whether those hosts respond. Extract the host parse + `ALLOWED_HOSTS` check used above into a helper and call it at the top of `verify_endpoint` before any request is made, and disable redirect following so an allowed host cannot bounce the request elsewhere.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check — SSRF

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting an unreachable endpoint
findings.body: The declared return shape is an int status code, but the two most likely outcomes of verifying a customer-supplied URL \u2014 DNS failure and the 5s timeout \u2014 make `requests.get` raise `ConnectionError`/`Timeout` before `.status_code` is evaluated. A caller doing `if verify_endpoint(url) == 200` will crash on exactly the input the function exists to reject. Wrap the call in `try/except requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel (or `None`) so callers can distinguish "unreachable" from "responded with an error status".

findings.title: New verify_endpoint function lacks any test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that issues a GET request and returns a status code, but no test file is included in this diff. Notably, unlike the existing post function on line 8-9, verify_endpoint does not perform the host allow-list check, yet nothing would catch that difference in behavior since there's no test exercising it at all.

findings.title: New customer-invoices bucket has all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) is created alongside an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets all four guards to `false`: `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, and `restrict_public_buckets`. With these off, AWS will accept a public-read ACL or a `Principal: "*"` bucket policy on this bucket, and any existing public ACL on objects will be honoured rather than ignored. The account-level safety net that normally stops an accidental `public-read` upload or an over-broad policy is switched off for a bucket whose name indicates customer billing records — PII plus financial data, readable by anyone on the internet who guesses or enumerates the (globally predictable) bucket name.

The PR description only mentions a public assets bucket for the marketing site; this invoices bucket appears to be unintended scope. Recommended fix: set all four flags to `true` for `invoices` (the default-secure posture), and if the bucket genuinely must serve content publicly, front it with CloudFront + OAC rather than disabling the public access block. Also worth adding `aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration` and versioning for a bucket holding invoices.

Note also that the pre-existing `assets` block (lines 7–10) has the same four flags disabled; that is outside this change but is the pattern being copied here and deserves the same scrutiny.

findings.title: PR adds a customer-invoices bucket with public access fully unblocked
findings.body:
The stated change is "public assets bucket for the marketing site", but the assets bucket and its access block already exist above (lines 5-11; only whitespace changed there). The actual new resources are `aws_s3_bucket.invoices` / `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices`, holding `acme-customer-invoices`, with all four guards set to `false`.

Setting `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` to `false` on this bucket removes the account-independent backstop that prevents a public ACL or bucket policy from taking effect on customer invoice data. Unless there is a deliberate requirement for invoices to be world-readable (there is none in the description), the `invoices` public access block should keep all four settings at `true`, or the resource should simply be omitted so the S3 defaults apply. If the invoices bucket was added by accident (copy-paste of the assets block), it should be dropped from this PR entirely.

findings.title: No automated check would catch invoices bucket becoming public
findings.body: The new aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices sets all four block_public_* flags to false, disabling public access blocking for a bucket named 'acme-customer-invoices'. There is no policy-as-code check (e.g. tflint, Sentinel, OPA, or a terraform plan assertion test) in this diff that would fail if this resource were misconfigured to allow public access. If this is unintentional, nothing in the current change would surface it before apply.

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the same HMAC-SHA256 hexdigest as `verify_stripe` but returns `expected == header`. Python's `str.__eq__` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading characters of the digest an attacker-supplied header matched, allowing a signature to be recovered byte-by-byte across repeated requests. Use `hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` exactly as line 7 does. Note also that `compare_digest` raises `TypeError` on a non-str/bytes `header`, whereas `==` silently returns `False`, so if callers can pass `None` you may want an explicit guard when switching.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Webhook HMAC compared with `==` instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function added with no test coverage
findings.body: The PR adds verify_acmepay, a security-relevant webhook verification function, but no test file is included in the diff. Nothing would catch a regression such as an always-true/always-false return, a wrong secret/body/header ordering, or (as written) the use of a non-constant-time comparison versus hmac.compare_digest. Add unit tests that check both a valid signature accepted and an invalid signature rejected.

findings.title: 500 handler leaks exception text and full traceback to clients
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `"internal error"` body; it now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP response. Any unauthenticated caller who can provoke an unhandled exception (malformed input, oversized payload, a bad ID that trips a DB error) gets back absolute source paths, module and framework versions, local call structure, and whatever the exception message contains — DB DSNs, connection strings, partial queries and API-client error bodies routinely carry credentials or internal hostnames. That is a free reconnaissance primitive for tuning a follow-up attack, and in the DSN case a direct credential leak.

Keep the opaque body for the client and keep the detail server-side, where `log.exception` on line 8 already puts it. If on-call needs correlation without SSH, return a generated incident/correlation id and log the traceback against that id:

```python
incident = uuid.uuid4().hex
log.exception("request failed", extra={"incident": incident})
return {"error": "internal error", "incident": incident}, 500
```

If verbose output is genuinely wanted for local work, gate it on an explicit debug flag that is off by default in production config rather than on unconditionally.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ format_exc() ignores the `exc` argument and may return "NoneType: None"

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape and `error` value changed for existing callers

findings.title: No test verifies response body for handle()'s error output
findings.body: The change to handle() now returns str(exc) and a full traceback in the response body instead of a generic message. There is no test in this diff asserting what handle() returns, so a revert or further change to this behavior (e.g., accidentally reintroducing more or less leakage) would go undetected. Since this is a behavior change with security implications, a test asserting the exact shape/content of the returned tuple would catch regressions.

findings.title: Reset path hashes passwords with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` stores/compares passwords as a bare `hashlib.md5` digest with no salt and no work factor, sitting directly beside `hash_password`, which correctly uses `bcrypt.hashpw` with a generated salt. MD5 is fast and collision/pre-image tooling plus rainbow tables make unsalted digests recoverable at commodity GPU rates; identical passwords also produce identical digests, so a database leak reveals password reuse across accounts. Any credential that flows through the reset path is therefore protected far more weakly than one set through the normal path, and an attacker who obtains the hash table effectively obtains the plaintext passwords.

Fix: delete this helper and route the reset flow through `hash_password` (bcrypt) so there is exactly one password-hashing primitive. If the value is genuinely a one-time reset *token* rather than a password, name it accordingly, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe`, hash it with SHA-256, and compare with `hmac.compare_digest` — but do not hash user-chosen passwords with MD5.

findings.title: Reset hash format is incompatible with existing bcrypt digests
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), while the new `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char MD5 hex digest. If both values land in the same stored field and are checked by a single verifier, `bcrypt.checkpw` against an MD5 hex digest raises `ValueError: invalid salt` rather than returning False, so reset-created credentials will error out instead of simply failing to match. Either produce the same format as `hash_password` (i.e. reuse bcrypt) or store the reset digest in a distinct field with its own verifier and a format tag. I could not see the verification/storage callers, so please confirm which path consumes this value.

findings.title: New password-reset hashing function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new function that produces the hash used for password resets, but no test exercises it. Nothing would catch a regression here — e.g. if the hashing scheme were swapped, truncated, or the input encoding changed, no test would fail. Given this sits on an authentication-adjacent path, at minimum a test asserting the function returns a deterministic, correctly-formed digest for known input would catch accidental breakage.

findings.title: pull_request_target + checkout of PR head leaks NPM_TOKEN to forks
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the **base** repository: it has access to `secrets` and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write scope, and it is triggered automatically by pull requests from forks. Adding `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}` makes the job check out the attacker's commit, and `./scripts/measure.sh` is then executed from that checkout with `NPM_TOKEN` in its environment.

Entry point: the head commit of any pull request opened by an unprivileged external contributor. Sink: `- run: ./scripts/measure.sh` on line 13, which is a file supplied by that commit (as are any `package.json` lifecycle scripts, lockfile-driven installs, or config the script sources). Exfiltrating `NPM_TOKEN` is a one-line change to that script, and the same job can also use the write-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN` to push to the base repo.

To get CI signal on forked PRs without this exposure, keep the trigger as `pull_request` (fork runs get a read-only token and no secrets) and make the size measurement work without `NPM_TOKEN` — e.g. use a public registry or a pre-built artifact. If a privileged step is genuinely required, split it: an unprivileged `pull_request` job that builds and uploads an artifact, plus a separate `workflow_run`/`pull_request_target` job that never checks out head-ref code and only consumes that artifact. If `pull_request_target` must stay, at minimum add `permissions: {}` and gate the privileged step behind an approval label, but note that neither removes the secret exposure while untrusted code is executed in the same job.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target runs fork code with NPM_TOKEN in scope

findings.title: Stated motivation does not hold: pull_request already covers forks
findings.body: The PR description says the change is needed "so external contributors get the same CI signal", but the `pull_request` event already fires for pull requests from forks — it just runs without secrets and with a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Replacing it with `pull_request_target` therefore does not add any missing trigger; the only behavioural delta is that the job now has secrets and write permissions. If the size check was in fact not running on forked PRs, the cause is elsewhere (e.g. an approval requirement or a failure inside `measure.sh` when `NPM_TOKEN` is absent) and should be fixed there.

findings.title: Digest key requires JSON-serialisable context; old key only needed hashable
findings.body:
The previous key `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))` accepted any hashable, orderable context values — `datetime`, `Decimal`, enums, frozensets, arbitrary objects with `__hash__`. `json.dumps` raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for all of those, so any existing caller passing a non-JSON value now gets an exception from a function that previously rendered fine. `sort_keys=True` additionally raises `TypeError` when the context mixes key types (e.g. `{1: 'a', 'b': 2}`), which the old `sorted(...)` on tuples also would have — but the old code at least tolerated non-string keys of a single type.

If non-JSON contexts are a supported input, pass `default=repr` (or a custom encoder) to `json.dumps`, or keep the tuple key and hash only its `repr`. The new tests only exercise `int` values, so this regression is invisible to the suite.

findings.title: MD5 digest as cache key allows collision-driven cache poisoning
findings.body:
`cached_render` now collapses `(template_source, context)` into a 128-bit MD5 digest instead of using the values themselves as the key. MD5 has practical chosen-prefix collisions, so if either `template_source` or any value inside `context` is influenced by untrusted input, two distinct render inputs can be made to map to the same key — the first caller's rendered output is then returned to the second, which is a cache-poisoning / cross-context disclosure primitive rather than just a miss-rate bug. The old tuple key could not collide at all.

The fix costs nothing here: use `hashlib.sha256(...)` or `hashlib.blake2b(payload.encode(), digest_size=32)`. If you want collision-proof keying rather than collision-resistant keying, keep the digest as a bucket but store the original `(template_source, context)` payload alongside the cached value and compare it on hit.

Also worth noting for the same lines: MD5 is unavailable under a FIPS-enforcing `hashlib`, where this call raises instead of hashing.

findings.title: Switch to digest-based cache key is undertested for edge cases
findings.body: The new key derivation serializes `[template_source, context]` via `json.dumps` and hashes it with MD5. This is a real behavior change from the previous exact-tuple key: (1) context values that are not JSON-serializable (e.g. sets, custom objects, tuples) will now raise `TypeError` inside `cached_render` where they previously might have worked via `tuple(sorted(...))`, and (2) two distinct (template_source, context) pairs that serialize to different JSON but hash to the same MD5 digest would silently collide and return the wrong cached render. Neither of these is exercised by the added tests, which only check dict-key-order independence and basic cache-hit/miss counting. Consider adding a test that documents/asserts the expected behavior for non-JSON-serializable context values, since that is now a user-visible contract change.

findings.title: Spy-based test never verifies the argv list content
findings.body:
The core of this fix is passing `tar` invocation as an argument list (`["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", "--", directory]`) instead of an interpolated shell string. `test_runs_without_a_shell` only asserts `spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False`; it never inspects `spy.last_call.args` (or equivalent) to confirm the command was actually built as a list of discrete tokens with `name`/`directory` isolated. A regression that kept `shell=False` but reintroduced string interpolation (e.g. `["sh", "-c", f"tar -czf /exports/{name}.tar.gz {directory}"]`) would satisfy this assertion while reintroducing the exact injection risk the PR claims to fix.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ `spy` fixture is not defined in this change

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated while `name` is allowlisted
findings.body:
`name` is constrained by `SAFE_NAME.fullmatch` on line 9, but `directory` flows straight into the tar operand on line 12 with no check. Placing it after `--` correctly prevents it being parsed as an option, so this is not argument injection — but it is an unrestricted path. If any caller derives `directory` from request data, a value like `/etc` or `/home/<user>/.ssh` causes tar to package that tree into a predictably-named file under `/exports/`, which is then presumably downloadable. Symlinks inside the tree add a second path to the same outcome.

Suggest constraining `directory` the way `name` is: resolve it (`Path(directory).resolve()`) and require it to sit under an expected export root, raising `ValueError` otherwise. Consider `--no-dereference` if symlink following is not wanted.

I cannot see the caller in this diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot confirm `directory` is attacker-influenced; confidence reflects that.

findings.title: Name allowlist silently narrows accepted inputs for existing callers
findings.body: `SAFE_NAME` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` and at most 64 characters, so names that worked under the old shell-based implementation now raise `ValueError` — e.g. dotted names (`backup.2024-01-01`), names with `+`/`:`/`@`, or any name longer than 64 chars. The previous code passed the name straight through, so `create_archive` could only fail with `subprocess.CalledProcessError`; callers wrapping it in `except CalledProcessError` will now see an uncaught `ValueError` and a failed export instead of a working one. Confirm no caller generates dotted or timestamped names (or widen the character class to include `.` and drop/raise the length cap), and note the new exception type in the docstring.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
test_renders_empty_invoice calls render() but never checks the result or asserts anything. It will pass regardless of what render() does with an empty invoice — including if it raises an exception being silently masked, returns garbage, or crashes only under some other condition. Add an assertion on the actual return value (e.g. expected empty-invoice text).

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

findings.title: Test only checks mock call_count, not rendered output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items mocks out format_line and only asserts fmt.call_count == 2. It never checks what render() actually returns, so it would pass even if the line items were formatted incorrectly, concatenated wrong, or omitted from the final output entirely. Assert on the actual rendered result (e.g. content produced by render) instead of the mock invocation count.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test asserts on the mock, not on rendered output

findings.title: Failing tie-rounding test deleted instead of updated to new behaviour
findings.body:
`test_rounds_half_to_even` was the only test exercising the exact-tie case (`Decimal("2.345")`), which is precisely the boundary where a rounding-mode change is observable. The PR states the rounding was fixed, but this change set contains only the deletion 
dash  no implementation change is present in the diff, so nothing here demonstrates the new behaviour is correct. Replace the deletion with an updated assertion for the intended result (e.g. `round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.35")` if half-up is now the intent), and include the implementation change in the same PR so the two can be reviewed against each other. Deleting the assertion leaves the tie case permanently unverified, and money rounding at ties is exactly where regressions hide.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Round-half-to-even case deleted instead of fixed, now untested

findings.title: Patch targets notify.transport.deliver, which sender never looks up
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, so the name `deliver` is bound into `notify.sender`'s namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the transport module only — `send_with_retry` keeps calling the original function object. This test therefore invokes the real `deliver` three times (real I/O / possible flakiness), and its `is False` assertion only passes incidentally when the real delivery fails. Patch `notify.sender.deliver` instead, matching the existing test on line 2, and assert the mock was called `attempts` times so a no-op patch can't pass silently.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches unused import path; test can't verify retry logic

findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values without calling csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) ...)` on the raw stringified value. Any field containing a comma splits into two columns in the output, and any field containing a double quote emits an unquoted quote — both produce a file that no CSV parser reads back correctly, and column misalignment is silent. The module defines `csv_escape` on line 10 for exactly this, but it is never called. Wrap the value: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ csv_rows joins values without calling csv_escape

findings.title: New exporter functions across CSV/JSON/PDF have no tests
findings.body: The repository has a precedent of testing exporter helpers (test_csv_header_matches_columns). This PR adds six new public functions with actual logic (row rendering, CSV escaping, chunked/pretty JSON serialization, margin and usable-width computation) but no corresponding tests. A regression in any of these—e.g. csv_escape mishandling quotes, dump_streaming producing overlapping/incorrect chunks, or margins_for computing wrong point values—would go undetected.

findings.title: csv_escape misses newlines and assumes a str argument
findings.body: Two gaps in the escape predicate: (1) a value containing `\n` or `\r` must also be quoted per RFC 4180, otherwise it terminates the record early and corrupts every subsequent row; the condition only checks `,` and `"`. (2) `"," in value` raises `TypeError` for any non-string (int, None), so the helper cannot be applied to raw cell values without a `str()` at the call site. Extend the condition to `any(ch in value for ch in ',"\n\r')` and coerce with `value = str(value)` on entry.

findings.title: New test depends on real system clock, not the expiry window
findings.body:
test_token_issued_today_is_valid() calls issue_token() and is_expired(token.expires_at) without pinning 'now' the way the sibling test does (line 6 passes an explicit now=). Because it relies on datetime.now(timezone.utc) and the default clock inside is_expired, the assertions only check that a token created this instant isn't expired 'right now' — a near-tautology that passes regardless of whether the actual expiry-window logic is correct. It also introduces flakiness around midnight UTC where token.issued_at.date() could differ from datetime.now().date() at the moment of comparison. This test does not exercise the boundary condition ('expiry window') the PR title describes, so a bug in the window calculation could ship undetected while this test still passes.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Test depends on wall clock; fails across the UTC midnight boundary

findings.title: No test covers the expired-coupon rejection path
findings.body:
apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses expires_at=tomorrow(), exercising only the non-expired branch. If the expiry comparison were inverted, always false, or the exception never raised, no test would fail.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ The new CouponExpired branch has no test

findings.title: expires_at of None or a naive datetime raises TypeError
findings.body:
`coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` assumes `expires_at` is always present and timezone-aware. Two reachable inputs break it:

- A coupon with no expiry (`expires_at is None`) raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'` instead of applying cleanly.
- An `expires_at` loaded as a naive datetime (common when reading a SQL `TIMESTAMP` without tzinfo) raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`.

Either surfaces as an opaque TypeError on a billing path rather than a discount being applied or a `CouponExpired`. Guard explicitly, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and _as_utc(coupon.expires_at) < datetime.now(timezone.utc)`, and normalise naive values at the boundary where coupons are loaded.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async def` but calls `requests.get`, a synchronous blocking call. Because it never awaits anything, the coroutine holds the event loop thread for the entire duration of the HTTP call \u2014 up to the 5 second timeout, and longer if DNS/connect stalls. Every other concurrent request handled by this loop is frozen for that period, so a slow `billing.internal` degrades the whole process rather than one request.

The module already imports `httpx` and the adjacent `fetch_plan` shows the intended pattern: take an `httpx.AsyncClient` and `await client.get(...)`. Either follow that (`async def fetch_plan_limits(client, tenant_id): r = await client.get(...)`) or, if the sync client must stay, drop `async` and run it via `anyio.to_thread.run_sync`/`loop.run_in_executor` from the caller.

Note also that declaring it `async` with no `await` means the function body runs entirely in the first `send()` \u2014 callers get none of the interleaving they would reasonably expect from an awaitable.

findings.title: No test covers fetch_plan_limits, including its blocking call
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but calls requests.get synchronously, which blocks the event loop — a real behavior bug. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so nothing would fail if the request errors, times out, returns malformed JSON, or blocks the loop under concurrent load. Add a test that runs this coroutine alongside other async work (or mocks requests.get) to catch the blocking-call regression and verify error handling.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing service URL
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with `f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}"`. `tenant_id` is not validated or percent-encoded before it becomes part of the path. If `tenant_id` originates from a request parameter (the PR description says this runs "during request handling"), a caller can supply values containing `/` or `../` and reach arbitrary paths on the internal billing host — e.g. `../../admin/keys` — which is a server-side request forgery against a service that is presumably not otherwise reachable from the outside. `requests`/urllib3 do not collapse dot segments, so the crafted path is sent as-is and the billing service resolves it.

Fix by constraining the value before it reaches the URL: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. UUID or `^[0-9]+$`), or at minimum pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. The same treatment should be applied to the pre-existing `fetch_plan` on line 6, which has the identical pattern.

findings.title: Bare `except:` swallows BaseException and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `MemoryError` raised while `_client.send` is running are converted into a silent `return None`. That makes the process unkillable via Ctrl-C during a push and can turn an intentional `sys.exit()` into a normal return. Narrow it to `except Exception:`.

Separately, the PR description says "catch and log, then continue", but the handler body is only `return None` — no logging call at all. Every push failure is now completely invisible: no metric, no traceback, no counter. Add `logger.exception(...)` (or the module's equivalent) inside the handler so failures remain diagnosable.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Bare except silently swallows all metrics push failures with no log

findings.title: No test covers the new exception-swallowing behavior in push_metrics
findings.body: push_metrics now catches all exceptions from _client.send and returns None instead of propagating them, per the PR's stated goal ('catch and log, then continue'). No test in this diff exercises the case where _client.send raises — nothing would fail if this bare except were removed, if it silently swallowed exceptions without logging (the diff shows no logging call despite the PR description promising one), or if it accidentally suppressed exceptions it shouldn't. Add a test that mocks _client.send to raise and asserts push_metrics returns None (or whatever the contract is) without propagating, and ideally asserts a log call was made.

findings.title: try_consume checks and updates the counter outside _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, decides against `LIMIT` on line 16, then yields to the event loop with `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18 before writing on line 19 \u2014 all without acquiring `_lock`. Two consequences on a reachable interleaving:

1. Limit bypass: N coroutines for the same tenant can each read the same `current`, each pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check, and each then write, so the effective total can reach `LIMIT + (N-1)*cost`. The `await` on line 18 guarantees a suspension point at exactly the wrong place, making this the common case rather than a rare one.
2. Lost update: line 19 assigns `current + cost` from the stale snapshot rather than re-reading. Any `consume()` (line 10) or `try_consume()` that committed while this coroutine was suspended is silently overwritten, so the counter under-reports usage permanently \u2014 the limiter then never fires.

Fix: wrap the whole read-check-write in `async with _lock:` (and do not await anything else inside it), or compute the new value from a fresh read taken under the lock:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ try_consume bypasses the lock: rate limit is defeatable by concurrency

findings.title: Insert failure is logged but WriteSettlement always returns nil
findings.body:
The error from `db.Exec` is scoped to the `if` statement on line 15 and is only logged. Lines 18–19 then declare a brand-new `var err error` (zero value `nil`) and return it, so `WriteSettlement` returns `nil` on every path after validation — including when the settlement row was never inserted. Any caller doing `if err := WriteSettlement(...); err != nil` will treat a failed insert as a success, so the end-of-day batch will mark settlements as recorded that do not exist in the database, and there is no retry or reconciliation signal.

If the intent is to propagate the failure, return it directly:
```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
    log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
    return err
}
return nil
```
If the intent really is log-and-continue per row, the swallowing should be explicit (return `nil` with a comment, or count failures) rather than laundered through a dead `var err error`, and the caller contract should say so — note that the sibling `WriteEntry` on lines 7–8 does propagate its `Exec` error, so callers are very likely expecting the same behaviour here.

findings.title: Rounding boundary silently changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5

findings.title: page_of_sorted returns one fewer record than page_of
findings.body:
The function `page_of_sorted` slices with `[start : start + PAGE_SIZE - 1]` while `page_of` uses `[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`. This means `page_of_sorted` returns `PAGE_SIZE - 1` records on most pages, violating the implicit contract that both functions return the same number of records per page. Callers expecting `PAGE_SIZE` records will receive one fewer, causing downstream logic (pagination counters, result set sizes, cursor calculations) to fail. Remove the `- 1` from line 12 to match `page_of`'s slice semantics.

findings.title: Dropped None guard makes header_lines crash when purchase_order is None

With it gone, `invoice.purchase_order.upper()` on line 4 raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` for every invoice without a PO — by the model's own docstring that is roughly nineteen accounts in twenty, i.e. the common path, not an edge case.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` is applied to `charge_card`, which calls `billing.gateway.charge`. The gateway's own docstring states "POST /charges. NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge" and that an Idempotency-Key header must be supplied to make retries safe. No such key is generated or passed here, so any failure that occurs after the gateway has already accepted the request (timeout, dropped response, 5xx after commit) will be retried and the customer will be charged two or three times. The read path (`fetch_charge` -> `get_charge`, documented "Safe to repeat") is fine; only the write path is affected.

Fix: generate a stable idempotency key per logical charge attempt (e.g. derived from the caller's order/payment id, not per-attempt) and pass it through `charge` so all retries of the same logical operation share it. Until the key is plumbed through, remove the retry decorator from `charge_card`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wrapper on non-idempotent charge() can double-charge customers

findings.title: Retry wrapper on non-idempotent call lacks safety documentation
findings.body: The `charge_card` function wraps the non-idempotent `charge` gateway call with automatic retries, but provides no docstring explaining the critical safety requirement. The wrapped function's docstring explicitly states: "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge" and requires an Idempotency-Key header for safe retries. A caller using `charge_card` would have no way to know they need to pass an Idempotency-Key, and might assume the retry wrapper makes it safe when it does not. Add a docstring documenting the idempotency requirement and how callers must satisfy it.

findings.title: Retry wrapping a non-idempotent charge call has no test guarding against duplicate charges

There is no test verifying that a transient failure followed by a retry does not produce multiple charges (e.g. a fake gateway that fails once then succeeds, asserting the underlying charge call happened only once or that an idempotency key was forwarded). Without such a test, a regression that silently double-charges customers on retry would not be caught.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`datetime.now()` on line 9 returns a naive local-time datetime. `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC, and subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`. This fires on every call, so `expires_within` can never return a value. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does; the `.replace(microsecond=0)` truncation is also unnecessary and biases the comparison by up to one second.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding", yet `contactEmail` accesses `.email` on it directly. findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body:
`fetch()` documents `timeout` as MILLISECONDS ("Callers wanting seconds must multiply") and passes it straight through as `timeout_ms`. The PR description says the timeout was "set generously since their API is slow", which indicates the intent was 30 seconds. As written the request gets a 30ms budget — shared across the default `retries=3` — so a slow partner API will fail on every nightly run, and the failure will look like a partner outage rather than a config mistake. Pass `timeout=30_000` (or define the value in seconds and multiply at the call site).

findings.title: Index duplicates existing invoices_tenant_created_idx from 0007
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_recent_idx` has exactly the same definition as `invoices_tenant_created_idx` created in migrations/0007_invoice_indexes.sql: same table, same column list, same sort direction. `IF NOT EXISTS` only matches on the index *name*, so it will not suppress creation — Postgres will happily build a second, functionally identical index. findings.title: Referer header is logged unscrubbed, leaking the auth token
findings.body:
The removed branch passed the `Referer` value through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before storing it in `headers`. The replacement copies `request.headers[header]` verbatim for every header including `Referer`, and line 6 serialises the whole dict into the log.

`token_authenticated_url` (jupyter_server/auth/identity.py) hands out notebook URLs of the form `{base}?token={token}`, so browsers send the full token back in the `Referer` header on every subresource request. Any 5xx therefore writes a live session token into the log, where it is readable by anyone with log access (operators, log shippers, error aggregators) and is replayable for full authenticated access.

Restore the scrub for `Referer` (and keep `extra_param_keys` threaded through), e.g. re-add the `if header == "Referer": value = _scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` step before assigning into `headers`. If the goal was to simplify, scrub unconditionally rather than dropping the call.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token leaked to logs via unscrubbed Referer header

findings.title: Removal of Referer scrubbing has no accompanying test change
findings.body: The diff deletes the call to `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` for the Referer header, meaning the raw Referer (which per `token_authenticated_url` can contain the auth token) is now logged unscrubbed on 5xx responses. No test file is included in this PR. If the surrounding test suite has a test asserting that logged Referer values are scrubbed, this change should fail it — but if such a test exists it isn't shown, and if it doesn't exist, this behavior change is going out with no test coverage catching the regression.

findings.title: `extra_param_keys` appears to become an unused parameter

After this change nothing in the shown body uses it, so the enclosing function keeps a parameter (and its callers keep passing a value) that has no effect — a silent no-op for anyone who configured extra keys to redact. If the scrub is intentionally dropped, the parameter and its call sites need removing too; more likely the scrub should be restored.

findings.title: xlink:href no longer scheme-checked, re-enabling SVG XSS
findings.body:
`validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the `unsafeLinkPrefix` schemes (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After this change `xlinkhref` falls through to whatever the default branch is, so a value like `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:...">` in user-submitted markdown is emitted into the DOM without any scheme check. `xlink:href` on `<a>`/`<use>` inside SVG is script-executable in browsers, making this a stored XSS in rendered content.

Restore `attribute === 'xlinkhref'` (and consider also handling the colon form `xlink:href`, plus `formaction`/`action`, if the normaliser can produce them) in the link-validation branch. If the goal is to shrink the allowlist, the safe direction is to drop the attribute entirely rather than to keep rendering it unvalidated.

No test in the diff exercises validateProp with attribute 'xlinkhref' before or after this change, so nothing would fail if this regressed the sanitiser's coverage of that vector.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID breaks buildPath's documented caller contract
findings.body:
`common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` was the only check applied to the caller-supplied `project` query parameter before it is used as a project identifier. The file DAO's `buildPath` explicitly documents the opposite contract: "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point." With the check gone, a value such as `../../etc` flows into `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)`, which cleans the `..` segments and resolves to a path outside `d.Folder` — the join does not scope anything, contrary to the PR description.

The remaining guard on line 4 only compares the query parameter against the path parameter; when `parameters.Project` is empty it performs no validation at all, and when both are supplied and equal it simply propagates the same unvalidated string. Restore the `ValidateID` call (or validate at the point the identifier is consumed) before removing it here.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removed ValidateID on project query param enables path traversal

findings.title: Removed validation contradicts buildPath contract
findings.body: The removed `ValidateID` call was the enforcement point for the documented requirement in buildPath's comment: 'callers are required to have validated the names before this point.' By removing this validation, the list() function no longer upholds that contract when passing projectQueryParameter to buildPath. Either the validation should be retained, or buildPath's documentation should be updated to reflect that validation may now be skipped if path-scoping is sufficient protection.

findings.title: No test covers removal of project-name validation path

findings.title: Buffer reserved from unvalidated client Content-Length
findings.body:
`Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory up front based on a value the client declares in the request, before a single byte of `body` has been read or verified. A request that advertises a huge Content-Length and then sends nothing (or is never completed) causes the server to reserve that much memory anyway; a handful of concurrent such requests exhausts the process. The previous code grew the RW a page at a time as bytes actually arrived, so the memory used was bounded by the bytes actually delivered.

Clamp the reservation to a sane ceiling before passing it in — e.g. `min(contentLength, maxPartSize)` using the S3 per-part limit — so the declared length can only ever reduce allocation churn, never drive it.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Buffer pre-reserved from attacker-controlled Content-Length (memory exhaustion)

findings.title: No test covers Reserve(contentLength) behaviour or its edge cases
findings.body: The change switches from lazy, page-at-a-time growth to eagerly reserving `contentLength` bytes via `multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)`. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that exercises this path with a large/attacker-controlled Content-Length, a Content-Length that mismatches the actual body size, or a zero/negative value. If Reserve mishandles any of these — e.g. allocating based on an untrusted declared length without a sanity bound — nothing in the test suite would fail, since no test touches this function at all.

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` downgraded to HTTP only when a caller explicitly set `is_secure = False`; every other case, including the overwhelmingly common one where `is_secure` is not present in `request.meta` at all (`.get()` returns `None`), produced `https`.

The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats `None` as falsy, so any request that does not explicitly opt in now goes out over plaintext `http://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com...`. That sends the AWS signature/authorization header and the object body over an unencrypted connection for all default-configured users, which is both a behaviour change and a credential-exposure risk.

If the ternary really should be simplified, keep the secure default, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` (unchanged) or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ S3 scheme selection logic inverted

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP after scheme refactor
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` was fail-secure: only an explicit `is_secure=False` opted into plaintext; a missing key (`.get` returns `None`) yielded `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` is truthiness-based, so the common case where `is_secure` was never set in `request.meta` now produces `http`, and the URL built on line 6 is fetched over an unencrypted channel.

S3 requests from this handler carry AWS authorization material (signature / session headers) and return bucket contents, so this silently exposes credentials-bearing requests and response bodies to any on-path network observer, and allows an active attacker to tamper with responses. Other falsy values (`0`, `""`) are likewise downgraded where they previously were not.

Restore the fail-secure default, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"` if the truthiness form is preferred.

findings.title: No test covers the default-scheme behavior change
findings.body: The old code defaulted to "https" unless is_secure was explicitly False. The new code defaults to "http" unless is_secure is truthy, meaning any request without is_secure set in meta (the common case) now silently downgrades to plaintext HTTP instead of HTTPS. There is no test in this diff exercising download_request with is_secure absent/None, so this default-scheme flip would pass unnoticed.

findings.title: DELETE now authorizes as "push", granting delete to push-only accounts
findings.body:
The old switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to the distinct action `"delete"`. The new two-branch form classifies anything that is not GET/HEAD as `"push"`, so a DELETE request produces `ResourceAction{Name: name, Action: "push"}` and is authorized against the caller's push grant.

Entry point: the HTTP method on the incoming request (fully attacker-chosen). Sink: `requestedAccess` on line 9, which is what the downstream policy check evaluates. An account provisioned with pull+push but deliberately not delete can now issue `DELETE /v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>` and have it pass authorization — destructive access granted to a principal that was denied it.

Restore the explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch (or an `if m == http.MethodDelete` before the push fallback) so the delete permission is still consulted.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ DELETE now authorises as "push", dropping the distinct delete action

findings.title: Action mapping no longer supports documented 'delete' action
findings.body: The code now maps all HTTP methods except GET/HEAD to 'push', eliminating the distinct 'delete' action that the repository's own documentation (pkg/api/config/config.go) explicitly states is intentional: 'The three actions are distinct on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones.' This change breaks the documented contract that callers may rely on to restrict delete permissions separately from push permissions.

findings.title: Unknown methods default to "push" instead of the previous "pull"
findings.body: The old `default:` arm assigned `"pull"` for any method outside the enumerated set (OPTIONS, TRACE, arbitrary verbs). The new condition treats every non-GET/HEAD method as a write, so those requests now demand push access and will be rejected for pull-only clients — e.g. CORS preflight OPTIONS requests against the registry. If the intent was only to simplify the mapping, keep the whitelist shape: assign `"push"` only for POST/PATCH/PUT, `"delete"` for DELETE, and `"pull"` otherwise.

findings.title: No test verifies DELETE now maps to 'push' instead of 'delete'
findings.body: The change removes the ActionDelete branch so http.MethodDelete now maps to 'push' rather than 'delete'. The repository's own documentation (pkg/api/config/config.go) states the three actions are intentionally distinct so that push and delete permissions can be granted separately. This is a significant behavior change (an account with push-but-not-delete rights would now be able to delete), yet no test in this diff exercises a DELETE request to confirm the resulting action/authorization behavior.

findings.title: Size guard clears the whole shared cache, evicting the fresh entry too
findings.body: When `_CACHE` exceeds 1000 entries, the entire dictionary is emptied — including the tenant just fetched and stored on line 10. Every existing entry that `get_tenant` (line 5) depends on is discarded at the same time, so one call to `get_tenant_fresh` turns into a cache stampede for all other callers, and the freshly fetched tenant is not actually retained despite being returned. If an eviction policy is wanted, drop a bounded subset (or use an LRU such as `functools.lru_cache`/`collections.OrderedDict.popitem(last=False)`) instead of `clear()`, and make sure the entry just written survives.

findings.title: A `None` result from `_fetch` is cached and indistinguishable from a miss
findings.body: `_fetch(tenant_id)` is stored unconditionally. If it can return `None` for an unknown or transiently unavailable tenant, that `None` is written into the shared cache, and `get_tenant` (line 5, `_CACHE.get`) then returns `None` for that tenant forever — a negative result is now indistinguishable from a cache miss and never re-fetched. Consider only caching truthy results, or using a sentinel so misses and known-absent tenants are distinguishable.

findings.title: Shared cache grows on caller-supplied keys and evicts by full clear
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` unconditionally stores `_fetch(tenant_id)` under the caller-supplied `tenant_id` in the module-level `_CACHE`, and the only eviction policy is `_CACHE.clear()` once the size passes 1000. Two consequences if `tenant_id` can be influenced by a request parameter:

1. Anyone able to drive lookups with distinct (including nonexistent) tenant IDs can push the cache past 1000 entries at will, wiping every other tenant's entry. Every subsequent `get_tenant` miss falls through to the backing store, so a cheap loop of ~1000 bogus IDs converts into a sustained load amplification / cache-stampede against whatever `_fetch` talks to.
2. Whatever `_fetch` returns for an unknown ID (likely `None`) is cached, so unresolvable IDs still consume a slot and count toward the clear threshold.

Suggested fixes: validate/authorise `tenant_id` before it is used as a cache key, skip caching when `_fetch` yields no tenant, and replace the flush-everything eviction with a bounded LRU (`functools.lru_cache` or `collections.OrderedDict.popitem(last=False)`) so one caller cannot evict all others.

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh has no test covering fetch/cache/eviction behaviour
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh introduces new behaviour: it always calls _fetch, writes the result into _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff. If _fetch were called with the wrong argument, if the cache write were skipped, or if the eviction threshold/logic were wrong (e.g. off-by-one, wrong clear condition), nothing would fail today.

findings.title: README documents renamed flag by old name
findings.body: The README still documents `--workers` as the flag name, but cli.py has renamed it to `--concurrency`. Users following the README will use the wrong flag name and the tool will not recognize it. Update line 7 to reference `--concurrency` instead.

findings.title: Flag rename changes argparse dest; existing callers of args.workers break
findings.body:
Renaming `--workers` to `--concurrency` also renames the argparse destination attribute from `args.workers` to `args.concurrency`. Any code that reads `args.workers` from this parser will now raise `AttributeError` at runtime, and any script, CI job, container entrypoint or docs snippet invoking `--workers` will fail with `error: unrecognized arguments`. The diff touches only the flag declaration — no consumer sites were updated in this change, and the README still advertises `--workers` on line 7.

If the goal is purely to align the user-facing name with the internal one, keep the attribute stable and/or keep the old spelling working:

    p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", type=int, default=4, dest="concurrency")

Otherwise, update every reader of `args.workers` in the same commit and call out the breaking change in the release notes.

findings.title: Flag rename from --workers to --concurrency has no test coverage
findings.body: The argparse flag name changed from --workers to --concurrency, which also changes the destination attribute name (args.workers -> args.concurrency). Any code elsewhere that reads args.workers would silently break (AttributeError or None), and nothing in this diff demonstrates a test exercising parser() and asserting the new attribute name. Since no test file for cli.py is shown or referenced, this rename's correctness is unverified.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts changed return type
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", but the implementation now returns a dictionary with per-day counts. A caller reading the docstring would expect an integer and receive a dict instead, causing their code to fail. Update the docstring to document the new return type and structure.

findings.title: monthly_usage return type changed from int to dict silently
findings.body:
`monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer; it now returns a `{day: count}` mapping. Any existing caller doing arithmetic, comparison, or formatting on the result (e.g. `monthly_usage(a) > limit`, `f"{monthly_usage(a)} calls"`) will now silently produce wrong output or raise a `TypeError`. The docstring on line 2 still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", so nothing in the code signals the break to callers.

Either keep a total-returning function and add a new `monthly_usage_by_day` alongside it, or rename this one and update every call site; in both cases update the docstring.

findings.title: No test covers the new per-day breakdown return shape
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict keyed by day instead of a single integer total, but no test in this diff verifies the new structure (keys, values, aggregation correctness) or that callers of this function were updated to handle a dict instead of an int. If the query or dict construction is wrong (e.g., wrong key names, day format mismatch, or count field name), nothing would catch it.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` is a public-looking function whose second parameter was renamed from `page_size` to `limit`. Any existing call site using the keyword form, e.g. `list_invoices(tid, page_size=100)`, now raises `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`. Positional callers are unaffected, so this will fail only on the keyword paths and may not show up until runtime. Either grep for and update every caller in the same change, or keep backward compatibility (accept `page_size=None` and map it to `limit` with a deprecation warning) before removing the old name.

findings.title: Docstring still documents the removed page_size parameter
findings.body:
The Args block still names `page_size`, which no longer exists in the signature. Update it to `limit` so the documented contract matches the code. Note also that the PR description says the rename is `page` \u2192 `offset`, but the code renames `page_size` \u2192 `limit` \u2014 worth confirming which rename was actually intended before this lands.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Docstring parameter name does not match signature

findings.title: No test exercises list_invoices after parameter rename
findings.body: The parameter was renamed from page_size to limit and the call to _query updated accordingly, but no test in this diff calls list_invoices to verify the positional argument still reaches _query correctly (e.g. with a non-default limit value). A regression that swapped argument order or broke the default would not be caught.

findings.title: verify/cert silently dropped — TLS verification no longer applied
findings.body:
The new `request()` signature still accepts `verify=None` and `cert=None` (lines 148-149), but the body never reads them: it populates the `Request` with method/url/headers/files/data/params/auth/cookies/redirects/proxies and then calls `self.send(prep)` (line 167). `send()` (lines 363-367) constructs a bare `HTTPAdapter()` and calls `adapter.send(request)` with no verify/cert argument either. Callers who pass `verify=True` (or rely on a session-level `verify`/`cert` config) get a connection whose certificate validation state is whatever the adapter defaults to, with no error and no warning — a silent downgrade that enables an on-path attacker to MITM HTTPS traffic, and that also breaks mutual-TLS client auth.

Thread `verify` and `cert` (merged with session/config defaults) through to `adapter.send(request, verify=..., cert=...)`, or raise `NotImplementedError` on this code path until it is wired up, rather than accepting the parameters and ignoring them.

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is not a package-relative import
findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this module is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will only resolve if a top-level module named `adapters` happens to be importable; under Python 3 (and Python 2 with `absolute_import`) importing `requests.sessions` will raise `ImportError`, i.e. the whole package fails to import. Change to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: New `request()` silently ignores timeout, verify, cert, prefetch, return_response, config
findings.body: The signature still accepts `timeout`, `return_response`, `config`, `prefetch`, `verify` and `cert`, but the body never reads them — they are accepted and discarded. Existing callers (including `get`/`post`/... which forward `**kwargs`) will believe they set a timeout or disabled/enabled TLS verification when in fact nothing is applied: requests can hang indefinitely and `verify`/`cert` are silently dropped, which is a security-relevant default change. Either thread these through to `req`/`self.send(...)` or remove them from the signature so callers fail loudly.

findings.title: `_send_request` deleted but `old_request` still calls it
findings.body: `_send_request` was removed in this diff, yet the retained `old_request` path still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call into `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep the helper until `old_request` is deleted, or delete `old_request` in the same change. Note also that `_send_request` was the only place `prefetch` was honoured.

findings.title: Connection pooling is disabled: new HTTPAdapter per send, close() is a no-op
findings.body: `send()` instantiates a fresh `HTTPAdapter()` on every call, so each request gets its own PoolManager and no socket is ever reused — the pooling behaviour previously configured from `pool_connections`/`pool_maxsize` is gone, and those config keys are now dead. Compounding this, `close()` was reduced to `pass`, so the sockets each per-request adapter opens are never explicitly released; `with Session() as s:` no longer frees anything. Hold a single adapter (or a mount map) on the Session in `__init__` and have `close()` clear it.

findings.title: Session.send() now delegates to HTTPAdapter with no test covering the new path
findings.body: Session.send previously called request.send() directly; it now constructs an HTTPAdapter and calls adapter.send(request). This is a core behavioural change to how every request is actually sent, but no test in this diff exercises it. If HTTPAdapter.send() has a different signature, return value, or error handling than the old request.send(), nothing here would fail.

findings.title: close() silently became a no-op with no test to catch the regression
